sources.title: How Ilias Ism buys backlinks: pay for top-ranking pages, bottom-funnel targets, short outreach and creator videos
sources.originalTitle: The Backlinks Worth Paying $2,000 For (w/ Ilias ISM)
sources.summary: Ilias Ism explains his developer-style approach to link building: email top-ranking pages and listicles, pay up to $1,000-$2,000 for links on pages ranking for bottom-of-funnel keywords, and mine competitor backlink data at scale. He also covers building real brand authority and hiring cheap retainer-based UGC creators.

principles.text: Pay heavily for links on pages already ranking top 10-20 for your keywords; they send referral traffic and AI citations.
principles.quote: Anything that is ranking in the top 10 or top 20 for keywords, I would just drop like infinite money on that. Like no limit up to like $1,000 or $2,000.

principles.text: Target bottom-of-funnel keywords, because AI fan-out searches end there and that's where products get picked.
principles.quote: So, just those bottom of the funnel keywords are the best ones.

principles.text: Keep link outreach short and direct; long vague emails get ignored even when the deal is good.
principles.quote: Often often like a direct request that is fairly short will get a good result.

principles.text: Find what drives referral traffic to competitors' backlinks, then write that topic yourself on other sites linking back.
principles.quote: I should look at the site that is giving Ahrefs this page traffic and look at that site and copy that page that gives them traffic

principles.text: Build deep, high-value authority content and a real brand rather than chasing shortcuts.
principles.quote: So you really have to be that deep authority content, super high value, super high quality.

principles.text: Hire UGC creators on a small monthly retainer with view bonuses; they self-test your funnel and post daily.
principles.quote: just pay people like 500 per month. They're going to put in all their effort.

sources.title: AI SEO and link building: tracking AI mentions and winning hard-to-get backlinks
sources.originalTitle: AI SEO and linkbuilding with Ilias Ism and Jesper Nissen - [SEO in 2026]
sources.summary: Ilias Ism explains how he learned SEO through a feedback loop on Google Search Console, why scarce links (your own sites, high-difficulty guest mentions) beat commodity ones, and how he gets mentioned in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. He shows his tracker workflow: monitor prompts, find the cited sources, email those authors with a specific value offer.

principles.text: Learn SEO by running a feedback loop: change something, check Search Console after a few days, keep what moves rankings.
principles.quote: you have like this funnel where you try things and you see has it been working? Did it actually have any impact? Am I ranking higher?

principles.text: Links that everyone can get only raise the baseline. Win with links nobody else can get, like your own network of real sites.
principles.quote: the only way to stand out is get the links that nobody else has.

principles.text: AI search cites sources everywhere (YouTube, Reddit, Medium, G2, blogs), so build awareness across platforms, not just on your site.
principles.quote: everything is kind of combining in like this overall uh awareness graph right and that will boost you more so than everything else because you just also appear everywhere

principles.text: To get into AI answers, find the pages the AI cites, then email those authors to be added to their lists.
principles.quote: look at all the sources that are feeding these results here in the bottom

principles.text: Low domain rating sites still get cited by AI search, unlike Google money keywords which need strong domains. Even small-site links help.
principles.quote: you don't need a super duper high domain authority or domain rating in in order to appear in AI search.

principles.text: Outreach works when it proves you read their article and offers real value (guest post, data, case study), not a bare backlink request.
principles.quote: it shows immediately that someone read the article, understood what they wrote about and so on.

sources.title: Ilias Ism: step-by-step SEO audit and content playbook from a live site teardown
sources.originalTitle: Step-by-Step SEO Guide from $20k/mo SEO agency founder | Ilias Ism
sources.outlet: Do It In Public | Startups & Marketing
sources.summary: Ilias Ism runs a live SEO audit of a founder's product site and explains how he grows on Twitter with "drop your site, get one tip" templates. He covers technical SEO basics, unique titles, redirects, domain authority, attacking one competitor keyword at a time with listicles, and distributing content so it actually ranks.

principles.text: Run a "drop your site, get one tip" template on Twitter and pair it with an auto-DM; it generates leads and helps people.
principles.quote: I combine it with like an autod DM of typ f or tweet Hunter and so you send like some links to people

principles.text: Keep each free favor under five minutes per person, or the volume buries you for weeks.
principles.quote: try to make it like under five minutes per person otherwise it it will really take you like a few days sleeping to go through there

principles.text: Entrepreneurship is pattern recognition: collect references, borrow the best parts, and apply proven templates.
principles.quote: entrepreneurship is is really about like seeing patterns and being able to understand them and and and use them right

principles.text: Build a swipe file of top-performing headlines, SEO titles and tweets, then use it to generate new ones.
principles.quote: I collected like 200 SEO titles and headlines that really work every time so I run them through jtp GPT

principles.text: Pick a target keyword first, then work out how to get into the ranking list, instead of deciding what to write first.
principles.quote: you don't have to you don't think like what is the content that I should write it's like which keyword should I focus on

principles.text: Writing the article is not enough; distribute it via newsletter, Pinterest, tweets and backlink outreach.
principles.quote: it's not enough to write an article right so it will give you nothing so it's important to like focus on this like distribution

sources.title: Ilias Ism on going from startup exit to indie hacking: productize services, systemize, sell SEO
sources.originalTitle: Ilias Ism — from startup exit to full-time indie-hacking. Do it in public Ep. 22
sources.outlet: Do It In Public | Startups & Marketing
sources.summary: Ilias recounts his path from teenage Chrome extensions and freelancing to co-founding Officient, an HR SaaS that reached 30 employees and about 20,000 customers. He explains why co-founders and written processes matter, then how to productize an SEO agency offer and win first clients with personalized outreach.

principles.text: Build only what customers already need; Officient sold the idea before writing code and built straight to customer needs.
principles.quote: we built it immediately and directly to like the the things that customers needed right so we didn't have like a long development cycle

principles.text: Co-founders let a company keep growing while you are away; solo founders must push everything themselves.
principles.quote: you realize the company still grew like 4% without you without doing anything and things moved on

principles.text: Most big companies were started by multiple people, so find a co-founder to spread responsibilities.
principles.quote: those companies have been actually co-founded by multiple people and you don't really uh notice it right

principles.text: Productize a service with a strict, clear offer: defined deliverables, price and next steps so clients know what they get.
principles.quote: you need to have like a very strict uh and clear structure in place of what you offer and um for what price

principles.text: Technical skill is a big edge in marketing and SEO because funnels, pixels and tracking are technical.
principles.quote: if you can do like technical marketing quite well you have a big Advantage because there's a lot of like even like Facebook pixels or other pixels that you need to set up

principles.text: Personalize cold emails with a screenshot of their site and their keywords instead of a generic pitch.
principles.quote: if you attach a screenshot and some very specific stuff it will help a lot

sources.title: Blitz SEO: how Ilias Ism pushed one page from #11 to #3 in 30 days
sources.originalTitle: Blitz SEO: the 30-day sprint to rank one page
sources.summary: Ilias argues most SEO fails from dilution, not quality. His Blitz SEO method puts all effort on one money keyword and one page for 30 days, with a daily ritual of internal links, backlinks, on-page tweaks, resubmission and logging. He reports page one by day 17 and position #3 by day 30.

principles.text: SEO usually fails because it is spread too thin, not because it is bad. Concentrate on one goal.
principles.quote: most SEO fails not because it is bad, but because it is spread too thin.

principles.text: Pick a money keyword: high intent, high volume, tied to the core offering, and something that hurts to lose.
principles.quote: Not a blog post keyword. Not a long-tail. A money keyword.

principles.text: Concentrate on one optimized landing page and make it the hero of your domain.
principles.quote: We rewrote and optimized a single landing page to own that keyword.

principles.text: Run a daily ritual for 30 days: internal links, new backlinks, one on-page tweak from competitor SERP analysis, resubmit, share, log.
principles.quote: Made one on-page tweak (based on competitor SERP analysis)

principles.text: Iterate fast instead of overthinking; speed and pressure beat content volume.
principles.quote: We did not overthink. We iterated fast.

principles.text: A business needs only about three top-3 keywords or pages for recurring revenue, not hundreds of pages ranking past position 10.
principles.quote: You just need 3 keywords or pages to rank in the top 3 to make a business.

sources.title: SEO vs paid ads: how $500 of content beat $1,000 of ads by 50x at GenPPT
sources.originalTitle: SEO vs Paid Ads: We Spent $1,500 Testing Both (Case Study)
sources.summary: Ilias Ism split $1,500 across Google Ads, Meta Ads and SEO content for GenPPT and tracked it for 12 months. Ads produced a handful of conversions and stopped the day spend stopped. $500 of content compounded into 100,000+ visitors, with one post driving most of the traffic.

principles.text: Paid traffic is rented attention: it vanishes the moment you stop paying, while content keeps producing.
principles.quote: The moment you stop paying, traffic stops. You're renting attention.

principles.text: SEO compounds over time; content published once keeps generating traffic long after the spend.
principles.quote: The $500 we spent on content in early 2025 is still generating traffic today. The $1,000 we spent on ads? Gone the day we stopped.

principles.text: Content results are power-law: one well-chosen, shareable post can drive most of your traffic.
principles.quote: one single blog post drove 70% of our traffic.

principles.text: Content earns backlinks that lift every page on the site, which ads can never buy.
principles.quote: Content doesn't just bring direct traffic. It attracts backlinks—which boost ALL your pages.

principles.text: Content plus distribution wins: promote on social, directories and listicles instead of only publishing.
principles.quote: Content + distribution = unstoppable. Our X/Twitter posts drove 20,000+ visitors. Directories and listicles drove thousands more. Don't just publish—promote.

principles.text: Use paid ads tactically (launches, demand validation, retargeting), not as the primary SaaS growth channel.
principles.quote: But as a primary growth channel? For most SaaS companies, SEO wins long-term.

sources.title: How Ilias Ism reduces SaaS churn: segment it, fix the product, shorten time to value
sources.originalTitle: How to reduce SaaS churn without lying to yourself
sources.summary: Ilias argues churn is a product-quality signal, not a funnel problem. He says to split churn into types, measure it honestly, get users to one real result fast, build honest cancellation flows, and price to attract customers with a real job to do.

principles.text: Churn isn't one number. Segment it by type (voluntary, involuntary, bad-fit, activation, value) before choosing a fix.
principles.quote: Most founders mix these together, then build the wrong fix.

principles.text: Fix the product before the funnel; churn mostly drops from fewer bugs, clearer setup and removing reasons users feel betrayed.
principles.quote: People churn when the value they get is lower than the cost they feel.

principles.text: Onboarding should get the user to one real outcome with as few choices as possible, not tour every feature.
principles.quote: Onboarding is not a museum tour. Nobody needs to see every room.

principles.text: Measure churn correctly. Don't mix trials, failed payments and serious customers; track logo, revenue, cohort and plan-level churn.
principles.quote: Do not mix free trials, failed payments, one-off users, and serious customers into the same emotional spreadsheet.

principles.text: Price like a bouncer: the wrong low price attracts browsers who churn; sometimes the fix is removing the plan that invites the wrong customer.
principles.quote: Sometimes the churn fix is not a discount. It is removing the plan that invites the wrong customer.

principles.text: Send value recaps showing what the customer achieved instead of 'we miss you' emails, so they remember the value before renewal.
principles.quote: If your product creates value quietly in the background, surface it. Otherwise the customer only feels the invoice.

sources.title: How Ilias Ism got a 107% trial lift by making Google Sign-In prominent (A/B test)
sources.originalTitle: Sign in with Google: 107% Conversion Lift (A/B Test)
sources.summary: Ilias Ism shares a live A/B test on GenPPT where a prominent Google Sign-In button in the hero plus a scroll-triggered sticky modal lifted trial starts from 7.48% to 15.5%. He backs it with six other case studies and a playbook for placement, fallbacks, measurement and controlled rollout.

principles.text: Making Google Sign-In prominent can double trial conversion by removing form friction.
principles.quote: prominently adding Google Sign-In more than doubled our trial conversion rate.

principles.text: Put the Google button in both navbar and hero, and add a scroll-triggered modal, for maximum visibility.
principles.quote: Show the Google button in both nav and hero for max visibility.

principles.text: Always keep email and other login alternatives visible; hiding them can reduce total conversions.
principles.quote: Keep an email fallback—hiding it can hurt conversions if Google is blocked.

principles.text: Measure completed, verified sign-ups per unique visitor, then check activation and retention, since social login may not lift long-term usage.
principles.quote: Social logins often boost sign-ups, but not always long-term usage.

principles.text: Validate with a controlled 2-week A/B test; use sequential or Bayesian testing if traffic is low.
principles.quote: Run a 2-week A/B test: 50% see the new, prominent Google CTA; 50% see the old flow

principles.text: Track every funnel step and respect One Tap cooldowns so you don't over-prompt.
principles.quote: Track each step: page view → button click → credential issued → onboarding.

sources.title: Sticky SaaS: how to keep $5-$50/month products low-churn
sources.originalTitle: Sticky SaaS: Low-Cost Wins & Low Churn in the $5-$50 Arena
sources.summary: Ilias Ism lays out a blueprint for low-ARPA SaaS retention: show value fast, price for commitment with annual plans and clear tiers, embed the product in workflows through integrations and automation, catch churn early, and bill ethically. It includes churn benchmarks by price tier and a testing roadmap.

principles.text: Stickiness means the product is so embedded, or delivers such steady background value, that canceling feels like a downgrade.
principles.quote: a product so deeply embedded in a user's workflow or providing such consistent background value that canceling feels like a downgrade.

principles.text: Sticky users are less price-sensitive, so small price hikes barely hurt churn if the product is indispensable.
principles.quote: high stickiness can be a leading indicator of price insensitivity.

principles.text: Pricing too low can signal poor quality, so price competitively but not so low that it devalues the product.
principles.quote: a price that is "too cheap" can be as detrimental as one that is "too expensive" if it inadvertently signals low quality or unreliability.

principles.text: Push annual plans with discounts and extras; sunk cost makes annual users extract more value and churn less.
principles.quote: The "sunk cost" psychology means users with annual plans are more motivated to extract value.

principles.text: For SEO, content and analytics tools, stickiness comes from indispensable outputs and automated processes, not only daily logins.
principles.quote: For SEO/Content/Analytics, stickiness is often about indispensable outputs (e.g., a thorough monthly SEO audit) or automated processes, not just daily logins.

principles.text: Low-ARPA SaaS cannot afford manual follow-up on failed payments, so automate dunning.
principles.quote: For low-ARPA SaaS, automated dunning is a necessity, not a luxury, as manual follow-up is too costly.

sources.title: Blitz Copy: the dopamine copywriting system for high-converting headlines
sources.originalTitle: Blitz Copy: The Dopamine Copywriting System
sources.summary: Ilias Ism lays out Blitz Copy, a copywriting framework built on the claim that emotion, not explanation, sells. It uses an identity trigger, emotional hook, mini cliffhanger and specific outcome, backed by a list of psychological triggers and deep audience empathy, with before/after rewrites of his own products' headlines.

principles.text: People buy what excites them, not what they understand; copy should provoke rather than explain.
principles.quote: People don't buy what they understand. They buy what excites them.

principles.text: Open with an identity trigger so the reader feels instantly recognized and thinks 'that's me'.
principles.quote: Make them think: "Wait, this person knows exactly what I'm feeling. They get me."

principles.text: Sequence the copy: identity trigger, emotional hook, mini cliffhanger, then a specific desirable outcome as the payoff.
principles.quote: Promise a concrete, desirable result. (The Payoff)

principles.text: Know your audience cold: reflect their real pains and desires in their own words, not generic hype.
principles.quote: To write copy that truly grabs attention, you need to reflect your audience's real pains and desires, using their own words and worldview.

principles.text: Pull specific emotional levers (curiosity, FOMO, surprise, relief, urgency, belonging, advantage) to move people from maybe to now.
principles.quote: These are the neurochemical triggers that move people from "maybe" to "I need this now"

principles.text: Replace feature-description headlines with pain-first, specific ones, e.g. naming the cost of the status quo.
principles.quote: Still Paying $5K/Month for Shady Backlinks?

sources.title: AutoDS CRO teardown: conversion tactics from a $1B dropshipping platform's funnel
sources.originalTitle: AutoDS CRO Teardown: 57 Screenshots + $1B Conversion Secrets
sources.summary: Ilias Ism breaks down 57 screenshots of AutoDS's funnel (homepage, pricing, blog, mobile) and distills the conversion tactics: specific timeframes, dual CTAs, third-party proof, value stacking, platform-based pricing, and content built to convert. The core lesson is that every page serves one role in a single journey toward paid customers.

principles.text: Use specific timeframes instead of vague speed claims; they feel believable and create commitment.
principles.quote: AutoDS doesn't say "quickly" or "fast"—they say **"2 minutes"**. This specificity serves multiple psychological purposes

principles.text: Run two CTAs aimed at different user mindsets: an action-oriented one and a process-oriented one.
principles.quote: Create 2 CTAs serving different psychological states

principles.text: Prefer third-party validation (app store and review-site ratings) over self-promotion.
principles.quote: Third-party validation over self-promotion

principles.text: Stack and quantify every trial benefit in dollars so a tiny price feels like a steal.
principles.quote: Quantify and stack every trial benefit with dollar values

principles.text: Adjust pricing by platform, billing frequency and segment rather than showing one price to everyone.
principles.quote: Adjust pricing based on traffic source or user segment

principles.text: Make AI feel controllable and tangible, with user control and concrete benefits.
principles.quote: Give users control over automated features

sources.title: How Ilias Ism runs minimal 1-file AI evals across 5 production products
sources.originalTitle: How I Run Minimal AI Evals Across 5 Products
sources.summary: Ilias skips eval SaaS and uses one co-located eval.ts plus eval.md per feature that imports production code and runs real models. He warns that model self-scoring rewards quantity over quality, and uses evals to cut costs, such as an 80% image margin. He also covers hillclimbing without overfitting.

principles.text: Skip heavy eval platforms; one eval.ts per feature plus a co-located eval.md is enough.
principles.quote: Skip heavy SaaS platforms: A single `eval.ts` file per feature co-located with `eval.md` is all you need.

principles.text: Never let models score their own output; self-scoring rewards quantity and confidence, not correctness.
principles.quote: Self-scoring rewards **quantity and confidence, not correctness**. A model that emits 7 loosely-relevant items looks like it beats a model that emits 4 precise ones, when the opposite is true.

principles.text: Summary tables hold only machine metrics; judge quality by reading raw outputs side by side.
principles.quote: Summary tables are for machine metrics only: Latency (ms), input/output tokens, total cost ($), and execution status (schema pass/fail).

principles.text: Always import production prompts and schemas into the eval instead of copying them, to prevent drift.
principles.quote: NEVER copy-paste prompts into `eval.ts`. If you duplicate prompts in your eval, production logic evolves while your benchmark tests obsolete behavior.

principles.text: Use evals to swap to cheaper models and raise margins; benchmark candidates on real production inputs.
principles.quote: That single benchmark unlocked an **80% profit margin** on standard credit packs. Without an eval, you either burn margin on overkill models or ship an untested cheaper model that ruins style transfer.

principles.text: Hillclimb carefully: split train/test, change one thing per round, and revert anything that lifts train but not test.
principles.quote: Keep it only if train and test both improve. Train up with test flat is overfitting, so revert it.

sources.title: Outputmaxxing: why AI tools should ship outputs, not reports
sources.originalTitle: Outputmaxxing: Your AI Tool Should Ship Outputs, Not Reports
sources.summary: Ilias Ism compares three of his own products and finds the tool that produces a finished artifact (GenPPT, ~$10k/mo) earns roughly 100x the pure detection tool (AI SEO Tracker, ~$200/mo). His principle, "outputmaxxing": AI made knowing free, so build tools that end with something that didn't exist before, and loop detection into production into verification.

principles.text: People don't pay to know; they pay for the thing to exist. Detection tools earn far less than tools that produce outputs.
principles.quote: People do not pay to know. They pay for the thing to exist.

principles.text: Test every product with one question: after someone uses it, what exists that didn't exist before? A decision or awareness is just a feature an agent will eat.
principles.quote: After someone uses your tool, what exists that didn't exist before?

principles.text: AI made detection and audits a commodity; the scarce, valuable bottleneck has moved from knowing to shipping.
principles.quote: The bottleneck moved from knowing to shipping, and almost every tool in my industry is still selling knowing.

principles.text: Turn every report row into an action: attach the contact, draft the personalized pitch or comment, and let the user fire it with one click.
principles.quote: The old version of this page is a report. You read it, nod, and the work still has not started.

principles.text: Close the loop across products so detection feeds production and production feeds verification.
principles.quote: Detection feeds production. Production feeds verification.

principles.text: Third-party placements can be your best-converting channel, and you can be blind to them if you only track assets you own.
principles.quote: I never saw it happen, because the page was never mine.

sources.title: How I generate Chrome extension store assets with AI: a three-phase skill
sources.originalTitle: How I Generate Chrome Extension Store Assets with AI
sources.summary: Ilias Ism turns the workflow he used for Peel UI into an open-source Cursor skill that generates a Chrome extension's icon, brand guide, promo tiles, benefit slides and listing copy. The core lessons: explore many icon concepts first, derive a brand guide from the winner, and use full-bleed promotional slides rather than popup screenshots.

principles.text: Explore several unrelated icon concepts before committing; never lock into the first mediocre direction.
principles.quote: Run phase 1. "Just make the icon" locks you into the first mediocre direction.

principles.text: Derive a brand guide from the winning icon so every later asset stays on palette.
principles.quote: After you pick an icon, generate a 16:9 brand guide: hex palette, typography direction, button mocks, 24px toolbar glyph, voice tags. Every store slide references this file.

principles.text: Store screenshots should be promotional benefit slides that explain the job, not zoomed popup screenshots.
principles.quote: Show what the extension _does_, not what the popup looks like zoomed to 90%.

principles.text: Fill the whole frame with multi-column layouts and concrete sample data instead of a small centered icon on empty background.
principles.quote: Multi-column layouts with sample data beat centered icon rows on empty background.

principles.text: One idea per slide; cramming hero, picker and export into one image reads cramped.
principles.quote: One slide, one idea. Hero + picker + export in one 1280×800 image reads cramped.

principles.text: Package repeatable workflows as open-source skills with a per-product config file, replacing per-product design work.
principles.quote: I wrote a three-phase workflow, packaged it as a Cursor skill, and stopped opening Figma for every extension.

sources.title: Backlink outreach: how MagicSpace SEO lands 15+ links a month with personalized email and follow-ups
sources.originalTitle: Backlink Outreach: How I Get 15+ New Links a Month
sources.summary: Ilias Ism lays out the repeatable backlink outreach process his agency MagicSpace SEO uses: pick keywords and competitors, find prospects, send short personalized emails, follow up 2-3 times, and track results. A Xnapper case study (100 emails, 10 links) shows what the numbers look like when outreach is personalized and incentivized.

principles.text: Manual outreach is one of the most effective link building methods because it targets relevant sites and wins contextual editorial links.
principles.quote: While there are many link building strategies out there, **manual outreach** remains one of the most effective.

principles.text: Start from competitors: pick target keywords, find the top 10 competitors per keyword, and mine their backlinks for prospects.
principles.quote: The first step is understanding what your competitors are doing and where they are getting links from.

principles.text: Write outreach emails that personalize, offer value, stay concise, and end with a clear CTA.
principles.quote: **Personalize**: Always use the recipient's name and reference something specific about their site.

principles.text: Never stop at one email: send 2-3 follow-ups spaced 5-7 days apart, each with a different angle, ending with a break-up email.
principles.quote: We typically send 2-3 follow-up emails spaced 5-7 days apart. Each follow-up takes a slightly different angle:

principles.text: Give prospects a concrete incentive, like a free pro license, to turn outreach into reviews and links.
principles.quote: **Offering a free pro license** was an effective incentive for reviews

principles.text: Track open rate, reply rate, links acquired and time to conversion, then refine templates and tactics from what performs best.
principles.quote: This data helps us continually refine our approach, identifying our best-performing email templates and outreach tactics.

sources.title: SEO strategy for SaaS startups: keywords, content, links, technical, and case studies
sources.originalTitle: SEO Strategy: How to grow Startups in 2026
sources.summary: Ilias Ism lays out a SaaS SEO playbook: know your audience and set 3-5 KPIs, research keywords by intent, publish content for each funnel stage, earn quality backlinks, fix technical SEO, promote, then measure and iterate. He backs it with Zapier, Ahrefs and Intercom examples.

principles.text: SEO compounds: it's a cheap, long-term channel that can become your top signup source within 6-12 months.
principles.quote: The results of SEO compound over time as you build authority and rankings. Within 6-12 months, SEO can become your top channel for new signups.

principles.text: Start from the customer: personas, journey and funnel stage decide which keywords and content you make.
principles.quote: Every effective SEO strategy starts with a deep understanding of your target customers.

principles.text: Pick only 3-5 core metrics, set aggressive but realistic targets, and get stakeholder buy-in.
principles.quote: Choose 3-5 core metrics to focus on and establish aggressive but realistic targets.

principles.text: Mix head keywords with long-tail ones tied to use cases and pain points, and tag every keyword by intent and funnel stage.
principles.quote: In addition to "head" keywords that define your product category, go after long-tail keywords that align with specific use cases, features, and customer pain points.

principles.text: For backlinks, a few relevant, high-quality links beat dozens of low-quality ones. Original data earns links naturally.
principles.quote: A few high-value links will do more for your SEO than dozens of low-quality ones.

principles.text: Publishing isn't enough. Promote content, then track results, reinvest revenue and scale what works.
principles.quote: Creating optimized content is only half the battle.

sources.title: Parasite SEO attack on .gov and .edu sites: how hijacked authority domains rank spam instantly
sources.originalTitle: Massive Parasite SEO Attack Hits .gov & .edu Sites
sources.summary: Ilias Ism documents a wave of parasite SEO attacks on high-authority .gov and .edu domains (Duke, Michigan.gov, ca.gov, Wayne State), where spam PDFs rank #1 almost instantly for lucrative keywords. He explains why domain authority bias makes this work and gives site owners concrete steps to detect and prevent compromise.

principles.text: Google weights domain authority so heavily that spam on a trusted domain inherits instant ranking power.
principles.quote: Google heavily weights domain authority. When spam appears on michigan.gov (DR 91) or duke.edu (DR 94), it inherits instant trust and ranking power.

principles.text: High-DR domains let content rank #1 in days for terms that would take years to win on a normal site.
principles.quote: This is why attackers target .gov and .edu domains—they get instant #1 rankings that would take years to achieve elsewhere.

principles.text: Authority is also a liability: a high-trust domain is a high-value target, so security is part of brand protection.
principles.quote: While it provides immense trust and ranking power, it also makes your domain a high-value target for attackers. Securing your web applications is no longer just a technical issue, it's a critical component of brand protection.

principles.text: Parasite SEO content is built to look legitimate and funnel traffic to monetized offers, not just stuff keywords.
principles.quote: The content on these pages is not just gibberish; it's often well-structured spam designed to look like a legitimate article, complete with calls-to-action, to funnel traffic to illicit sites.

principles.text: Monitor Google Search Console for unrecognized indexed URLs; a sudden spike in indexed pages is a red flag.
principles.quote: Regularly check the "Pages" report in GSC for any URLs that you don't recognize. A sudden spike in indexed pages is a major red flag.

principles.text: Most compromises come from outdated CMS, vulnerable plugins or misconfigured upload forms, so audit those first.
principles.quote: The most common attack vectors are outdated CMS versions, vulnerable plugins, or misconfigured file upload forms.

sources.title: How to use AI to write blog posts without hurting your SEO: a 7-step workflow
sources.originalTitle: How to use AI to write blog posts without hurting your SEO
sources.summary: Google penalizes bad content, not AI content. Ilias lays out a repeatable workflow: pick a query with real intent, outline by hand, draft section by section with AI, then inject experience, optimize on-page, fact-check and iterate. A full post fits in about 90 minutes.

principles.text: Google doesn't penalize AI content; it penalizes bad content. Experience, intent match and usefulness decide rankings, not the drafting tool.
principles.quote: Google does not penalize "AI content." It penalizes **bad content**. If your post demonstrates experience, satisfies intent, and is useful, it can rank, regardless of the tool you used to draft it.

principles.text: Pick topics where a strong post can win: use Search Console positions 3-20, validate the SERP, and decide your unique angle.
principles.quote: Skip vague ideas. Pick a query where a strong post can actually win.

principles.text: Always write the outline by hand around search intent before letting AI draft anything.
principles.quote: Drafting starts with a human outline. Keep the structure laser-focused on intent:

principles.text: Draft with AI section by section using short, specific prompts scoped to your outline, with capped length and no clichés.
principles.quote: Work section-by-section. Keep prompts specific, short, and scoped to your outline.

principles.text: Rankings are won by adding what AI can't fake: your own screenshots, results, failures, primary sources, author bio and internal links.
principles.quote: This is where rankings are won.

principles.text: Treat AI drafts as starting points: verify every stat, strip generic filler, read aloud, cut 10-20%, then publish and iterate with one improvement a day.
principles.quote: AI drafts are starting points. Before publishing:

sources.title: Will ChatGPT replace SEO? SEO is shifting to AI visibility and narrative optimization
sources.originalTitle: Will ChatGPT Replace SEO? Here's the Real Answer
sources.summary: Ilias argues ChatGPT won't kill SEO but is rewriting it: the goal moves from ranking on Google to being cited, summarized and spoken about by AI answer engines. He lays out four bets: track AI visibility, earn citations from quotable content, write for AI summarization, and control your narrative.

principles.text: The SEO goal is shifting from ranking #1 to being the brand AI chooses to talk about.
principles.quote: Be the brand AI chooses to _talk about_ when users ask questions

principles.text: If AI tools don't mention you, a #1 Google ranking matters much less.
principles.quote: If ChatGPT doesn't mention you, it doesn't matter if you're #1 on Google.

principles.text: Earn citations by creating assets worth quoting, not PBNs or spammy guest posts.
principles.quote: Not PBNs or spammy guest posts. Create assets worth quoting.

principles.text: Write with AI summarization in mind: clear structure, entity names and helpful formatting give AI the signal it needs.
principles.quote: Clear structure, entity names, helpful formatting. AI needs signal!

principles.text: Define what you want AI to say about you and seed that narrative across your content, blog and partnerships.
principles.quote: Define what you want AI to say about you, and seed that across your content, blog, and partnerships.

principles.text: Old-school SEO tactics fail because AI favors sources that feel trustworthy, useful and common across sources.
principles.quote: Old-school tactics (keyword stuffing, random backlinks) won't cut it.

sources.title: Generative Engine Optimization: how to get cited by ChatGPT, Perplexity and AI Overviews
sources.originalTitle: What is Generative Engine Optimization (GEO)?
sources.summary: Ilias Ism explains GEO as optimizing content to be cited by AI search engines, not just ranked. He covers the three engine types, the Princeton study's tactics, and his daily manual routine of finding AI-cited listicles and paying for placement.

principles.text: GEO builds on SEO rather than replacing it; master traditional SEO first, since AI engines rely on the same crawling and rankings.
principles.quote: AI systems cite content that ranks well in traditional search.

principles.text: Optimize for citations in AI answers, not blue-link rankings; being the top citation can beat ranking #1 in Google.
principles.quote: Being the top citation in generative AI systems often outperforms ranking #1 in Google for credibility and conversion

principles.text: Add concrete statistics and credible citations; they were the biggest levers in the Princeton GEO study.
principles.quote: Transform vague claims into concrete data points.** AI models prioritize factual, quantifiable information.

principles.text: Tailor tactics to content type: opinion, factual, historical and business content each respond to different optimizations.
principles.quote: One-size-fits-all doesn't work in GEO. **Tailor your strategy to your content type**.

principles.text: Track GEO manually for 10 minutes daily: ask AI engines your money queries and see which listicles get cited.
principles.quote: So every morning, I spend **10 minutes** checking where I stand.

principles.text: Pitch authors of AI-cited listicles and offer to pay for placement; leading with 'your article is cited by AI' gets replies.
principles.quote: I'm not begging for links. I'm offering to pay for placement in content that AI already trusts.

sources.title: Why Ilias Ism chose a location independent lifestyle and how to sustain it
sources.originalTitle: Why I Chose a Location Independent Lifestyle
sources.summary: Ilias recounts going remote at 18 with design and web dev skills, freelancing, then founding Officient and moving through Paris, the Canary Islands and Switzerland. He distills a survival checklist (steady cash flow, in-demand skills, insurance, adaptability) and a mindset built on balance, constant learning, networks and embracing change.

principles.text: Have a reliable income and an emergency fund before going location independent.
principles.quote: Whether it's online jobs, freelancing, or running your own biz, you need a reliable income. Having an emergency fund for those unexpected hiccups is a smart move.

principles.text: Build skills that are in demand online; they are what let you thrive remotely.
principles.quote: the key to thriving as a digital nomad is having skills that are hot online.

principles.text: Freelancing with marketable skills is a low-barrier way to start before launching your own business.
principles.quote: Freelancing was my golden ticket to the world of digital nomad jobs

principles.text: Never stop learning; every project and place teaches something, however much you've hustled.
principles.quote: Every new job, project, and city teaches you something.

principles.text: Your network is a lifeline; connect with peers and build a social presence early.
principles.quote: Connect with other digital nomads, join Facebook groups, and build a strong social media presence. You never know when these connections might come in handy.

principles.text: Adaptability is key; plans, income and circumstances will shift, so roll with it.
principles.quote: Learning to adapt and roll with the punches is key.

sources.title: Why hire a team to scale: the ramen chef vs. the sushi owners
sources.originalTitle: Why You Should Hire a Team to Scale Your Business
sources.summary: Ilias contrasts a ramen chef who hired staff and can leave on busy nights with sushi owners who do everything themselves and never get a day off. He applies it to his SEO agency: document processes as SOPs so new hires can replicate quality, which also raises valuation and helped him sell his previous SaaS at a premium.

principles.text: If you do everything yourself, you are the business; it stops when you stop.
principles.quote: When they're sick, the restaurant is closed. **They are the business!**

principles.text: Scale by hiring a team so the business runs without you being present.
principles.quote: This is because the ramen chef has focused on scaling up and hiring a team to run things without him needing to be there.

principles.text: Scale without losing quality by documenting processes as SOPs that new team members can replicate.
principles.quote: The key to scaling without losing quality is developing standardized systems and procedures that can be replicated by future team members.

principles.text: As clients grow, capacity must grow with them or you risk losing them.
principles.quote: Because as my customers grow, I will need to grow with them. I will need to hire more people to help me with the work of providing for my clients or risk losing them.

principles.text: Documented processes speed onboarding, keep consistency, free the founder, and raise valuation.
principles.quote: Increases business valuation if I ever want to sell

principles.text: A business that runs without the founder earns a premium from acquirers.
principles.quote: I had built a team and processes that allowed me to step away from the business and focus on other things. And the acquirer was willing to pay a premium for that!

sources.title: Perfect Landing Page Formula: headline, description and bullet-point benefits
sources.originalTitle: Perfect Landing Page Formula [Free Template]
sources.summary: Ilias Ism lays out a simple landing page formula: a short headline showing value and USP, a description with specific numbers and reasons, and 3-5 benefit bullets. He illustrates it with Pieter Levels' Nomad List, Interior AI and Photo AI pages and packages it as a reusable AI prompt.

principles.text: Headline should be very short, simple, concise, and show value and the USP.
principles.quote: Title: Very short, simple to understand, concise, shows value and USP

principles.text: Description carries the specifics: numbers, benefits, reasons why, and the mission.
principles.quote: Description: Specific numbers, benefits, reasons why, mission

principles.text: Use 3-5 bullet points with numbers and key points to summarize the product.
principles.quote: Bullet points: 3-5 bullet points with numbers & key points

principles.text: Bullet points are the most important part of a landing page because they summarize benefits in an easy-to-remember way.
principles.quote: The bullet points are the most important part of the landing page. They summarize the product and its benefits in a way that's easy to understand and remember.

principles.text: Design for scanners: most visitors skim to decide if the page is worth their time.
principles.quote: They're also easy to scan, which is important because most people don't read every word on a landing page. They scan it to see if it's worth their time.

principles.text: Reuse a proven landing page style across products; copying one style lifted Nomad List conversion from 1% to almost 4%.
principles.quote: I copy-pasted Photo AI and Interior AI's landing page style and put it on Nomad List and conversion is now up from 1% to almost 4%

sources.title: SEO page titles: formula, patterns and an audit loop from SEO Roasts
sources.originalTitle: SEO Page Titles: How to Write Them (Formula + Examples)
sources.summary: Ilias Ism explains how to write SEO titles by treating the SERP as the brief: lead with the main query, stay around 40-55 characters, mirror winning patterns, match page type, and align title, description, H1 and slug. He adds a 10-step audit loop and a Cursor skill for bulk rewrites.

principles.text: Treat the SERP as the brief: study what already ranks, then write the clearest version for your page.
principles.quote: The better way to write page titles is to treat the SERP like the brief. Look at what already ranks, identify the pattern, then write the clearest version for your page.

principles.text: Bad titles fail by being vague, bloated, mismatched or clever, not by missing a magic word.
principles.quote: bad titles usually do not fail because they are missing a magic word. They fail because they are vague, bloated, mismatched, or trying to be clever when Google wants obvious.

principles.text: Point title, meta description, H1 and slug at one primary query, with the main phrase first.
principles.quote: SEO title -> meta description -> H1 -> URL slug They should all point at the same primary phrase.

principles.text: Keep titles around 40-55 characters so the words that matter appear before truncation.
principles.quote: Shorten until the words that matter appear before the ellipsis.

principles.text: Mirror the SERP's modifiers and format instead of inventing your own phrasing; this is matching the market, not copying.
principles.quote: If every top result says "best AI presentation makers" and your title says "AI slide creation solution," congratulations, you have invented a worse phrase.

principles.text: Make the title say what the page is (pricing, docs, login); a title like 'Home' wastes the most important SEO real estate.
principles.quote: Vague titles waste the most important SEO real estate on the page. Say what the page is.

sources.title: Programmatic SEO: data, templates and automation to generate thousands of ranking pages
sources.originalTitle: What is Programmatic SEO & How to Do It (with Examples)
sources.summary: Ilias Ism explains programmatic SEO as data plus templates plus automation producing thousands of useful pages. He backs it with client examples (MagicBuddy, WorkbookPDF, GradientPage), a four-stage implementation process, and a firm stance that quality beats page count.

principles.text: Programmatic SEO is a formula: data source plus templates plus automation yields thousands of valuable pages.
principles.quote: Data Source + Templates + Automation = Thousands of Valuable Pages

principles.text: Build a system instead of writing pages one by one; effort stays flat while output compounds.
principles.quote: Traditional SEO often scales linearly with effort—more content means more work. Programmatic SEO can scale exponentially once you build the right systems.

principles.text: Page count is not the goal; every page must serve a real user need.
principles.quote: The key to successful programmatic SEO isn't just creating many pages - it's creating valuable pages that serve real user needs.

principles.text: Pick keywords with clear intent that can be templated, then shape your URL structure around them.
principles.quote: Focus on keywords with clear commercial or informational intent that can be templated

principles.text: Let user activity spawn pages on demand, such as a new page each time someone clicks an example.
principles.quote: we created thousands of pages dynamically when the user clicks on a ChatGPT example they like.

principles.text: Use AI to generate variations, but always review the output before it ships.
principles.quote: Always review AI-generated content for accuracy and value

sources.title: X (Twitter) marketing: build an audience in public, engage, and convert followers into customers
sources.originalTitle: X (Twitter) Marketing: How to Grow and Get Customers in 2026
sources.summary: Ilias Ism's playbook for using X as a founder: post consistently, reply a lot, build in public, and weave product mentions into value-first content. Covers niche research, profile optimization, engagement tactics, cross-promotion of top content, analytics, and tooling, with examples of founders who grew via X.

principles.text: X is one of the few channels where a solo founder can compete with companies 100x their size, because buyers follow people, not brands.
principles.quote: It is also where a lot of buyers hang out: founders, developers, marketers, and investors who follow people, not brands. That makes it one of the few channels where a solo founder can compete with companies 100x their size.

principles.text: Build in public with value-driven show-and-tell content instead of self-promotion; expertise attracts clients better than ads.
principles.quote: The results prove the power of "building in public" on Twitter with tactical, value-driven content. His expertise attracted clients more effectively than any ads could.

principles.text: Build the audience on X before launching, so social proof backs the debut.
principles.quote: This social proof helps ensure a successful debut.

principles.text: Get endorsed by the right bigger person in your niche; one mention can generate leads almost overnight.
principles.quote: After my friend and bigger Indie Hacker Marc Louvion tweeted about my SEO services at MagicSpace, I received 20 solid leads in my direct messages almost overnight! It’s important to connect with the right people.

principles.text: Avoid hard selling; weave product mentions subtly among lots of value so followers see your product as the go-to solution.
principles.quote: The key with Twitter marketing is avoiding overly promotional content. Followers are quick to tune out hard sells.

principles.text: Reply to everyone and engage with the community; it boosts algorithmic visibility, and track analytics to double down on what works.
principles.quote: Reply to questions and comments from followers. This improves the algorithmic visibility of your tweets.

sources.title: AI Apps 50 SEO report: what separates winning AI tools in organic search
sources.originalTitle: AI Apps 50: SEO & Traffic Analysis of Top Startup AI Tools (2025) - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: MagicSpace (Ilias Ism, Sasha, Hiren) pulled Ahrefs data on the a16z AI Apps 50 list. Traffic is highly concentrated, organic dwarfs paid, and winners ship large indexable content libraries and category-owning educational content rather than relying on links.

principles.text: Organic search is the only sustainable acquisition channel at scale; even well-funded AI tools barely use paid search.
principles.quote: Even these well-funded tools barely use paid search. Organic is the only sustainable acquisition channel at scale, something we also see with our clients.

principles.text: Don't chase long-tail keywords that bring 1-2 visits a month. Focus on the few keywords that actually matter.
principles.quote: Most tools waste resources chasing long-tail keywords that generate 1-2 visits/month. Focus on the 1-5 keywords that matter.

principles.text: Programmatic SEO: every template, tool or asset is a new indexable page, so content volume beats selective link building.
principles.quote: Every new template/tool/asset = new indexable page = new ranking opportunity.

principles.text: High domain authority is wasted without a content strategy to turn it into visitors.
principles.quote: Links without content strategy = wasted authority.

principles.text: Own your category's educational content: teach how to use the category, not why to use your tool.
principles.quote: "How to use [category]" content > "Why use [our tool]" content.

principles.text: Go deep in one category rather than spreading thin across many; ideally narrow to one keyword.
principles.quote: Own one category completely > weak presence in multiple categories.

sources.title: Content distribution: turn 1 article into 7 channels for 7X the reach
sources.originalTitle: Content Distribution Guide: Turn 1 Article Into 7X the Reach - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: Ilias Ism argues that publishing is only the start and distribution is the real work. He lays out a 7-channel framework (Twitter thread, LinkedIn article, Pinterest pins, Reddit, Medium, newsletter, Quora) with timing and tactics for each, plus how to measure ROI per channel.

principles.text: Distribution is the work, not extra work; one well-distributed article beats ten undistributed ones.
principles.quote: One well-distributed article will outperform ten undistributed ones.

principles.text: Repurpose one article into seven channels: thread, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Reddit, Medium, newsletter, Quora.
principles.quote: Same content. 7X the reach.

principles.text: Don't just post a link on Twitter; turn the article into a hook-driven thread.
principles.quote: Don't just tweet a link. Nobody clicks those anymore.

principles.text: On Reddit, skip traditional self-promotion: answer real questions helpfully and be early.
principles.quote: Sort by "new" and be the first valuable commenter.

principles.text: Make one Pinterest pin per example in a list article, since Pinterest users are actively searching.
principles.quote: Create one pin for EACH example

principles.text: Shift from writing more to distributing better; audit your top posts against all channels.
principles.quote: Stop thinking: "I need to write more content" Start thinking: "I need to distribute better"

sources.title: Programmatic SEO with Next.js: building thousands of pages from one template
sources.originalTitle: Programmatic SEO with Next.js: The Complete Tutorial - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: A hands-on tutorial on building a programmatic SEO site in Next.js. Prefer static generation for speed, drive many pages from one dynamic-route template and a data file, give every page unique metadata, ship a dynamic sitemap, and deploy on Vercel. Includes scaling notes for very large sites.

principles.text: For pSEO at scale, prefer static site generation: pre-render pages at build time for fast loads.
principles.quote: SSG generates static HTML files at build time, resulting in incredibly fast page load times – a key ranking factor. For pSEO, SSG is often the ideal choice, especially for large sites.

principles.text: One template plus a data source plus dynamic routes yields hundreds or thousands of pages.
principles.quote: Next.js makes it incredibly easy to create dynamic routes, which are essential for generating hundreds or thousands of programmatic pages from a single template.

principles.text: Give every programmatic page unique metadata (title, description) built from its own data.
principles.quote: This is _essential_ for programmatic SEO, as you need unique metadata for each page.

principles.text: Put a clean slug in your dataset so URLs are readable and SEO-friendly.
principles.quote: We've added a `slug` field to each city object. This will be used for creating clean, SEO-friendly URLs.

principles.text: Past 50,000 URLs or 50MB, split into multiple sitemaps with a sitemap index file.
principles.quote: If you have more than 50,000 URLs or your sitemap file exceeds 50MB, you'll need to create multiple sitemaps and a sitemap index file.

principles.text: On very large sites, update sitemap entries incrementally instead of regenerating everything.
principles.quote: For very large sites, regenerating the entire sitemap on every change can be inefficient.

sources.title: How MagicSpace SEO took StoryChief from 8k to 44k monthly clicks and cut CPA
sources.originalTitle: StoryChief SEO Case Study: 6x Traffic, 80% lower CPA - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: Case study of a 6-month SEO engagement for StoryChief, a content marketing SaaS up against Ahrefs, SEMrush and Backlinko. A mix of content, technical SEO, backlinks and conversion work grew organic clicks 6x, made SEO the source of 80% of leads, and replaced PPC that had a CPA above $2,000.

principles.text: SEO is a long-term, cost-effective alternative to PPC for acquiring customers.
principles.quote: Sustainable growth: SEO provided a long-term, cost-effective solution compared to PPC.

principles.text: Combine content, technical SEO and off-page work; the mix beats any single lever.
principles.quote: Holistic approach: Combining content, technical SEO, and off-page strategies yielded powerful results.

principles.text: You can beat industry giants in a crowded market with a focused multi-faceted SEO strategy.
principles.quote: Competitive edge: StoryChief successfully competed against industry leaders in a crowded market.

principles.text: Judge channels by acquisition cost; shifting from PPC to SEO dramatically cut CPA.
principles.quote: ROI focus: The shift from PPC to SEO dramatically reduced customer acquisition costs.

principles.text: Pair SEO with conversion optimization, email nurture and distribution so traffic becomes leads.
principles.quote: Conversion rate optimization

sources.title: Why SEO is so hard in 2025: algorithm churn, technical debt, AI search and link building
sources.originalTitle: Why is SEO So Difficult? - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: Ilias Ism lists five reasons SEO is difficult: frequent core updates, technical SEO, scaling quality content, weaker link building tactics, and AI Overviews. His tactical advice: hybrid AI plus human content, diversified traffic, digital PR, and interactive tools. It ends as an agency pitch and the statistics are loosely sourced.

principles.text: Scale content with AI for ideation and drafts, but keep human editors for expert interviews and data validation.
principles.quote: Successful brands adopt hybrid models—leveraging AI for ideation and drafting while retaining human editors for EEAT-enhancing elements like expert interviews and data validation.

principles.text: Don't depend on organic search alone; diversify traffic sources to survive algorithm updates.
principles.quote: Diversifying traffic sources to mitigate reliance on organic search

principles.text: Monitor continuously and audit content regularly so you can adapt when core updates hit.
principles.quote: Continuous monitoring through tools like Google Search Console and third-party platforms

principles.text: Modern link building leans on digital PR built around newsworthy data studies.
principles.quote: Digital PR campaigns tied to newsworthy data studies

principles.text: Design for mobile first, because Google always crawls the mobile version of your site.
principles.quote: Google always crawls your website on mobile!

principles.text: Build interactive tools like calculators and quizzes that AI summaries can't replace.
principles.quote: Create interactive tools (calculators, quizzes) that resist AI summarization

sources.title: How Ilias Ism got Aikido Security to #1-#3 rankings in one month of SEO
sources.originalTitle: Aikido Security -  - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: A case study of a one-month SEO engagement with Aikido Security when it had 5 founders. Instead of publishing lots of new content, the work improved existing posts, restructured keywords, and used third-party listicles plus self-owned backlink pages to reach top-three rankings.

principles.text: Improve and restructure existing content before writing new content.
principles.quote: Improve existing content first. Look at all the blog posts you have. Improve every article. Do a keyword restructure. Make your existing content rank.

principles.text: Get into other people's listicles and articles to rank fast instead of publishing hundreds of posts.
principles.quote: Instead of writing tons of content, use other listicles and articles to get into top results immediately. Do comprehensive backlink and listicle research.

principles.text: Add backlinks from your own pages by writing pages that feature the company.
principles.quote: Leverage your existing authority. Write pages featuring the company. This boosts domain authority.

principles.text: A short, focused SEO engagement can be enough to build a foundation.
principles.quote: One month can be enough. We worked together for one month. We decided together that was enough for their SEO.

principles.text: Focus effort on the top keywords that matter and aim for the top three positions.
principles.quote: Look at all the top keywords. Make sure you get into the results. Acquire #1, #2, #3 spots for what matters.

sources.title: Bank.Green case study: how focused SEO took a non-profit from launch to #1 for green banking
sources.originalTitle: Bank.Green: From Launch to #1 Rankings in Green Banking - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: Case study of MagicSpace SEO's work with non-profit Bank.Green: growth strategy, brand identity, website and a tightly targeted keyword plan. Organic traffic grew from near zero in 2021 to 3.8K monthly visits with #1 rankings for the core topic keywords.

principles.text: Target a small set of high-intent, relevant keywords instead of chasing thousands.
principles.quote: Rather than trying to rank for thousands of keywords, focusing on a smaller set of highly relevant, high-value terms led to better rankings and more qualified traffic.

principles.text: Capture people already searching for the solution by going after specific, high-intent terms.
principles.quote: By targeting specific, high-intent keywords related to sustainable banking, Bank.Green was able to capture significant organic traffic from users actively seeking eco-friendly banking solutions.

principles.text: A clear brand identity helps you stand out in a competitive space and build trust.
principles.quote: Establishing a clear brand identity helped Bank.Green stand out in a competitive space and build trust with environmentally conscious consumers.

principles.text: SEO compounds: a solid foundation keeps paying off years later.
principles.quote: The SEO strategy continues to pay dividends years after implementation, demonstrating the value of building a solid foundation.

principles.text: Build the website for both users and search engines from the start.
principles.quote: The site was optimized for both user experience and search engines.

principles.text: Mission-driven non-profits can win with SEO using the right strategy and execution.
principles.quote: This case study shows that non-profit organizations can achieve significant SEO success with the right strategy and execution.

sources.title: Black & White Idea Framework: writing sub-60-character titles that catch attention
sources.originalTitle: Black & White Idea Framework: Viral Copywriting Guide - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: Ilias Ism explains Wono's attention framework (catch, hook, retain, convert) and the idea of Black & White ideas: concepts that reduce to a binary, sub-60-character title. He shows how to build one with ChatGPT using the "How Japanese Housewives Outsmarted Global Finance" example.

principles.text: Manage attention as a funnel: the more you catch, the more flows into hook, retain and convert.
principles.quote: The more attention you can catch, the more you can funnel into the subsequent steps.

principles.text: Good ideas split into layered (retain attention) and black & white (catch attention); titles need the latter.
principles.quote: Layered Ideas: These are complex, multi-dimensional ideas that are hard to convey with simple words. While they are effective for retaining attention, they are not as effective for catching attention.

principles.text: Test an idea by compressing it into a binary under 60 characters; if it survives, you have something to work with.
principles.quote: Black & White Ideas: These are ideas that can be broken down into a binary format in less than 60 characters.

principles.text: Build the title from two counterpart thoughts (e.g. Japanese vs Global, Housewives vs Finance) to create tension.
principles.quote: The power of this attention management framework is that it create a conflict and tension in the mind of the reader, causing them to be intrigued and hooked

principles.text: Focus on the ingredients of an idea rather than the idea itself when generating content ideas.
principles.quote: the Black & White Idea Framework emphasizes the importance of focusing on the ingredients of the idea, rather than the idea itself.

principles.text: Simplicity without losing substance is what makes an idea catch attention and spark curiosity about the nuance.
principles.quote: Because it can be understood in a few words without losing its substance, it is highly effective at catching attention.

sources.title: How MagicSpace audited 1000 Framer sites and grew into ongoing SEO and AI SEO consulting
sources.originalTitle: Framer - From Audit to Ongoing AI SEO Growth - MagicSpace SEO
sources.summary: Case study of auditing Framer.com and its top 1000 customer sites by scraping them all and spotting shared problems. Shows how platform-wide SEO fixes beat per-site work, why clear Notion documentation matters, and how a one-off audit became a long-term AI SEO partnership.

principles.text: Audit at scale: scrape many sites at once, find the patterns, and fix them for everyone together.
principles.quote: Audit at scale when possible. Don't check sites one by one. Scrape 1000 sites. Find patterns. Fix problems for everyone at once.

principles.text: For platforms, ship broad fixes that help every customer rather than custom work per site.
principles.quote: Platform-wide fixes beat individual solutions. Framer needed improvements that helped thousands of customers. Not custom work for each site. Broad solutions scale better.

principles.text: Document deliverables clearly (Notion with screenshots) so dev teams can reuse them and stop repeating questions.
principles.quote: Document everything clearly. Notion reports with screenshots work great. Dev teams can reference them later. Clear documentation prevents repeated questions.

principles.text: Turn one-off audits into ongoing relationships; long-term partnerships compound.
principles.quote: One-time SEO audits help. Ongoing consulting helps more. Questions come up. Strategy shifts. Long-term partnerships deliver compounding results.

principles.text: Common platform issues are findable by crawling: missing H1s, canonicals, nofollow, staging domains indexed, leftover lorem ipsum.
principles.quote: Found patterns everywhere. Missing H1 tags on 25% of sites. Canonicalization problems across domains. Nofollow issues hurting crawl budget. Lorem ipsum still live on customer sites.

principles.text: Being a founder in the client's own space (SEO as the product) gives an edge in recommending product-level improvements.
principles.quote: Their core Product is SEO! So as SaaS founders ourselves, we were uniquely positioned to take this on and to provide product improvements on how each Framer customer could rank better.

sources.title: Ilias Ism's 12 link building strategies for 2026, with real costs and a 90-day plan
sources.originalTitle: 12 Link Building Strategies That Work in 2026 (With Real Costs)
sources.summary: Ilias Ism ranks 12 link building tactics by cost, speed and scalability, based on 10,030 publisher quotes. Start with competitor link-gap outreach and "Best X" listicle insertions, compound with data pages and free tools, and filter targets by real traffic rather than DR. Links should also win citations in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews.

principles.text: Mine competitors' backlinks: pitch editors who already link to 2+ rivals, since relevance is built in.
principles.quote: pull the exact pages already linking to 2 or more of your direct SERP competitors. Because those editors have already linked to tools in your category, your pitch is relevant by definition.

principles.text: Filter link targets by organic traffic, not Domain Rating alone.
principles.quote: 43% of DR 30+ websites have under 1,000 monthly visits—always filter by organic traffic, not just DR

principles.text: Link building should also feed AI search: pages in Google's top 10 are what answer engines cite.
principles.quote: Pages ranking in Google’s top 10 are the #1 source pool cited by ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews

principles.text: When doing niche edits, write a genuinely useful addition rather than forcing an exact-match anchor.
principles.quote: Never force an awkward exact-match anchor into an unrelated paragraph. Write a 1–2 sentence addition that genuinely improves the section so the editor keeps it permanently.

principles.text: Publish proprietary data so writers cite you for free; it compounds with no publisher fees.
principles.quote: When you publish proprietary numbers from your own database or customer base, writers cite and link to you for free.

principles.text: Build narrow, zero-signup free tools instead of another generic beginner's guide to earn links.
principles.quote: A narrow, zero-signup calculator, checker, or generator earns far more organic links than another 2,000-word beginner's guide.

sources.title: Link building statistics 2026: what guest posts cost, what drives price, what publishers demand
sources.originalTitle: Link Building Statistics 2026: Prices From 10,030 Sites
sources.summary: Ilias Ism's LinkDR essay analyzes a catalog of 10,030 publisher sites to show real link prices. Median guest post is $100 on DR 30+ sites, price is flat from DR 30 to 59, traffic matters as much as DR, and most publishers want upfront payment. It ends with practical buying rules.

principles.text: Check a site's organic traffic before buying a link, not just its Domain Rating.
principles.quote: Almost half of the DR 30+ sites that sell links get fewer than 1,000 visits a month. DR measures a site's own backlinks, and those can be bought too. **Check organic traffic before you buy, not only DR.**

principles.text: Don't overpay for a few extra DR points: median price is flat from DR 30 to DR 59, so pay for traffic and relevance.
principles.quote: Do not pay DR 60 prices for DR 50 sites.** The median price is flat from DR 30 to DR 59. Pay more for traffic and relevance, not for a few DR points.

principles.text: Publishers price on traffic about as much as DR, so price climbs steadily with traffic.
principles.quote: Across DR 30+ sites, log price correlates with log traffic at 0.49 and with DR at 0.45. Publishers price on both, and traffic edges out DR.

principles.text: Compare multiple resellers: the same site can cost twice as much from one seller as another.
principles.quote: The most expensive reseller asks a median of **1.44 times** the cheapest. On **30%** of these sites, the gap is 2 times or more.

principles.text: Skip news sites unless you truly need them; they carry a large price premium.
principles.quote: Skip news sites unless you need them.** They cost about 11 times more than other DR 30+ sites.

principles.text: Link insertions are rarely cheaper than guest posts, so choose based on fit, not expected savings.
principles.quote: The insertion saves the publisher work, but many charge for the link, not the article.

sources.title: Backlink pricing in 2026: what links cost by Domain Rating and how to budget
sources.originalTitle: How Much Do Backlinks Cost in 2026? Real Prices by DR
sources.summary: Managed backlinks cost roughly $150 to $500 each, driven mainly by Domain Rating, real traffic and niche. The essay covers per-DR price tiers, red flags in cheap links, the true cost of doing it yourself, and budgeting from the link gap versus competitors.

principles.text: Backlink price is driven mostly by the linking site's Domain Rating.
principles.quote: The biggest price driver is the Domain Rating (DR) of the site that links to you.

principles.text: Judge a link by real traffic, not DR alone.
principles.quote: A site with real readers is worth more than a high-DR site with none.

principles.text: Restricted niches cost more because fewer publishers accept them.
principles.quote: Casino, crypto, CBD, and finance links cost much more because fewer sites accept them.

principles.text: Cheap links are a false economy: spam or PBN links get ignored by Google and can hurt you.
principles.quote: A cheap link that Google ignores is not cheap. A link on a spam network can also hurt you.

principles.text: Count DIY link building as your time plus the publisher fee; that is why teams outsource.
principles.quote: if one link takes five hours and your time is worth $50 an hour, that is $250 before the publisher's fee.

principles.text: Budget from the gap: count competitors' referring domains, then buy a steady monthly pace.
principles.quote: Count the referring domains of the top three pages for your keyword.

sources.title: Cold email outreach for link building: warmup, setup, and what to put in the email
sources.originalTitle: Cold Email Outreach for Link Building (2026)
sources.summary: A practical guide to running cold email campaigns for backlinks. Covers using a separate outreach domain, warming it up, configuring DNS and mailboxes, and writing short, incentive-led emails that avoid common mistakes like broken variables and generic greetings.

principles.text: Never run cold outreach from your primary domain; buy a lookalike domain and warm it up first.
principles.quote: you shouldn’t use your primary business domain for cold email outreach. Purchase a domain that’s similar, e.g. try(name).com.

principles.text: Warm up new sending domains so you build a positive reputation and land in the inbox, not spam.
principles.quote: you need to create a positive email sending reputation so that your emails are delivered to your prospects inbox, not their spam/junk folder.

principles.text: Use three mailboxes per domain with human-sounding names, basic signatures and forwarding to your real inbox.
principles.quote: 3 email accounts per domain is the standard for cold email outreach. For best results, create US-sounding names e.g. ‘James Williams’

principles.text: Give prospects a strong incentive to link: affiliate access, free product access, or ready-made assets.
principles.quote: You need to have a strong incentive to be included - this is key for any campaign.

principles.text: Keep subject lines short (5-7 words) and the email body concise, with hyperlinks instead of long explanations.
principles.quote: Short, catchy subject lines get 2x higher open rates than long, detailed ones. Aim for 5-7 words max.

principles.text: Lead with value: use Ahrefs or SEMrush to find broken or outdated links and offer to fix them.
principles.quote: Use tools like Ahrefs or SEMrush to identify broken backlinks or outdated references on their site. Offering to fix these adds immediate value.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism explains his developer-style approach to link building: email top-ranking pages and listicles, pay up to $1,000-$2,000 for links on pages ranking for bottom-of-funnel keywords, and mine competitor backlink data at scale. He also covers building real brand authority and hiring cheap retainer-based UGC creators.

chunks.heading: Backlink buying: what makes a link worth paying for
chunks.text:
- Ilias will pay "up to $1,000 or $2,000" for a link on any page that ranks in the top 10 or top 20 for a relevant keyword. His reasoning:
  - A top-5 ranking page sends real referral traffic to humans.
  - Those pages also get picked up by AI models.
  - A page ranking that high is likely a legitimate site, even with a low domain rating.
- Bottom-of-funnel keywords matter most, such as "best link building tool". An AI fans out to this kind of query in its final research step, so a mention on a page ranking for it can lead to citations in AI answers.
- Top-of-funnel pages (e.g. "how to get more traffic") are worth less. They are still worth paying for if he can get a direct mention, such as a "best tools" H2 with a screenshot, an H3 with his tool and a description. A bare anchor-text insert is worth less.
- His minimum baseline for a link site:
  - 500 to 1,000+ monthly traffic across the domain in Ahrefs or Semrush.
  - Some domain rating.
  - Top pages roughly relevant to his topic.
- He treats a link as spammy when the site isn't relevant, has low domain traffic, or looks like slop (casino pages, random content). He avoids blogs that look like link farms, where every post is a paid recommendation.
- He sees a no-follow link on a ranking page that gets clicks as valuable. A brand mention inside the content (H3 plus screenshot plus description) is a signal even without a link.

chunks.heading: Finding link opportunities at scale (LinkDR)
chunks.text:
- Ilias's product LinkDR (linkdr.com) automates link building. It pulls the top 100 to 1,000 backlinks for each of 5 to 10 competitors and combines them. Pages linking to several competitors (the "intersect") are strong prospects.
- It also adds every page ranking in the top 20 for his keywords. Expanding to the sites that link to those pages gives thousands of prospects, and everyone gets emailed.
- Email style: short, direct requests work best. He dislikes four-paragraph vague emails himself and ignores them. A typical ask is "I saw your page, you didn't mention me, can you please mention me?"
- Templates: AI-written templates were bad (unless using Opus, which was expensive), so he hard-coded real human-written examples. The AI picks from them depending on the opportunity:
  - Listicle: ask to be added.
  - Competitor has an affiliate program and he does too: offer a better deal.
  - Guest-post site: pitch a new guest post.
- Early on he offered $100 to $200 payments, affiliate links, or free credits.
- Recent rebuild: he deleted much of a two-year codebase. The app now runs mostly in Claude Code, a thin wrapper around an MCP and a database. He tells the AI to build its own MCP tools as needed. He says the emails are now very high quality.

chunks.heading: Ahrefs workflow for discovering topics competitors miss
chunks.text:
1. Open a top competitor in Ahrefs (the example was NapLab) and go to best-by-links.
2. Filter to one link per domain and sort by page traffic.
3. Find the linking pages that get the most real traffic. Those pages are what to copy or write about, not the competitor's own top pages, which everyone already copies (e.g. "how to wash pillows").
4. Write that content yourself, either as a guest post on a similar site or on your own, and link back.
5. Go one level further: look at who links to the 200 sites that link to the competitor. This expands to thousands of prospects.

- He also exports 10 to 20 CSVs from Ahrefs (keywords, top pages, links across competitors) into a single Claude Code chat to analyze them together.
