- He uses Ahrefs batch analysis on all your YouTube videos to see what keywords your video content already ranks for (his example: a video ranking number one for "maximize SEO").

chunks.heading: Where SEO is heading and what still works
chunks.text:
- He sees AI overviews as convenient and uses them himself. Pure content sites are dying, so he focuses on bottom-of-funnel pages that lead to a product.
- He believes the best long-term tactic is a real brand. He used Semrush's blog to learn link building, and he'd search "link building Semrush" because they publish deep, researched content. Build a site with "super high value, super high quality" resources.
- Real virality and brand mentions (YouTube, X, LinkedIn, even a billboard) help rankings. His view is that Google ingests data from every platform, so being known matters more than any single link.
- He predicts 2027 SEO becomes broader: Instagram, YouTube, LinkedIn and Twitter content for top of funnel, with the bottom of funnel converting on your own site. AI recommendations are fed by authority across all those sources.
- Paying YouTubers to make videos about you will be the next frontier. He expects social to follow the same path SEO did, with spam eventually pushing out low-authority accounts.
- Wisdom matters more than raw AI knowledge. Seeing patterns across SEO, retention loops, coupons and metrics lets him apply ideas AI wouldn't suggest. Example: a share feature in your app is itself an SEO tactic, because users share your links.
- AI gives conflicting SEO advice, and he says he can prove both sides from sources.
- He notes link exchanges such as Ultra Rank "are working" for now, though he doesn't know how long.

chunks.heading: UGC creator campaign for a SaaS product
chunks.text:
- He ran UGC for genppt.com, an AI presentation maker he bought on Acquire.com. He said it already had paying customers, and he tripled its MRR by building SEO content with Claude Code and a month of good backlinks.
- The setup: five creators, 30 videos per month each, for $500 per month each, posting to TikTok, Instagram and YouTube Shorts. (He said "30 videos per day across three channels" for the combined output and "30 videos per month for $500" per creator.)
- He found creators through a platform (he named SideShift). Retainers worked better than per-video pay. The platform tracked views automatically and paid bonuses at 20k, 50k and 100k views.
- Hiring test: he sent a link to the site and asked for a test video. If the creator's video was good, he hired them. Creators tested the app themselves for free, found the "wow moment," and made videos without any briefing, which showed whether they had taste.
- He chose this over buying phones, SIM cards and proxies to run warmed-up accounts. Real US-based creators make their own accounts and are motivated by bonuses.
- Results: some videos hit a million views. People swipe past in 3 to 10 seconds and rarely buy immediately, but may remember the brand. He thinks he needs a better product to test it with.
- His benchmark is Gamma, which spends heavily on creator and affiliate content.
- New accounts take time to warm up. His guideline is to interact with relevant content for a few weeks before posting.

chunks.heading: Public SEO roasts and what builds authority on X
chunks.text:
- His best-performing X posts are concrete tactics, skills and step-by-step templates, which people bookmark.
- The content that actually wins clients is the hardest to make: 20 to 30 minute unfiltered audits where he looks at a site for the first time and shows every step (Ahrefs, top pages, links, exporting into his tools, customer journey map, AI SEO tracker). He says that proves skill far better than a tweet.
- He did a public roast of Levels' sites (Peter Levels). Levels paid him to audit his sites in public. Ilias tweeted topics and ideas per site, and Levels implemented them himself.
- He enjoys the roasts because they teach viewers and show the opportunities he sees.
- Long-term, authority-based tactics stay white hat-ish. Short-term exploits are risky to publicize.

chunks.heading: AI SEO testing and protecting content from AI scrapers
chunks.text:
- On his SEO roast site (seoroast.com), he sells transcripts and videos for a $50 payment. To stop people pointing ChatGPT or Claude at the content, he detects AI agents and shows them a message that they must buy the content.
- It works 100% of the time, he says. Mechanisms: notes in robots.txt and llms.txt, and content negotiation (checking the Accept header for text/markdown). He also detects ChatGPT browsers and serves different content.
- It is similar to cloaking, which Google bans, but he says the AI companies don't have that rule and want markdown-optimized content.
- His method for AI SEO and for testing this:
  - Open a new incognito ChatGPT and run a prompt simulation.
  - Copy the steps the AI took.
  - Give them to the agent building your site and have it fix what went through.
  - Retest in a loop until everything is blocked.
- He also runs a tool called SEO tracker (the recording gave "seotracker.com") that checks rankings and runs prompt scans for AI search. He says he was early, then big companies entered.

chunks.heading: Customer journey prompt
chunks.text:
- He recommends the customer journey skill from his SEO skills repo. It maps the problems and queries people type in.
- He ran it on NapLab. One output was "Why do I sleep better in a hotel than at home?"
- It suggests non-SEO tactics where fitting, like YouTube demonstrations or troubleshooting guides, for each step.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism explains how he learned SEO through a feedback loop on Google Search Console, why scarce links (your own sites, high-difficulty guest mentions) beat commodity ones, and how he gets mentioned in ChatGPT, Gemini and Perplexity. He shows his tracker workflow: monitor prompts, find the cited sources, email those authors with a specific value offer.

chunks.heading: Ilias's background and how he learned SEO
chunks.text:
- Ilias started as a developer and front-end designer, building sites with Vue.js, React and JavaScript, and SaaS software with a team.
- He moved into SEO because side projects had no distribution: "nobody finds your apps", so he had to figure out traffic.
- He learned by doing: search a keyword, implement strategies, then watch Google Search Console every few days to see whether rankings improved or dropped.
- He argues SEO suits developers because it can be engineered: build a site, understand the algorithm, make it rank higher. He contrasts it with TikToks, brand marketing or social media where you need to learn Photoshop.
- He notes SEO advice conflicts constantly (backlinks matter or don't, descriptions matter or don't, entities, topical clusters), so the only way to find the truth is your own experiments.
- Today he runs an SEO agency plus side products. The agency is Magic Space SEO in Switzerland: strategy, consulting, blog posts and backlinks, fully done-for-you with Slack access. The tools are AI SEO Tracker, Link Dr and GenPPT.

chunks.heading: How he tests SEO
chunks.text:
- He does not run formal A/B tests with five near-identical pages. He thinks single-variable tests are time-consuming and only give marginal gains: a table instead of an image won't matter against a competitor with a higher domain rating.
- He tests ideas on his own live sites or directly with clients, for example backlinks plus entity stacking.
- If something works, he repeats it later to confirm. He also keeps doubting it, "because everything changes all the time" as the algorithm shifts.

chunks.heading: Links over content in 2026
chunks.text:
- Ilias says both on-page and links matter, but more mentions and links is the best strategy.
- Anyone can now publish 100 blog posts instantly. Tools make about 30 articles a month with images and links for around $100 per month. Content alone is no moat.
- The advantage is links nobody else can buy. His main version is a private network of his own legitimate sites that get their own traffic and don't link out to anyone else.
- Commodity links (parasite pages, profile links, directories, Link Tree style pages) raise the baseline for everyone. His analogy: in Switzerland everyone wears luxury, so basic gets you nothing. "The only way to stand out is get the links that nobody else has."
- Beyond blog links he wants broad awareness: listicles, guest posts, YouTube videos, Reddit, Medium, TikTok, Facebook, Twitter. Google's AI overviews and "people also ask" pull from all of these, so appearing everywhere builds one overall awareness graph.
- He notes AI overviews attach videos to paragraphs, and he thinks YouTube videos that mention you get extracted for content.

chunks.heading: AI SEO Tracker: how it works
chunks.text:
- The product tracks whether a site is mentioned in ChatGPT, Gemini, Copilot, Perplexity, AI Mode and AI Overviews. It costs $79 per month, and he expects the industry to settle around $799 per month at the high end.
- Setup: it scrapes the site, converts it to markdown, and runs a set of prompts to infer what the site is about.
- It builds a customer journey map of prompts from awareness through solution-aware to bottom-of-funnel. Example for a cloud-links tool: "how do I scale an SEO agency", then "automated backlink building software", then "what is cloud stacking".
- It runs each prompt in an incognito browser, copies the AI answer, and checks whether the brand is mentioned. It extracts every brand and entity mentioned, shows competitors and their order, and re-scans weekly.
- It lists the source pages feeding each answer and groups source domains by domain rating bucket.
- Roadmap goal: click a button to generate the missing blog post and backlinks. He expects customers want the least work possible: put in a credit card and be mentioned everywhere next month. He thinks people would pay about $500 per month for five posts plus five backlinks.

chunks.heading: Getting cited in AI answers: the GenPPT case
chunks.text:
- GenPPT is bootstrapped (zero funding) and competes with tools that raised around $50M. Ilias says it is mentioned in several AI answers, though usually around position 9 to 18 and about number 10 in ChatGPT listicles.
- Method: look at the sources feeding AI answers for a prompt (for example "best AI presentation maker"), then get into those sources.
  - He emailed the author of a "best AI presentation makers" listicle (Cripesh) and got GenPPT added.
  - He wrote a guest post himself on a Story Chief style guest-post site, and commented on a Reddit thread.
  - He emailed GCS Network and got a link there too. Roughly four sources now feed ChatGPT results.
- Result: after a few mentions the brand started appearing in AI results. He says AI results differ from Google because people scan the whole list, so even position 12 is useful.
- To rank higher in those lists, the product itself must improve: better conversion and features.
- Source patterns from his tracker data:
  - YouTube had about 460 mentions across 31 keywords, the most common source, so a decent YouTube presence helps a lot.
  - Medium, G2, Reddit, Wikipedia and blog or guest-post sites also appear.
  - Many cited domains have domain rating 0 to 20 or under 40, unlike Google money keywords where high domain rating is needed. Example: a security-site network ranked high at DR 40.

chunks.heading: The email outreach process for hard links
chunks.text:
- His AI email writer scrapes the target article and the sender's site, then checks whether the sender is already mentioned and whether a backlink exists. It works out the author's angle and what the publisher cares about (keeping the article current, giving readers actionable tools, partnerships and traffic).
- The email references specifics from the article and a gap in it. Example: the listicle ranks a tool at number six but doesn't link GenPPT in that section, so "readers are asking where to actually buy".
- He offers real value instead of asking for a free link: a link to their article from his sites, a guest post, co-created content, social promotion to his audience, and original data or a case study.
- For a hard target like Shopify, he says a plain link ask won't work. Offer data they would love, for example scraping the top 1,000 Shopify stores' schema/structured data and charting which schema (such as product offer with date and coupon) correlates with ranking in the top 100.
- He calls it "hardcore enterprise B2B sales", and says this is how he got the links that cheap spam never would.

chunks.heading: Link Dr: SERP-based backlink prospecting
chunks.text:
- Core idea: backlinks from pages ranking in the top 100 for your keyword are worth far more than random links.
- Given a keyword (for example "best link building tools"), the tool pulls the top 100 results, which costs about 10 scrapes. For each site it:
  - screenshots the homepage to check it is legit,
  - records domain rating and visits,
  - saves the pages it ranks for and related similar sites,
  - scrapes contact details from homepage and contact page, and uses the Hunter API for emails,
  - flags available parasite opportunities.
- Output: one exportable list of contacts you can paste into a Google Sheet and start outreach. He uses the same method for clients and for his own GenPPT link.
- Fast domain rating growth for Link Dr (reaching about DR 55 within roughly a month): he linked the new brand from his own sites (the agency, AI SEO Tracker, GenPPT, clients), plus profile links (calendar page, rank tracker), Indie Hackers guest posts and directories. His own sites don't link out to anyone else, which helps.
- Link Dr itself gets little organic traffic because SEO tools are extremely competitive. He relies on:
  - a free "top directories to submit to" list on LinkedIn, offered in exchange for a comment,
  - Reddit: a post about building an AI-powered link building tool (with feedback requested, no link) that still ranks in the top 3 on parasite SEO a year later,
  - press mentions, Twitter and LinkedIn.

chunks.heading: Social and free-offer tactics
chunks.text:
- Giveaways and freebies work well on social. His examples: "put your domain in the comments and I will give you one SEO tip", or "one free entity stack link" for followers.
- People love free stuff, and SEO people respond especially well to domain-review style offers.
- Facebook (discussed by the host) can be used with ads that drive people to a page profile; Ilias adds that this is a cheap way to gain visibility there.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism runs a live SEO audit of a founder's product site and explains how he grows on Twitter with "drop your site, get one tip" templates. He covers technical SEO basics, unique titles, redirects, domain authority, attacking one competitor keyword at a time with listicles, and distributing content so it actually ranks.

chunks.heading: Ilias's pattern-recognition view of entrepreneurship and templates
chunks.text:
- Ilias argues entrepreneurship "is really about seeing patterns and being able to understand them and use them", including for Twitter viral marketing and growth ideas.
- He says his speed on SEO audits comes from volume: he opens a website and already knows what to change for SEO or a blog post, because the knowledge "sticks in your brain" from years of trial and error ("learn through pain" from products that didn't ship or sell).
- He uses templates for tweets, headlines, SEO titles, landing-page descriptions and email subject lines, because the same templates keep working on people's psychology.
- He keeps swipe files: he collected about 200 SEO titles and headlines that work and fed them to ChatGPT/Claude, so he now has a quick tool that outputs an optimized SEO title. He did the same for tweets and wants to productize it one day.
- He also saves good emails (e.g. from Danny Postma) in a folder to reuse and optimize.
- His design method: collect references, take the best parts of about 10 products, and combine them into one unique page. He built an OG image tool this way: the top line from one tool, buttons from another, popups from others (e.g. ShipFast).
- He advises finding five references and spotting what they share before building something, rather than starting from scratch.
- On product timing, he says he used to launch many products with no audience and nothing happened. If he did it again he would build in public first, talk to people, find recurring problems, and then build for specific groups.

chunks.heading: Twitter "drop your domain" SEO tip template
chunks.text:
- Ilias runs a reply-bait tweet: "drop your site domain, I'll give you one tip to improve your SEO strategy", combined with an auto-DM (Typefully or Tweet Hunter style) that sends links.
- First run, November 2023: about 330 replies, many bookmarks, around 70,000 views.
- Rerun the same week as this recording to prove the template works: about 110k views and 460 replies, with an account that had grown from roughly 100-200 followers to almost 4,000.
- His earlier variant was "You deserve a break, I'll give your site a mini SEO checkup for free, I'll record a video analysis" (a testimonial video attached). It got only about 7,000 views, which he calls a good thing: the video reviews took up to 13 minutes each, and at 20 minutes per person, 100 replies is about two weeks of work.
- His rule: keep the deliverable under about 5 minutes per person, otherwise you spend days answering.
- Friends copied the template with their own specialty: a conversion-rate-optimization version (300-follower account roughly doubled followers), a "one idea to grow your product" version (about 200 replies in a day), "explain to your mom what your product does" (130 replies), and a product-hunt pre-launch version with a DM sent to everyone. Landing-page redesign offers also went viral for another founder (about 120 comments).
- It did not work on LinkedIn for him.
- Side benefits he lists: DMs from leads, content you can compile into a Notion doc, blog post or paid info product, social proof from testimonials, and followers who see you as an expert without it being spam.

chunks.heading: How tweets go viral in stages, and Twitter vs LinkedIn
chunks.text:
- Ilias describes three stages for a viral tweet: first it is shown to close friends and followers; if they engage it spreads to a slightly bigger group; after about 6-8 hours, when American traffic wakes up (for him in Europe), views can jump from about 20K to 100K+. He says a tweet must pass all stages to go super viral.
- He thinks LinkedIn's algorithm differs and people there are more hesitant: Twitter rewards "build in public" and admitting "my website needs help", while LinkedIn culture leans toward "my website is already perfect", so different content is needed.
- On Twitter, he says it is one of his best channels for generating leads and getting high-quality clients, and gives immediate feedback from other founders.
- He promotes products he genuinely finds underexposed (e.g. a blog-to-Pinterest scheduler tool), because he feels better products deserve visibility.

chunks.heading: Technical SEO audit checklist
chunks.text:
Ilias's quick audit uses the Ahrefs SEO toolbar and checks the following:
- Domain rating and backlink/referring domain counts at the page level.
- **Canonical URL:** missing canonicals mean Google treats URL variants (e.g. with query parameters) as separate pages; a canonical concentrates link juice on one page.
- robots.txt and sitemap.xml, including removing pages from the sitemap that shouldn't be in it.
- **Structured data:** e.g. person schema for a personal site, article schema for blog posts, review schema for review snippets. He says star-rating snippets help a page stand out versus a plain result; which schema to use depends on niche (courses, books, e-commerce).
- **Open Graph images:** auto-generate them (he notes they can be generated, and suggests adding a title and type). He says OG is for social/chat previews and does not impact rankings.
- Add alt text to images.
- **Unique titles on every page:** he says titles are among the most important things to manage. Check them with a Google `site:` search; if every page shows the same or duplicated title, fix it.
- Make sure the homepage explains what the tool is. On the audited product, he preferred a longer "about" style front page over a one-screen demo page, and suggested adding social proof such as stars from a testimonial tool.
- A one-page site will struggle to rank for much, and blogs written randomly "waste a lot of time" if not done in a specific way.

chunks.heading: Domain migrations and building domain authority
chunks.text:
- To move from one domain to another, Ilias sets up 301 redirects (e.g. Cloudflare rules, dynamic regex redirects, or on Vercel) mapping every page to its equivalent (/blog to new /blog), not just the root domain, since redirecting only the root destroys the purpose.
- He also says to use Google Search Console's "change of address" tool.
- He recommends hosting everything under one domain or subdomains where possible, because it concentrates domain rating. Separate domains for user-generated pages are acceptable, especially if they backlink to the main product.
- He frames SEO as building domain authority as an asset: with a domain rating of 60-70+, every new product or page launched from that domain gets an advantage.
- His example is Canva: domain rating about 92, around 370 domains linking in, many tools on one domain, so any new tool or blog post can outrank rivals even for keywords where Midjourney or ChatGPT seem like the obvious winner. He compares domain rating to a social account with many followers.
- Another tactic he's seen: competitors redirect expired domains that had backlinks to their landing pages.

chunks.heading: Competitor keyword research and ranking for listicles
chunks.text:
- Ilias picks a few competitors (for the audited tool: Webflow, Framer, Unicorn Platform), compares their top pages and keywords in Ahrefs, and goes keyword by keyword. He treats it as "which keyword should I focus on and what can I do to get into this list?" rather than "what content should I write".
- He skips low-intent keywords (e.g. "ChatGPT website") that bring people looking for something else.
- **Alternatives pages:** make "X alternatives" pages, list your tool on G2 and Product Hunt (mark yourself as the tool you use instead of the competitor so you appear as an alternative), and go through the top 100 keywords even though it takes long.
- **Get listed in existing lists:** open the pages Google ranks, find their contact or partner page, and reach out even if they say they don't accept guest posts. Offers include: a free article (paid placements typically cost roughly $200 to $1,000 per post), a link exchange, a free product, or a social shout-out. Being mentioned as a tool, even without a dofollow link, already wins part of that keyword. Also reach out to YouTubers who made reviews.
- Write for Starter Story-type sites: he says Starter Story has strong SEO ratings, and submitting your own story creates a high-value backlink (he has been featured).
- **Listicle format is mandatory:** if Google shows lists (5, 7, 14, 22 tools), you can only rank with a list. The title starts with a number and includes the keyword (e.g. "5 Best Website Builders for Beginners in 2024"), followed by an introduction, a numbered list, and a conclusion. He says deviating from the format wastes time.
- Keep titles within about 60 characters or they get cut off in search results.

chunks.heading: How to make a listicle outrank the competition
chunks.text:
- Ilias analyzes the page ranking first and explains why it wins: it shows a feature comparison table, an overall score, pricing, whether there is a free plan, pros and cons, images/screenshots of the software, a "since our last update" note, expert tips, and "best for" labels (e.g. best for e-commerce, best for beginners, easiest design).
- He criticizes a weaker page (ranked ninth): the intro skips explaining what website builders are, the evaluation criteria come too early, the list items are too short, with no images, pricing or detail, and an unnecessary extra H2. His view: listing pros and cons alone provides "no value".
- To outrank it, he says make a better page with unique insights: who each tool is best for, screenshots, use cases, example sites, reviews of users, and comparison with competitors (e.g. one focused on AI content vs another on simple directories).
- His rule: the more unique information you can provide, the better, and AI-written generic content loses against pages with real insights and images.
- For content planning, he suggests building a sitemap/directory structure beforehand, looking at competitors, and choosing specific keywords. A feature-explainer page for the product is fine as a landing page, but blog effort should go to competitor keywords.
- He uses Zebra-brief-style content-brief tools (he names Stefan's tool, "Z brief") for outlines and keyword ideas, and Story Chief for agencies with multi-writer workflows, scheduling and multi-channel distribution.

chunks.heading: Distribution after publishing and podcast repurposing
chunks.text:
- Ilias says writing an article is not enough; distribution is what makes it rank. His repurposing list: send it in your newsletter, link it from your top pages, make a Pinterest pin in portrait format, schedule tweets or a thread (using Typefully or similar, asking an AI for tweet ideas from the article), post to LinkedIn and everywhere else, and reach out for backlinks ("I built this page, do you want to link to it?").
- He says there is a lot of effort involved, so focus on the most important keywords one by one: do the maximum effort per keyword.
- For podcasts, he suggests making episode pages with transcripts and embedded tweets to rank for the content, then posting everywhere (Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, email).
- He offers free quick audits to people who reach out on Twitter, but notes the real cost of SEO is time and prioritization: "pick a few keywords, focus on those" instead of writing random blogs.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias recounts his path from teenage Chrome extensions and freelancing to co-founding Officient, an HR SaaS that reached 30 employees and about 20,000 customers. He explains why co-founders and written processes matter, then how to productize an SEO agency offer and win first clients with personalized outreach.

chunks.heading: Starting from a Chrome-extension tinkerer to a 30-person HR-software exit
chunks.text:
- Ilias began at about 13, learning graphic design and making Chrome extensions for wikiHow. He helped with around 20,000 articles. One extension showed a sun, cloud, rain or thunderbolt icon depending on how urgent the article-verification queue was.
- Building and hosting those extensions himself taught him domains and websites by around age 15. He later studied software at college, partly for fundamentals self-taught people miss ("how TCP works", servers, Linux, system architecture).
- He freelanced during college, going from logos to web design to front-end development after a UK ticketing client asked him to build his design in HTML. A friend's referral led to a Belgian startup, and then a co-founding role.
- He says curiosity drives it: you want to learn something, Google it, ship it, and the feedback and traffic (for example from a Reddit post) motivate you to do more.
- He thinks seeing other people build in public makes building feel possible, and that the indie-hacker community and Product Hunt make this much easier than it was 10-15 years ago.

chunks.heading: How officient was started: sell the solution before writing code
chunks.text:
- Officient was an HR platform that centralized employee data: assets (laptops, keyboards, monitors), documents (passports, IDs, pay slips), holidays and sick days. This information normally sits scattered across Excel and other systems.
- The idea came from a co-founder who was a sales director at a large Gent startup. He had met the problem at every company he sold to, and had already sold the solution to a customer before any code existed or the product was online.
- Development began around February, built straight to what customers had asked for, with no long development cycle. The first modules were things like asset planning.
- Growth: about 30 employees and around 20,000 B2B customers in three years.
- Ilias credits a strong salesperson on the founding team for how smoothly and quickly it grew.

chunks.heading: Why co-founders and a spread-out team beat going solo
chunks.text:
- Officient had four co-founders. The first employees came within about half a year (a marketing person and an extra developer), which led to quick growth.
- After a year, Ilias could take a two-week holiday or time off sick and come back to find the company had grown about 4%, added around 10 customers and shipped a big feature without him.
- He describes solo work as constant doubt: is this the right plan, how to split time between marketing, dev, sales, support, cold emails, referral campaigns and design. Without outsourcing, many things get done "a little bit but nothing that happens amazingly well".
- He notes that most big companies that look like one-person stories were co-founded by several people, and that finding co-founders makes things much smoother.
- Officient's founders split roles: two development co-founders, one salesperson, and a product/CEO/finance person. Others covered funding, accounting, hiring, security (important for HR data), product information and customer support.
- He admits he's currently more solo, with one co-founder, and that this is a struggle: the structure that a team enforced is now only in his head instead of written down.
- He respects the solo path (own your ideas, no one to answer to) and notes that Danny recently decided to stop going solo and hire.

chunks.heading: Running an async, documented company
chunks.text:
- Officient's Notion was about 200-500 pages, covering HR processes, product processes and ways of working, including what makes a good pull request and good code (for example, return early instead of if/else).
- When someone made a mistake in a PR, a reviewer would link the relevant Notion page in Slack or as a PR comment, so the team learned from the documentation.
- The company was split into four teams (development, customer success, product, sales). Each had its own documentation and a responsible person at the top who set the rules for that area.
- They were pretty async. No meetings without an agenda or plan.
- Slack conventions: emojis to claim and finish tasks (an eye emoji for "I saw it", a checkbox for done), a weekly to-do list in Slack, and Jira (today he'd use Linear) to track work.
- No standups ever. In the early years you just posted the PR link in Slack and @-mentioned the reviewer. Later (around year three) they added a dev/progress channel where people wrote what they were working on that week.
- Sales and customer success ran through a defined flow: inbound call, sign-up as a lead, a salesperson calls, then onboarding (visit the office or online) and customer support.

chunks.heading: Productize an SEO and marketing service
chunks.text:
- Ilias learned marketing in officient's second year, when he left the dev team for a while. He learned landing pages, search, Ahrefs and Semrush, optimized ads, and studied AdWords and Facebook ads.
- He believes technical people have an advantage in marketing, because it's full of technical work: Facebook pixels, conversion tracking, retargeting funnels, Zapier flows into email sequences, keyword research and backlinks, or a Next.js blog instead of just WordPress.
- His advice for launching a service like his agency: have a strict, clear offer for a set price. Example: for $1,000 per month, 3-5 blog posts a month, on-page SEO (titles, descriptions, image alt tags, internal links), then off-page link building, and improved Google Business Profile and Google Maps presence.
- Without a defined structure, work becomes random, such as a few blog posts here and there. The client then asks "what are you actually doing for us?" and leaves because they don't see an outcome.
- Spell out the expected outcome: for example 60 quality posts over a year, 5-10 links per month, a weekly or monthly strategy check, and a target such as being top 10 for a keyword. Then each month sells the next step ("five more posts, ten more links").
- Make the onboarding and expected result clear so the client can say why they're paying you.

chunks.heading: Getting the first clients
chunks.text:
- He says to pick one acquisition method that works for you.
- Step one: ask people you already know whether they need the service (a hot email or call), and ask for referrals.
- Post a lot of free, useful content on Twitter, such as how to find keywords or a secret way to find backlinks, so people see you as an expert.
- Cold email works if it's very specific to a niche. At officient, which targeted HR companies and startups with roughly 10-50 employees, they found a list in the local area and sent a personalized video, with the prospect's name on the thumbnail, attached to the email.
- Automation idea for an SEO agency: find a list of websites in a niche, run them through Hunter for emails and names, and use a screenshot API to capture each site. Then email a screenshot of their site, three keywords they currently rank for, and how you could improve those rankings. He says that beats a generic "we offer marketing services" email, since prospects get around 50 of those per month.
- He mentions Lemlist as a tool that can personalize emails with custom text and images.

chunks.heading: Plan, write down processes and set expected outcomes
chunks.text:
- His main advice is to brain-dump everything onto one page: how you get customers, onboarding, the emails you send, the benefit you provide, future plans, growth targets for the year and coming months, how revenue turns into hires. Then structure and systemize it over time.
- He says this gives much better results than "messing around trying things in the arena", and compares it to programming before programming: you spell out the algorithm in words or flowcharts, and then it's easy to automate.
- At officient, every experiment started with an expected outcome. For example, if they added another email to a sequence, they checked whether it actually improved anything. Without an expected result written beforehand, you can't know whether you succeeded.
- Recommended books: Alex Hormozi's "$100M Offers" and "$100M Leads" for building a good offer and getting leads to it, and "The E-Myth" for standard operating procedures.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias argues most SEO fails from dilution, not quality. His Blitz SEO method puts all effort on one money keyword and one page for 30 days, with a daily ritual of internal links, backlinks, on-page tweaks, resubmission and logging. He reports page one by day 17 and position #3 by day 30.

chunks.heading: Blitz SEO: the core idea and when it applies
chunks.text:
Ilias argues that most SEO fails because it is "spread too thin," not because it is bad. He calls the problem "death by dilution": publishing blog posts, building links and updating metadata without anything moving. His company was stuck at position #11 for a mission-critical keyword while competitors with worse products outranked it, and time was going to keywords that would not produce revenue.

- Blitz SEO is a short, aggressive sprint that puts every resource on ranking one high-value page for one money keyword (1-3 max).
- It is "not about scale" or content volume. It is about "focus, speed, and pressure."
- He frames it as a growth-hacking "SEO war room": pick the keyword, identify the target page, then deploy daily optimizations, backlinks, internal links and social signals until the page moves onto page one.
- He rejects the usual advice (6-12 months, 40 blog posts, "SEO is a marathon") for cases where you do not have time for a marathon, such as being on page two for a keyword that matters.
- Mindset: "choosing to win one battle instead of fighting ten at once."

chunks.heading: Business logic: why only a few pages matter
chunks.text:
Ilias's view is that SEO exists to make repeated, recurring revenue for a business, not to rank everywhere.

- "You do not need hundreds of pages that rank past position 10. You just need 3 keywords or pages to rank in the top 3 to make a business."
- Good fit for the skill version of the playbook: stuck on page 2 for a keyword that actually matters, launching something new that needs one page to win fast, or weaker competitors outranking you.
- Poor fit (per the skill): brand-new domains with zero authority, or keywords with no revenue attached.
- A page already sitting at roughly position 5-20 is the ideal target, since it is indexed and only needs pressure.

chunks.heading: Step 1: Pick one money keyword
chunks.text:
- Choose a high-intent, high-volume keyword tied to the core offering. Not a blog-post keyword and not a long-tail.
- Test: "Your Blitz target should be something that hurts to lose."
- Check the SERP. If competitors with weaker products outrank you, that is the target.
- Ilias researched the keyword in LinkDR, his own backlink and SEO tool.
- Limit to 1 keyword, 3 absolute max. "Saying no to everything else is the strategy."
- Ask whether ranking top 3 would directly produce signups or sales.

chunks.heading: Step 2: Rewrite one page to own the keyword
chunks.text:
Ilias rewrote and optimized a single landing page, then made it "the hero of our domain."

- Tight H1 containing the keyword.
- Keyword in the title tag, URL and meta description.
- LSI/related phrases in subheads.
- Fast load speed and mobile optimization.
- Visual trust: screenshots, logos, charts (the skill adds testimonials).
- Make it the hero of the domain: link to it from the homepage and main nav where possible.

chunks.heading: Step 3: The 30-day daily optimization ritual
chunks.text:
For 30 days straight, every day:

- Add internal links from older blog posts to the target page.
- Build 3-5 new backlinks to the page using LinkDR.
- Make one on-page tweak based on competitor SERP analysis.
- Re-submit the page in Google Search Console (and check Search Console every 24 hours).
- Share the page contextually on Reddit, Quora and X.
- Log every change and the daily rank position.

He stresses not overthinking any single change: "We did not overthink. We iterated fast." The skill's tracking log format is date, change made, position, notes. The skill sets a benchmark of page-one movement around day 14-20 if the pressure holds.

chunks.heading: Results from the original sprint
chunks.text:
- Started at position #11 (page 2) for a mission-critical keyword.
- Cracked page one by day 17 and hit position #3 by day 30.
- Organic traffic to the page up 720%.
- Click-through rate 2.8x higher.
- Leads were "qualified. Focused. Converting."
- The bigger win, in his words: "We stopped wasting time. We stopped ranking for useless terms. We focused like hell."

chunks.heading: Packaging and tools
chunks.text:
- Ilias turned the sprint into an installable agent skill, `blitz-seo`, for Cursor or Claude Code (`npx skills add Illyism/seo-skills --skill blitz-seo`). It reads project context if present and outputs a target keyword with reasoning, an on-page rewrite checklist, a 30-day calendar, a tracking log and benchmarks.
- A free Notion tracker template accompanies the essay.
- Tools mentioned: LinkDR (backlinks and keyword research), Google Search Console, MagicSpace SEO (his agency, which runs Blitz SEO for others).
- Companion playbook for conversion copy on the winning page: Blitz Copy (blitz-copy skill).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism split $1,500 across Google Ads, Meta Ads and SEO content for GenPPT and tracked it for 12 months. Ads produced a handful of conversions and stopped the day spend stopped. $500 of content compounded into 100,000+ visitors, with one post driving most of the traffic.

chunks.heading: The $1,500 test: SEO vs Google Ads vs Meta Ads on GenPPT
chunks.text:
Ilias split $1,500 evenly ($500 each) across Google Ads, Meta Ads and SEO/content for GenPPT, an AI presentation generator, and tracked it for 12 months.
- **Google Ads:** targeted "ai presentation maker", "AI PPT generator" and related keywords. Result: 1 trial signup, about $500 per acquisition, zero traffic after stopping.
- **Meta Ads:** interest-based targeting (entrepreneurs, students, startup founders). Result: 2 purchases, about $250 per acquisition, roughly 2x return ("barely break-even"), zero traffic after stopping.
- **SEO/content:** 5-6 long-tail blog posts, 10-15 outreach backlinks, tool directory and listicle listings. Result after 12 months: 100,000+ visitors, 3%+ conversion rate, 5,000+ monthly organic visitors, 50x+ return on $500.
- His conclusion: "The math isn't even close. For sustainable SaaS growth, content wins."
- Paid total was $1,000 for 3 conversions (about $333 per conversion). He says the $500 of content is worth 5-figure value over the next 3 years.

chunks.heading: One post drove 70% of traffic: "Gen Alpha Slang"
chunks.text:
- One shareable, fun article, "Gen Alpha Slang: The Complete Guide", drove 70% of GenPPT's traffic. The audience (students, young professionals making presentations) matched the product's users.
- Results from that single post: 35,000+ visits in 12 months, 3,500+ visits per month now, 80+ ranking keywords, top 10 for "gen alpha slang" (20,000+ monthly searches).
- It cost about $100 to write. Getting 35,000 visitors through Google Ads at their CPC would have needed $10,000+.
- Caveat he acknowledges: viral posts like this bring traffic but not high-intent buyers.

chunks.heading: Why SEO compounds and ads are rented attention
chunks.text:
- Ads are linear: spend $500 for about 200 clicks a month, stop paying and traffic drops to zero. "You're renting attention."
- SEO compounds. His example trajectory for a post: month 1 about 100 visits, month 3 about 500, month 6 about 1,500, month 12 about 3,500+ per month.
- Site-wide traffic: about 500/day in Dec 2024, about 700/day in Jun 2025, about 2,000/day in Jan 2026.
- The $500 spent on content in early 2025 still produces traffic; the $1,000 on ads was gone when he stopped.
- Cost per visitor: about $0.003 for SEO vs $5+ for ads.
- Timeline: expect 4-6 months for meaningful traffic. Posts started ranking at 3 months and peaked around months 8-12.

chunks.heading: Backlinks as a multiplier
chunks.text:
- Content attracts backlinks that lift every page on the site, which ads cannot buy.
- In the last month GenPPT earned 40+ quality backlinks from DR 40-80 sites, including:
  - Chatbase Blog (DR 80): "ChatGPT Enterprise Alternatives" listicle
  - Tolt Blog (DR 65): founder mentioned GenPPT in an income report
  - VoiceNotes Blog (DR 53): "Meeting Summary Tools" roundup
  - Global Cybersecurity Network (DR 40): "Best AI Presentation Makers 2026"
  - StoryChief: tool directory listing, about 1,000 visitors a month alone
- Each backlink sends referral traffic, builds domain authority and improves rankings across the site.

chunks.heading: Traffic sources and AI search
chunks.text:
12-month visitors by source:
- Google organic: 50,000+
- Direct: 25,000+
- X/Twitter: 20,000+
- Bing: 8,000+
- DuckDuckGo: 4,000+
- ChatGPT referrals: 3,000+
- StoryChief: 1,000+
- TAAFT directory: 500+
- Perplexity: 200+

- Paid traffic was so small it didn't appear in the sources at all.
- In the last 30 days, ChatGPT sent 300+ visitors and Perplexity 200+. Ilias says AI assistants recommend GenPPT because it ranks well in traditional search and has quality content. He calls this a channel "that literally didn't exist 18 months ago" and says only content can tap it.
- To monitor brand visibility in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews he points to his own tool, AI SEO Tracker.

chunks.heading: When paid ads still make sense
chunks.text:
Ilias sees paid as useful for:
- Product launches that need immediate visibility
- Validating demand with a quick test before investing in SEO
- Retargeting visitors who didn't convert
- Competitive keywords where SEO would take years

For most SaaS companies as a primary growth channel, he says SEO wins long-term. Start SEO first if you have 6+ months of runway; the best strategy combines both, using PPC data to pick keywords and then building SEO content around them.

chunks.heading: What he'd do differently and the SEO starter playbook
chunks.text:
Regrets:
1. Start SEO earlier. They waited 6 months before investing seriously; starting sooner would have given about 2x the traffic.
2. Write more bottom-funnel content. Now adding "GenPPT vs Canva" (comparison), "How to make an AI presentation" (how-to) and "Best AI pitch deck generator" (listicle).
3. Build distribution first. "Content + distribution = unstoppable." X/Twitter posts drove 20,000+ visitors, and directories and listicles thousands more. "Don't just publish, promote."

Playbook:
1. Find one long-tail keyword with 1,000-10,000 monthly searches.
2. Write the best article on it (2,000+ words, actually useful).
3. Build 5-10 backlinks via guest posts, directories or outreach.
4. Wait 6 months.
5. Measure traffic value by comparing what the same visitors would cost in ads.

He also recommends indexing tools to get new pages crawled in minutes instead of weeks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias argues churn is a product-quality signal, not a funnel problem. He says to split churn into types, measure it honestly, get users to one real result fast, build honest cancellation flows, and price to attract customers with a real job to do.

chunks.heading: Churn is a segmentation problem before it is a tactics problem
chunks.text:
Ilias refuses to treat churn as one number ("Our churn is 8%. Cool. What kind?"). He splits it before fixing anything, because mixing causes leads to building the wrong fix.

- **Voluntary:** they chose to cancel.
- **Involuntary:** failed card or billing problem.
- **Bad-fit:** never matched the customer you serve.
- **Activation:** never reached a first meaningful result.
- **Value:** used it, understood it, still not enough value.
- **Success:** project ended or the job disappeared.

Matching fixes: if people can't connect Stripe, fix setup; if they don't want to pay, fix qualification; if the product is buggy, stop adding features and "fix the kitchen." Also segment by plan, acquisition channel, cohort and customer segment. 20% churn on impulse B2C users is a different problem from 20% on $500/month B2B accounts.

chunks.heading: Measure churn correctly or you celebrate nonsense
chunks.text:
He warns that "churn dashboards can lie in a very polite font." He cites a founder whose churn dropped only because trials stopped being counted as active; that is a measurement cleanup, not a product win.

Track separately:
- Logo churn (share of customers lost)
- Revenue churn
- Net revenue retention (expansion minus contraction and churn)
- Trial-to-paid dropoff (often confused with churn)
- Cohort retention
- Plan-level churn (cheap monthly plans behave differently from annual or team plans)

Don't mix free trials, failed payments, one-off users and serious customers in one spreadsheet. Churn is not always bad: the goal is to reduce "avoidable churn from customers you actually want."

chunks.heading: Fix the product before the funnel
chunks.text:
Ilias says the real churn fix is usually product quality, not a clever cancellation popup or retention newsletter ("if your product is leaky, newsletters are just scented candles on a house fire").

- People leave when felt cost (setup time, switching pain, bugs, confusion, dread of opening the app) exceeds value.
- The tempting move is adding more features, emails, discounts and AI. Churn often drops when you remove reasons for users to feel betrayed.
- Checklist: the core job works every time; first result is fast; users don't need support for basics; docs answer the top 20 confused-user questions; UI uses customers' words, not database words; bugs blocking value get fixed before new features ship.
- He points to Chatbase (a MagicSpace SEO client) and its founder Yasser's public focus on quality over "feature confetti," and its falling churn. The levers: fewer bugs, clearer setup, better docs, stronger activation, smarter pricing, human save calls for valuable accounts, cancellation feedback reaching product decisions, promises matching reality. "No magic sauce. Just fewer reasons to leave."
- For GenPPT, the retention question is whether a founder can paste rough notes and get a deck they'd actually send, not how many export formats exist.

chunks.heading: Onboarding: shorten time to value "until it feels almost rude"
chunks.text:
Onboarding is "not a museum tour." Get users to the first real outcome with minimal choices. Examples: first usable deck, first ranked SEO opportunity, first resolved support conversation, the "oh, that's why revenue moved" moment.

- Simple product: self-serve onboarding. High-ticket or complex: get people on a call, but the call should complete setup and remove blockers, not be "customer success theater."
- Suggested first 14 days:
  - Day 0: welcome email, one login link, one goal, one 5-minute setup path.
  - Day 1: help complete the core action.
  - Day 3: show one advanced use case based on what they did.
  - Day 5: plain reply-to email asking if they got the promised result.
  - Day 7: value recap of what they created, saved, launched or fixed.
  - Day 14: invite to upgrade, add a teammate, or book help if stalled.
- The sequence should be "a guided shove toward the thing they came for," not a feature drip.
- Define the one action that predicts retention, rewrite onboarding around it, and cut every step that doesn't help reach it.

chunks.heading: Watch behavior before cancellation day
chunks.text:
By the time someone clicks cancel they've usually been gone a while. Warning signs: setup never completed, a couple of logins then silence, only one feature used, repeated docs visits on one topic, frustrated tickets ("again," "still," "why," "broken"), usage drops after a failed export, integration or billing moment.

Blunt rules he suggests (no ML needed):
- No login for 3 days during trial: send a human-looking check-in.
- Zero projects created by day 2: trigger setup help.
- Same error twice: route to support before they ask.
- Billing page viewed three times: offer plan help or annual savings.
- Heavy usage but no upgrade: show ROI or the next limit.

Tools: Hotjar, Microsoft Clarity, PostHog. The aim is finding the moment the product made someone feel "dumb, blocked, or doubtful," like ten trial users stalling on the same "connect workspace" screen ("a tiny product crime scene").

chunks.heading: Stickiness without hostage-taking, and cancellation flows
chunks.text:
Bad sticky is a cancel process hidden behind phone calls. Good sticky is saved context that would hurt to lose because it's useful: history, automations, team workflows, integrations, trained preferences, recurring reports, shared libraries, benchmarks over time. If canceling changes nothing in the customer's week, churn stays high.

His cancellation flow:
1. User clicks cancel.
2. Ask the main reason with honest options.
3. If the reason is confusion, missing setup, bug or price, offer the matching path.
4. If they still want out, let them cancel.
5. Send a short win-back or feedback email based on the reason.

- Reasons to collect: too expensive, missing feature, confusing, bug/quality, switched to competitor, no longer needed, project ended, wanted free plan, other (with required comment).
- The comment matters more than the category: "too expensive because I only needed one deck" is a packaging signal (sell a one-off credit pack), not a reason to discount.
- Don't overreact to one angry note; do react when ten people say the same thing.
- Worst flows: instant cancel with zero learning, and dark-pattern mazes.

chunks.heading: Talk to customers, use community carefully, send value recaps
chunks.text:
- Lightweight customer contact: a monthly founder email asking "What almost made you cancel this month?", a Slack or Discord for power users only, monthly office hours, a 15-minute rescue call for high-intent accounts, a public changelog of fixes users asked for, a "Was this confusing?" prompt on docs and empty states.
- Support tickets are "churn research written by people who cared enough to complain." Close the loop by telling users when you fix what they reported.
- Community helps with examples, accountability, implementation help, benchmarks, templates and momentum. It is no substitute for clarity: "If users need a Discord to understand your app, your app is not community-led. It is confusing."
- Send value recaps instead of "we miss you" emails ("brand sadness in HTML"). Examples: 12 decks created, 6 hours of editing saved, 18 more keywords ranked, 320 support chats resolved, 43 trials generated. "People renew what they remember." Surface quiet background value or the customer only feels the invoice.

chunks.heading: Pricing as a bouncer, plus a 30-day cleanup plan
chunks.text:
**Pricing:** cheap plans attract experimenters. A $9 plan may bring volume and feedback but also users who judge you like a free Chrome extension. Higher prices attract people with a real problem, budget and urgency, but raise expectations (no B2B prices with toy onboarding). "Think of pricing like a bouncer, not just a cashier."

Pricing audit questions: which plan and which acquisition channel churn worst; which plan creates the most support tickets per dollar; which customers expand; who complains about price before seeing value. Sometimes the fix is removing the plan that invites the wrong customer, not discounting.

**30-day churn cleanup:**
- Week 1, measurement: separate trial dropoff from paid churn; split by plan, channel, segment; pull the last 50 cancellation comments and tag them (fit, activation, value, price, bug, support, project ended, other).
- Week 2, activation: define the retention-predicting action, rewrite onboarding around it, send a day-3 rescue email to users who haven't done it.
- Week 3, cancellation: add reasons, offer save paths only when they match, route high-value confused users to a call, let the rest cancel cleanly.
- Week 4: ship one concrete fix for the most repeated reason (a confusing empty state, broken export, missing template, bad integration error, hidden docs page, pricing surprise), then tell users.

Closing line: "Fix the bucket. Then go buy traffic."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism shares a live A/B test on GenPPT where a prominent Google Sign-In button in the hero plus a scroll-triggered sticky modal lifted trial starts from 7.48% to 15.5%. He backs it with six other case studies and a playbook for placement, fallbacks, measurement and controlled rollout.

chunks.heading: Why Google Sign-In lifts conversion and how it works
chunks.text:
- Ilias treats "Sign in with Google" as a conversion booster, not just a convenience. It is built on OAuth 2.0: the user clicks the button, approves access at Google, and Google returns a secure token (JWT). The backend verifies it and signs in or creates the user, receiving name, email and optionally a profile picture.
- His reasons it lifts conversion:
  - It removes friction: no new password or form.
  - It gives instant onboarding with a single click.
  - It builds trust through Google's familiar UI.
  - It yields verified, deliverable emails.
- Google One Tap overlays an account prompt directly on the site with no redirect.
- He cites Pinterest, Reddit and Zapier as seeing 20-126% conversion lifts from Google Sign-In or One Tap.

chunks.heading: GenPPT A/B test: +107% trial conversion
chunks.text:
- Ilias ran a live A/B test on GenPPT (his own product) to validate what other case studies showed.
- Control: the standard "Start Trial" flow with no social login. Trial conversion was 7.48%.
- Test variant: a Google Sign-In button in the hero section, plus a scroll-triggered sticky modal prompting login. Trial conversion was 15.5%, a 107% lift.
- Funnel tracked in PostHog: pageview, logged in, landing on `/app` (counted as trial start).
- Stack: PostHog for conversion tracking, React/Next.js for layout variants, and Cursor AI to ship the changes quickly.
- His takeaway: "prominently adding Google Sign-In more than doubled our trial conversion rate," with zero form friction and better visibility.
- He has a full video tutorial on his A/B testing process (Cursor AI, React, Next, PostHog, TypeScript).

chunks.heading: Other case studies he uses as proof
chunks.text:
- **Promptwatch:** a prominent "Join with Google" button in both navbar and hero, placed before the "Start 7-day trial" CTA, reportedly lifted sign-up conversion to 10.5%. Key value props and social proof sit above the fold.
- **KISSmetrics:** adding "Log in with Google" raised sign-up engagement from 11% to 59.7%, a 314% improvement. Takeaway: social login drives big gains when prominent and easy.
- **Reddit:**
  - Google button: +50-60% sign-ups (desktop and Android).
  - One Tap: +90% sign-ups (desktop).
  - Combined: about 185% total increase.
- **Iron Company (fitness equipment retailer):**
  - 8x more sign-ups after Google One Tap.
  - 70x more sign-ups via One Tap than via the old Google button.
  - 25x more new accounts than all other social logins combined.
  - 32% of orders came from One Tap users, with a 16% rise in total orders.
  - Signed-in purchase rate rose from 24% to 40%.
- **The News Minute (subscription publisher):**
  - 8x more sign-ups in 90 days.
  - Nearly 100% of new sign-ups now via One Tap.
  - +15% subscription revenue in 90 days.
  - Implemented in about a week via a third-party service.
- **Heap 2025 benchmark (79 SaaS sites):** adding one-click OAuth (usually Google) raised signup conversion by 8.2%. Extra form fields such as company name or phone reduced conversion. Companies using A/B testing tools nearly doubled signup rates.
- His broader point: removing registration friction compounds into purchases, subscriptions and revenue, not just sign-ups.

chunks.heading: How to implement it (his 2025 checklist)
chunks.text:
1. Make the button obvious: put it in the navbar, hero and any sign-up modals, on desktop and mobile. Enable One Tap for returning users or content gating.
2. Always offer alternatives: keep email/password and Apple ID visible, because hiding them can reduce total conversions.
3. Measure what matters:
   - Primary: completed, verified sign-ups divided by unique visitors.
   - Secondary: activation (first key action) and retention, since social logins boost sign-ups but not always long-term usage.
4. Be transparent and secure: show a clear consent notice ("We'll receive your name & email from Google..."), store OAuth tokens securely, and support account deletion (GDPR/CCPA).
5. Test with a controlled rollout: run a 2-week A/B test, 50% on the prominent Google CTA and 50% on the old flow (or Google hidden under "More options"). With low traffic, use sequential or Bayesian testing.

chunks.heading: SaaS benchmarks he cites for Google login
chunks.text:
| Funnel stage | Baseline | With Google login |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Landing-page sign-up rate | 2-5% | 6-15% |
| Activation (first action) | 25-40% of sign-ups | 30-50% (product fit matters more) |
| 30-day retention | 20-25% | 25-35% (if onboarding uses the richer profile data) |

chunks.heading: Which Google option to use
chunks.text:
- **Maximum lift, few compliance constraints:** use One Tap. It is a zero-click overlay that follows visitors across pages and catches them while they are still evaluating.
- **Already redesigned the hero, want a low-code test:** use an inline button in the hero and nav. It is easy to A/B and piggybacks on the existing CTA hierarchy.
- **Fintech/health-tech or explicit consent screens needed:** use a login-page option only. It keeps the main UI unchanged while still trimming friction for motivated users.

chunks.heading: Implementation tips
chunks.text:
- Show the Google button in both nav and hero for maximum visibility.
- Keep an email fallback; hiding it can hurt conversions if Google is blocked.
- Track each step: page view, button click, credential issued, onboarding.
- Respect One Tap cooldowns; over-prompting makes it disappear.
- Share before/after sign-up charts to prove the impact.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism lays out a blueprint for low-ARPA SaaS retention: show value fast, price for commitment with annual plans and clear tiers, embed the product in workflows through integrations and automation, catch churn early, and bill ethically. It includes churn benchmarks by price tier and a testing roadmap.

chunks.heading: Low-cost SaaS stickiness: what it is and how Ilias measures it
chunks.text:
Ilias defines a "Sticky SaaS" as a product so embedded in a user's workflow, or delivering such consistent background value, that canceling feels like a downgrade. He focuses on the $5-$50/month range, where users are price-sensitive and switching costs are low, so value must be obvious immediately and delivered consistently.

**Metrics he uses**
- DAU/MAU (stickiness score) = Daily Active Users / Monthly Active Users x 100. He says average rates run 13-20% and a good target is 20-30%.
- For tools used less often (analytics checked weekly, SEO audits a few days a month), he suggests WAU/MAU instead, and says "active use" must be defined per tool.
- LTV = (ARPA x Gross Margin %) / Customer Churn Rate. A healthy LTV:CAC is at least 3:1. With low ARPA, retention is what drives LTV.
- Other engagement metrics: feature adoption rate, session duration, and "Lness" (e.g. L4+/7 = at least four visits a week).
- He notes high stickiness is a leading indicator of price insensitivity: a 5-10% hike on a $10 or $20 plan barely matters to users who depend on the tool.

chunks.heading: Pricing perception in the $5-$50 range
chunks.text:
- Price signals value. A low price can feel expensive if the value is unclear, and a price that is "too cheap" can signal low quality, which is especially suspicious for SEO or analytics tools (doubts about data accuracy, support, long-term viability).
- Value drivers: solving a well-defined pain point, saving time or money, offering insights free alternatives lack, and low friction.
- He calls the "value gap" (expected vs actual value) a primary churn driver.
- Use loss aversion in messaging: highlight the "cost of inaction" of not using the tool, not just features.

**Pricing models for low-cost SaaS**
- Freemium: low acquisition cost but typical conversion is 1-10%. Canva converts about 6%.
- Tiered: his default recommendation for SEO, content and analytics tools in this range, with clear value metrics and upgrade paths. Too many tiers cause decision paralysis.
- Usage-based: feels fair but can cause billing anxiety unless there are caps and alerts.
- Flat-rate: simple but inflexible. Hybrid: e.g. $10/month core analytics + $5 per premium report pack.

**Psychological tactics**
- Anchoring: show "Agency $99" next to "Pro $29" and "Starter $9" so $29 looks reasonable.
- Decoy: Plan A $10 (5 reports), Plan B $18 (7 reports), Plan C $20 (20 reports plus advanced analytics) makes C the obvious pick.
- Charm pricing: $4.99, $19.99, $49.99.
- Goldilocks: customers often pick the middle of three tiers (e.g. Solo, Growth, Team), so make the middle the best value.

chunks.heading: Churn benchmarks for low-ARPA SaaS
chunks.text:
He treats churn as structurally higher at low prices, leaving less room for error.
- General SaaS median monthly churn is about 3.5% ("good" is under 3%, ideally under 2%).
- ARPA under $25/month: median 6.1% (top decile 2.5%, top quartile 4.0%, bottom quartile 9.3%), per ProfitWell/Paddle.
- ARPA $25-$50/month: median 4.2% (top decile 1.7%, top quartile 2.8%, bottom quartile 7.4%), per ChartMogul. He flags that other research puts this bracket at 8.7%.
- ARPA $50-$99/month: also about 4.2% in the ChartMogul $25-$100 band.
- 20-40% of churn can be involuntary (payment failures).

chunks.heading: Annual plans, price increases and onboarding
chunks.text:
**Annual vs monthly**
- Offer annual plans with a 10-20% discount or 1-2 months free. He says this cuts churn, improves cash flow and raises LTV.
- Sweeteners beyond discount: annual-only features, higher usage limits, priority support, special onboarding.
- Sunk-cost psychology makes annual subscribers work harder to extract value. Nudge toward annual after users have seen initial value, often in the second month.

**Price increases**
- 5-10% increases framed around added value usually have minimal churn impact on a sticky product.
- Give 30-90 days notice and consider grandfathering loyal customers.

**Low-touch onboarding**
- At this price, users judge value in the first session, so engineer the "aha" moment fast. For an SEO tool: a rapid site scan that surfaces 1-2 critical errors.
- Tactics: minimal sign-up and social logins, clear welcome message, interactive walkthroughs, checklists and progress bars, role-based personalization, self-service docs. "Low-touch" does not mean "no-touch": add chatbots or triggered emails to unblock users.
- He cites that 63% of customers say onboarding quality is key to subscribing, and that good onboarding can raise retention by up to 50%.

**Email triggers**
- Welcome email immediately (open rates around 86%).
- Product tour unfinished: follow up at 24-48 hours.
- Key activation event missed: nudge about 3 days after sign-up.
- First quick win: congratulatory email right away.
- Trial ending: reminders at 7, 3 and 1 day before.
- Inactivity: re-engagement at 7-14 days.

chunks.heading: Product levers that create stickiness
chunks.text:
- Integrations (Google Analytics, Search Console, WordPress publish, Google Sheets export) embed the tool in workflows and raise switching costs.
- Automation of recurring work: weekly rank reports, scheduled reports, error alerts.
- "Set-and-forget" monitoring that gives background value with little active use: continuous broken-link checks, competitor keyword monitoring, brand mention tracking.
- Customizable, shareable reporting (white-label reports as a premium feature, shareable dashboard links).
- Actionable dashboards that become the go-to place for specific data.
- Key point: for SEO, content and analytics tools, "stickiness is often about indispensable outputs (e.g., a thorough monthly SEO audit) or automated processes, not just daily logins."

**Demonstrating value continuously**
- Automated progress reports such as "You've saved X hours this month", and personalized tips based on usage.
- Case studies and regular product update communications.
- Grammarly's weekly stats email is his example.

**Moats**
- Community (forums, social groups), loyalty and referral programs (referred customers often have higher LTV), and micro-upgrades or add-ons that let users unlock small features without a full plan jump.

chunks.heading: Churn prevention and cancellation handling
chunks.text:
**Why low-cost users cancel**
- Perceived lack of ongoing value, the "forgotten subscription," easy switching, budget limits, and "passive churn" (they neither dislike nor need it enough).
- Learn why through exit surveys, interviews and support tickets. He cites Canva's cancellation flow as a model.

**Early warning signals**
- Falling login frequency, reduced use of key features, billing issues, unresolved complaints. Trigger automated outreach with help or resources.

**Involuntary churn**
- Automated dunning is "a necessity, not a luxury" at low ARPA because manual follow-up costs too much.
- Components: reminders before payment or card expiry, smart retry logic, clear failed-payment messages, easy payment update, account updater services.

**Graceful offboarding**
- Easy cancellation (1-2 clicks, no guilt trips) that reminds users of value and data they will lose and offers pause or downgrade.
- Exit survey, then win-back campaigns (a discount if price was the issue, a feature announcement if one was missing).

chunks.heading: Ethical billing and testing priorities
chunks.text:
**Ethical billing practices**
- Email paying users inactive for 30-60 days (checklist mentions 30/60/90) with a re-engagement tip, a pause offer and an easy cancel link.
- Offer a 1, 3 or 6-month pause, and a free or low-cost "data hold" or hibernation tier for long-inactive accounts.
- Send annual renewal reminders 30 and 7 days before charging, with amount and date.
- Clear pricing pages with no hidden fees, plain data-retention policies, and no dark patterns. He says genuine value is "the only sustainable path to stickiness," and that proactively addressing inactive subscriptions builds trust.

**Pitfalls**
- An overly generous free tier that cannibalizes paid conversions, complex pricing, ineffective onboarding, ignoring feedback, no proactive value demonstration, hard cancellation, pricing too low, and "value obscurity" (valuable product, but users never discover it).

**What to test first**
- For low-touch SaaS he says A/B testing the automated journey has the highest ROI: pricing page (price points, tiers, tactics, annual incentives), onboarding flow, email nurture sequences, in-app upsell nudges, and the cancellation flow (retention offers, exit survey questions).
- Case-study pattern across Canva, Grammarly, Notion, Zapier, Ahrefs and Semrush, Mailchimp and HubSpot: "land and expand," with compelling free or low-cost core utility first, then upgrades as users come to rely on it.

His closing principle: enduring stickiness comes from delivering such compelling value that the product becomes "an indispensable, yet almost invisible, part of your user's success."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism lays out Blitz Copy, a copywriting framework built on the claim that emotion, not explanation, sells. It uses an identity trigger, emotional hook, mini cliffhanger and specific outcome, backed by a list of psychological triggers and deep audience empathy, with before/after rewrites of his own products' headlines.

chunks.heading: Blitz Copy is built on emotion, not explanation
chunks.text:
- Ilias created "Blitz Copy" as a copywriting method for landing pages, emails, LinkedIn posts, cold emails, tweets, YouTube intros, TikToks and SEO titles.
- His core claim: "People don't buy what they understand. They buy what excites them."
- He argues that explanation doesn't sell, and that emotion does. Copy should interrupt, ignite and provoke within seconds, because people face infinite scroll and endless options.
- The target reaction is: "Wait. That's me. I need this. Why haven't I seen this before?"
- The goal is a dopamine-driven "YES! Aha! Wow! I need this!" feeling that drives action right now (click, visit, share, buy).
- He describes it as "chemical warfare for conversions" and wants it to feel almost "illegal" in its effectiveness.

chunks.heading: The four parts of a Blitz headline and the four-step sequence
chunks.text:
Blitz Copy uses four ingredients: dopamine triggers (tension, curiosity, instant relief), identity spikes (readers feel "that's me"), pattern interrupts (stop the scroll cold) and emotional payoffs (drive action immediately). It follows a fixed sequence:

1. **Identity Trigger.** Make them feel instantly recognized. Example: "You're not disorganized. You're drowning in 42 browser tabs and guilt."
2. **Emotional Hook.** Surface a hidden frustration or desire. Example: "You've tried every productivity app. None of them stuck past day 3."
3. **Mini Cliffhanger.** Build tension to keep them reading. Example: "We tested this on 1,324 people. Here's what happened next..."
4. **Specific Outcome (the payoff).** Promise a concrete, desirable result. Example: "Reclaim 2 hours a day, without changing your habits."

chunks.heading: The neurochemical triggers
chunks.text:
Ilias lists the hidden levers that move people from "maybe" to "I need this now":
- **Curiosity:** "What am I missing?"
- **FOMO:** "Others are getting ahead, am I?"
- **Surprise:** "Wait, I didn't expect that!"
- **Relief:** "Finally, a solution that just works."
- **Urgency:** "If I don't act now, I'll lose out."
- **Validation:** "This is for people like me."
- **Desire to belong:** "I want to be part of this."
- **Power / advantage:** "I finally found an edge no one else knows."
- **Unique secret:** access to something exclusive or hidden.
- **Domination / exclusivity:** being among the first, or the only ones, to benefit.

chunks.heading: Know your target cold (the "empathy engine")
chunks.text:
- Blitz Copy only works if the writer understands the audience deeply: not just who they are, but what keeps them up at night and what they secretly want.
- Generic hype doesn't work. The copy should reflect the audience's real pains and desires in their own words and worldview, so it feels personal and urgent.
- Ilias turned this into an installable agent skill called `understand-customers`, which works in Cursor, Claude Code or any AI (`npx skills add Illyism/seo-skills --skill understand-customers`).
- The prompt he uses has four research blocks:
  - **Core identity and role:** who they really are (e.g. "ambitious SaaS founder", "overwhelmed marketing manager", "freelancer struggling to scale") and their primary goal related to the problem.
  - **Deepest pains (the "nightmare scenario"):** their most visceral nightmare, the exact words they use, their inner monologue, what they tried that failed and why, and the emotional consequences (feeling stuck, wasting money, falling behind competitors, imposter syndrome).
  - **Unspoken desires (the "magic wand" outcome):** the almost "too good to be true" outcome, what it means emotionally or for status (market leader, peace of mind, industry recognition, freedom), and what would feel like a "cheat code" or "unfair advantage".
  - **Language and worldview:** their jargon, tools and influencers, and a core belief about the problem that the product can affirm or satisfyingly challenge.
- Output of the prompt: initial Blitz Copy angles (identity triggers, emotional hooks, pattern interrupts, dopamine-driven payoffs).

chunks.heading: Before and after: GenPPT headline rewrite
chunks.text:
- **Before:** "AI Presentation Generator. Make presentations with AI. Save time. No experience required."
- **After:** "Still Wasting Hours on Slides? Let AI Build Your Deck in Seconds. Stop fighting templates and design blocks. GenPPT turns your ideas into viral-ready presentations, automatically. No design skills, no wasted time, just instant wow."
- The pattern: replace a feature label with a pain-first question (identity trigger plus emotional hook), then a concrete speed outcome.

chunks.heading: Before and after: LinkDR and AISEOTracker
chunks.text:
**LinkDR**
- **Before:** "AI Link Building Tool. Find backlinks for your website."
- **After:** "Still Paying $5K/Month for Shady Backlinks? LinkDR automates high-quality placements, for $100 each. No agencies. No retainers."
- The rewrite leads with a specific painful number ($5K/month), then contrasts it with a concrete price ($100 per placement) and removes the objections (agencies, retainers).

**AISEOTracker**
- **Before:** "Get AI to recommend your brand, not your competitors. Stop losing sales to AI recommendations. See exactly which brands AI mentions when users search your industry, and get actionable data to improve your position."
- **After:** "Invisible in AI Search? See Who's Winning, and Steal Their Rankings. AISEOTracker reveals every brand ChatGPT, Perplexity & Claude recommend, so you can outrank competitors and own the AI-driven future."
- The rewrite uses a pain question, names the specific AI products, and adds a "steal their rankings" advantage angle.

chunks.heading: Blitz Copy as the engine behind a campaign
chunks.text:
- Ilias treats Blitz Copy as "the emotional engine behind every Blitz campaign": it turns attention into action and powers the rush that makes people buy, share and join.
- He wants the final jolt ("I'm not 100% sure, but I need this") to be engineered, not accidental. It's the same dopamine-driven spark behind his Blitz SEO approach (a focused 30-day sprint to rank one high-value page for one money keyword).
- His stance: "We don't write to impress. We write to convert. To provoke. To dominate attention."
- His summary: "Be first. Be loud. Be unignorable."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism breaks down 57 screenshots of AutoDS's funnel (homepage, pricing, blog, mobile) and distills the conversion tactics: specific timeframes, dual CTAs, third-party proof, value stacking, platform-based pricing, and content built to convert. The core lesson is that every page serves one role in a single journey toward paid customers.

chunks.heading: Ilias's CRO teardown method: study the whole funnel, page by page
chunks.text:
- Ilias spent "40+ hours" capturing and analyzing 57 screenshots of AutoDS's funnel (homepage, pricing, integrations, blog, mobile, login). AutoDS serves 1.8M+ dropshippers and claims $1B+ in user earnings.
- His thesis: the lift comes from optimizing the entire user journey, not isolated elements. Each page has one job, and all of them build toward converting visitors into paying customers through trust-building and value demonstration.
- Page roles he identifies: the homepage builds awareness, features create desire, pricing enables comparison, content builds authority, mobile ensures accessibility.
- His advice: audit your own site page by page, map each page's role in the funnel, and optimize accordingly. "Every page has a purpose. Every element drives toward conversion."
- Generic CRO tactics fail unless you know your audience deeply. Before A/B testing headlines or CTAs, understand customer fears and desires so well that the copy "feels like mind-reading". He points to his Blitz Copy system for this.
- AutoDS example: their copy speaks to dropshippers' specific fears (product research taking forever, suppliers disappearing, shrinking margins) and desires (automated success, reliable income, business growth).

chunks.heading: Homepage hero: specific promises and dual CTAs
chunks.text:
- AutoDS says "2 minutes", not "quickly" or "fast". Ilias's reasoning: it is believable, users can picture investing 2 minutes, and it nudges immediate action. His action item: replace vague speed claims with specific timeframes.
- Dual CTAs serve different intents: "START DROPSHIPPING" (action-oriented, for ready users) and "LAUNCH YOUR STORE IN 2 MINUTES" (process-oriented, for those needing context). This reduces choice paralysis while keeping options open.
- On mobile the dual CTAs are kept and stacked vertically for thumb reach, with social proof, the AI badge and the trial offer still visible.
- A realistic Shopify mockup with actual products makes the AI store builder promise tangible.
- Show real data, not mockups: the order fulfillment view uses customer names, photos, status badges and tracking; product import shows real pricing ($5.45-9.48). Ilias says this proves active use by real businesses.
- A simple 3-step setup visual (numbered, connected steps, AI emphasis) makes a complex business look simple.
