- AutoDS sells its own print-on-demand merchandise through its platform ($18.50-20.50), which Ilias calls "the ultimate credibility move".

chunks.heading: Making AI feel controllable and tangible
chunks.text:
- AutoDS's AI description generator shows a real product interface and "high-converting" descriptions "instantly", tying AI to revenue rather than vague automation.
- Tone options (Professional, Funny, Creative, Balanced) make AI feel controllable and let users match brand personality, without overwhelming them with choices.
- The product import example offers "Make it funny" and a one-click promise, which shows AI isn't robotic and lowers perceived complexity.
- His action items: give users control over automated features, and demonstrate AI value with specific, relatable use cases.
- The triple-benefit framing is time ("seconds"), money (theme cost savings) and sales (revenue), with icons for scanning.
- Journey segmentation: a beginner path ($1,060 dashboard as an achievable goal, "all-in-one", setup assistance) and a grow-your-business path (order management, VIP support, automation, multiple marketplaces).

chunks.heading: Trust and social proof
chunks.text:
- Video testimonials feature recognizable entrepreneurs (e.g. AC Hampton) with specific achievements and 5-star ratings, not random users.
- Success stories span different achievement types, including a Forbes 30 Under 30 name and a specific revenue figure ($7,426.64), with real names and photos.
- Impact numbers are massive and specific: 1.8M+ dropshippers, $1B+ earned, 800M+ products. The "Our impact" framing takes credit for user success.
- Third-party ratings beat self-promotion: Shopify 4.7/5 and Trustpilot 4.9/5 with review counts (the login page cites 23,047 Trustpilot reviews). His action: feature external review platform scores.
- Social proof appears at signup too: the login page shows an AC Hampton quote, the Trustpilot score and a Google one-click login to cut friction.
- Support is humanized: a real agent photo ("Laura"), a "1h average" response time, a live chat preview and a 24/7 promise.
- The FAQ handles objections up front ("Can I cancel anytime?", beginner-friendly), and the footer repeats the trust badges.
- He recommends Senja (affiliate link) for collecting testimonials from 30+ platforms and displaying them as "Walls of Love". He notes he earns a commission.

chunks.heading: Pricing and value psychology
chunks.text:
- Value stacking: the $1 trial is presented with itemized benefits, each with a dollar value, including a $1,500 course, totaling $2,095. In his words it makes "$1 feel like theft". The AI Shopify store access is emphasized as FREE. His action: quantify and stack every trial benefit with dollar values.
- Pricing tiers highlight the middle tier with a pink border and a "MOST POPULAR" badge. Product limits are the differentiator (200, 500, 1K on Shopify). Annual savings are shown ("Save $84", "Save $120", "Save $204").
- The same $1 trial appears across all tiers and throughout the journey, which reduces friction.
- Pricing is dynamic by platform and billing frequency: Shopify annual runs $19.90-$49.90; TikTok monthly runs $26.90-$73.90 with different limits (200, 400, 800). His action: adjust pricing based on traffic source or user segment.
- Add-ons form a price ladder from $9.90 to $39.97, from automation up to mentorship (the most expensive), as revenue expansion.
- Educational value is quantified too: a $499 course and a $10k/month goal as aspiration.
- The final CTA sits on a dark background to cut distraction, with an "all-in-one tool" message and the same trial offer.

chunks.heading: Platform and supplier ecosystem as credibility
chunks.text:
- Platform pages show 8+ major marketplaces in an equal-weight logo grid with "applies to all sellers" messaging, which signals universal compatibility and lowers platform risk.
- Platform-specific landing pages (e.g. Facebook Marketplace) use that platform's colors and a "day-to-day" automation promise.
- The supplier map uses a hub-and-spoke visual: AutoDS in the center, major brands (Amazon, Walmart, Costco) around it, for trust transfer. Scale claims include 500M+ products and 100,000 sellers.
- A two-sided marketplace angle (browse products, become a supplier) uses revenue examples such as $1,899 and $4,679.
- A private suppliers dashboard shows transparent pricing and European local warehouses.
- Free tools act as lead magnets: the eBay calculator shows a concrete $41.60 profit example and an updated date. Resources are organized in three columns (Blog, Tools, Guides).

chunks.heading: Content and SEO: the blog as a conversion machine
chunks.text:
- Ahrefs data shows 54.2K monthly organic visitors, with posts ranking for high-intent keywords such as "amazon dropshipping" (7.8K monthly searches). Ilias credits systematic planning around high-intent keywords. His action: research the high-intent keywords your customers use.
- Strategy: solve problems before selling the solution. Educational content builds trust before the platform is introduced, and the product is positioned as the enabler.
- Content targeting: geographic (a European market piece with a "€565 billion by 2029" figure, EU warehouses and customs), niche long-tail (UK suppliers, TikTok, SHEIN, dogs, dresses, baby care) and seasonal (monthly product lists). Read times of 10-35 minutes are shown.
- His list of what makes a post convert:
  - Table of contents ("ON THIS PAGE").
  - Short paragraphs (2-3 sentences) for mobile.
  - Strategic bold on key numbers.
  - Key takeaways with checkmarks, placed before CTAs. He notes this also helps featured-snippet eligibility and reduces bounce.
  - Author bio with credibility signals such as "since 2017" (E-E-A-T).
  - Related-content links at the end to prevent exit.
- Persistent sidebar CTA: dark background, pink on navy contrast, a specific promise ("Find private suppliers in seconds"), benefit stacking and risk reversal ("14 day trial + cancel anytime"). Most sites bury CTAs at the bottom. His action: add persistent sidebar CTAs to all content pages.
- Email capture shows a visual value demo (a $10.21K dashboard mockup), a clear frequency ("Every two weeks") and specific copy ("Free dropshipping resources").
- A community CTA ("Join 10.5K ecom leaders") converts blog readers into the $1 trial.
- Blog videos use a professional presenter and a custom thumbnail with a "FAST SHIPPING" overlay.

chunks.heading: Ilias's own testing workflow and services
chunks.text:
- He shares a video of his A/B testing workflow using Cursor AI, React, Next.js, PostHog and TypeScript, covering the path from hypothesis to statistical significance.
- He offers content strategy through MagicSpace, claiming 20+ businesses grew organic traffic by 300%+ through content meant to convert rather than only rank.
- He positions this teardown itself (4,000+ words, 40+ hours) as proof of concept for authority-building, SEO content that converts.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias skips eval SaaS and uses one co-located eval.ts plus eval.md per feature that imports production code and runs real models. He warns that model self-scoring rewards quantity over quality, and uses evals to cut costs, such as an 80% image margin. He also covers hillclimbing without overfitting.

chunks.heading: Eval structure: one `eval.ts` per feature, co-located `eval.md`
chunks.text:
Ilias skips eval SaaS platforms, vector databases and scoring dashboards. He runs minimal evals across five products (AISEOTracker, LinkDR, GenPPT, headshot-generator.ai, MagicBuddy), covering voice TTS, image generation, presentation decks, long-form markdown and structured JSON.

- Each feature gets one `eval.ts` plus a co-located `eval.md` that diffs cleanly in git, so cost, speed and output changes are visible in pull requests.
- Rules he enforces:
  - Import the production function, prompt constants and Zod schemas directly. Never copy-paste prompts into the eval, because production evolves and the benchmark ends up testing obsolete behavior.
  - Run real API calls to record true latency, tokens and cost. Models can't predict their own streaming throughput.
  - One script, three modes: `bun eval.ts` runs the production model only, `--matrix` runs all candidates, `--models=a,b` runs a subset.
  - Log progress with ✅/❌ and write results to `eval.md`, not just stdout.
- He packaged this as an open-source skill: `npx skills add Illyism/dev-skills --skill eval`.
- His definition: an eval is "a unit test for non-deterministic AI outputs". It runs real inputs through production code and records latency, token usage, cost, schema validity and a surface for judging quality.

chunks.heading: Why he runs evals: regressions, prompt drift, margins, schema failures
chunks.text:
Ilias gives four reasons to eval every AI feature:

- **Silent model regressions:** providers change checkpoints and API behavior behind the scenes. An eval flags when a new model version breaks tool calling or JSON formatting.
- **Prompt drift:** fixing one edge case in a system message often breaks three others. A repeatable suite catches that.
- **Margins:** benchmarking candidates side by side on real production inputs lets you swap an expensive flagship for a lightweight model. He cites cutting API costs 75%+ this way.
- **Silent schema failures:** even strong reasoning models can fail structured JSON or loop on tool calls. Evals catch this before users see broken UI.

Without evals, he says, every prompt update, model upgrade or provider swap is a gamble.

chunks.heading: The self-score fallacy: never let models grade themselves
chunks.text:
Ilias's AISEOTracker competitor-suggestion benchmark (Framer alternatives) showed why auto-scoring lies.

- The summary counted candidates each model scored above 80/100. `gpt-5.6-luna` got 7/10 and `gemini-3.6-flash` got 4/10, so luna appeared to win.
- The raw outputs said otherwise. `gemini-3.6-flash` returned four precise direct competitors: Webflow, Wix, Squarespace, Elementor. `gpt-5.6-luna` returned those four plus bare "WordPress" (redundant with Elementor), Builder.io (a headless visual CMS, not a Framer replacement) and Bubble (a full-stack app builder, wrong category).
- Luna confidently scored its own weak suggestions highly, so the eval rewarded it for producing more items.

His conclusion: self-scoring "rewards quantity and confidence, not correctness".

Rules that follow:
- Summary tables hold machine metrics only: latency (ms), input/output tokens, total cost, schema pass/fail. Any item count is captioned as a count, never "Relevant" or "Quality".
- Quality is judged from raw outputs grouped verbatim under each test case, by a human or a strong independent judge model (`gpt-5.6-sol` or `claude-opus`). The judge must never be the generating model.
- A "✅ Passed" only means the API call succeeded and the JSON matched the Zod schema. It says nothing about accuracy or quality.

chunks.heading: Image evals: cutting headshot-generator.ai cost to lift margin to 80%
chunks.text:
On headshot-generator.ai users upload photos to generate style clones (subway film portraits, studio headshots, cinematic editorial). Failures either lose the scene grammar (tiles, lighting) or copy the reference subject's face. His `clone-eval.ts` runs style analysis, calls image generation, and passes the output image path to an independent visual judge model.

Benchmark on the `fuji-street` subway portrait case:

| Model | Latency | Result | Cost/image | Margin on $0.17 credit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gemini-3-pro-image-preview` (default) | ~30,000ms | PASS 7/10 | $0.134 | 20% |
| `gemini-3.1-flash-lite-image` | ~12,000ms | PASS 6/10 | $0.034 | 80% |

Flash Lite kept the hard scene grammar (white subway tile, orange stripe, red/white curb), scrubbed the subject's identity cleanly, ran 2.5x faster at a quarter of the cost. He says that one benchmark unlocked an 80% margin on standard credit packs.

He also admits the eval is weak: one case, one run, a 1-10 score, so 7 vs 6 is noise. To hillclimb it he'd want a judge that checks yes/no claims (white subway tile, orange stripe, a new face) and more cases, each run three times.

chunks.heading: Tool-calling evals: GenPPT's 18-slide deck benchmark
chunks.text:
GenPPT turns articles, documents or prompts into 18-slide decks. It's a multi-turn tool-calling task (`addSlides`, `setTheme`, `insertImages`), not a single prompt.

Results against the baseline `gpt-5.4-nano`:

| Model | Pass | Slides | Duration | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gpt-5.4-nano` | 100% | 18 | 94.3s | $0.0206 |
| `gpt-5.6-luna` | 92% | 18 | 72.1s | $0.1127 |
| `gpt-5.6-terra` | 91% | 18 | 52.3s | $0.1867 |
| `gpt-5.6-sol` | 90% | 18 | 115.3s | $0.5047 |
| `gemini-3.6-flash` | 21% | 0 | 55.3s | $0.2126 |

- `gemini-3.6-flash` looped 13 times on malformed `addSlides` arguments, produced 0 slides and still burned $0.21. Public leaderboards rated it a top fast reasoning model, but it choked on his tool schema.
- The lesson he draws: an eval stops you shipping a hyped model update that breaks your core workflow.
- He notes this eval has no headroom (nano already scores 100%), so it works as a cost eval, not something to hillclimb. Every pricier model scored lower and cost more.

chunks.heading: Voice evals on MagicBuddy and pitfalls in benchmark fairness
chunks.text:
MagicBuddy is a Telegram AI bot that sends voice notes via TTS providers like Grok Voice TTS and Gemini. His `voice.eval.ts` tests voices (`Sulafat`, `Eve`), languages (English, French, Spanish) and inline emotion tags. Example case: voice `Sulafat`, input "[whispers] Mon chéri... come closer. I have a secret.", instructions "Soft Parisian French accent. Slow, intimate, whispered delivery."

- It writes `.ogg` and `.mp3` files to `voice-samples/` plus an `eval.md` with audio duration, payload size and latency.
- Instead of prompting the bot on his phone, he runs `bun voice.eval.ts` and listens to the exported files.

Other benchmark traps he flags:
- **Control output constraints.** If one model emits 60 tokens and another 1,400, the second looks 20x slower and pricier, but you're measuring verbosity. Force identical `top_k`, character limits or array lengths.
- **Count real billed cost.** Reasoning models (Gemini Flash thinking, OpenAI o-series) burn hidden reasoning tokens. Pull total billed cost from response metadata, not visible output length.
- **Use absolute dollars.** "94x more expensive" sounds scary, but a backfill at $0.22 vs $20.70 may be trivial against the quality or speed gain. Judge against your margins.

chunks.heading: Hillclimbing without overfitting
chunks.text:
Ilias treats an eval as a place to stand and hillclimbing as the next step: read failures, change one thing, rerun, keep it only if the score rises. He draws on Anthropic's Lance Martin post (Sep 28, 2026), whose `claude-api` skill ships `/claude-api build-eval` and `/claude-api hillclimb`.

**Check the eval first.** Hillclimbing a bad eval optimizes the bad eval. Cases should mirror production (real inputs, bug reports, support tickets before synthetic ones), stronger models should score higher, the best model should land well below 100%, and the same setup should score about the same twice.

**The loop:**
1. Split cases into train and test, roughly two-thirds and one-third. The agent reads train failures only.
2. Measure noise: run the baseline three times per split. If identical runs swing 4 points, a 3-point gain means nothing.
3. One patch per round, aimed at a root cause. Rerun both splits.
4. Keep it only if train and test both improve. Train up with test flat is overfitting, so revert. Revert any regression too.
5. Log every round in `hillclimb.md` next to `eval.md` and ship the version with the best test score.

**Don't let it cheat.** Never paste failing cases or expected answers into the prompt. Don't add tools or rules that fix only one case. Keep the answer key out of the model's reach.

**When it stalls.** After two or three flat rounds, stop patching and group remaining failures by root cause. In Anthropic's example, `claude-api` went from 66% to 88% over 24+ rounds. At one stall the right docs were present but Claude kept writing older API shapes from training data, so they added a table mapping old forms to current ones. The last jump came in the round where they fixed a broken grader.

**Hillclimbing cost.** Anthropic's 44-ticket support benchmark started on Opus 4.8 at high effort, 4.6¢ per ticket. They trimmed the prompt, lowered effort, dropped to Sonnet 5, then added routing rules. On 14 held-out tickets the final setup scored 90.5% vs the baseline's 78.6%, at about a fifth of the cost.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism compares three of his own products and finds the tool that produces a finished artifact (GenPPT, ~$10k/mo) earns roughly 100x the pure detection tool (AI SEO Tracker, ~$200/mo). His principle, "outputmaxxing": AI made knowing free, so build tools that end with something that didn't exist before, and loop detection into production into verification.

chunks.heading: Outputs, not detection, are what people pay for
chunks.text:
- Ilias frames the rule as outputmaxxing: AI tools should ship outputs (artifacts), not reports or dashboards.
- His test, one question: "After someone uses your tool, what exists that didn't exist before?"
- If the answer is "a decision" or "awareness", he says you built a feature, and "an agent will eat it".
- If the answer is an artifact (an email sent, a post published, a link placed, a deck exported), people will pay, because the tool "collapsed the distance between knowing and done".
- His line: "People do not pay to know. They pay for the thing to exist."

chunks.heading: The portfolio comparison: same founder, 100x revenue gap
chunks.text:
Ilias treats his product portfolio as an accidental controlled experiment. Same founder, same distribution playbook, same market:

| Tool | What it does | Revenue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AI SEO Tracker | Detects: tracks AI search visibility | ~$200/mo |
| LinkDR | Detects and places links | Low five figures/mo |
| GenPPT | Produces: prompt to finished deck | ~$10,000/mo |

- AI SEO Tracker gives a list of where ChatGPT mentions you and where it doesn't, then the user has to go do the work elsewhere.
- LinkDR also finds link opportunities, but it gets the link placed. He says that is the entire difference.
- The one detection tool in his portfolio that makes real money is the one that ends with something that did not exist before.

chunks.heading: Why detection is becoming a commodity
chunks.text:
- Five years ago a good audit was worth $5,000 because finding problems was hard.
- Today any decent agent can crawl a site, pull rankings, diff against competitors and produce a better audit than most agencies for about $0.50 of tokens.
- Every insights dashboard, tracker and audit tool now competes with a ChatGPT prompt.
- The bottleneck moved "from knowing to shipping", and he says most tools in his industry still sell knowing.
- What is still expensive and manual in his growth playbooks:
  - The insertion email actually sent to the author ranking #7 for your money keyword.
  - The comment actually posted in the Reddit thread sitting at #3 on Google.
  - The listicle actually published on your own domain.
  - The creator outreach actually delivered to the YouTuber whose comparison video got 39k views.
  - The LinkedIn post, video script, image or deck, actually made.

chunks.heading: The $18,000 listicle: a blind spot in detection tooling
chunks.text:
- GenPPT's revenue dashboard showed a 16% drop. Ilias pulled 90 days of attribution by channel, page and plan tier, as he would for a MagicSpace SEO client.
- His best revenue month ever was mostly someone else's blog post: StoryChief's December listicle "Best AI Presentation Makers".
- It ranked on Google through January and February and sent about 18,000 visitors to GenPPT.
- Conversion rates: that referral traffic converted at 11.9%, versus 4.7% for Google organic and 1.9% for direct. Hundreds of paying customers came from one article on a domain he doesn't own.
- When the post slipped off page one, referrals decayed 95%, which explained most of the "revenue drop".
- Lesson he draws: he never saw it happen because the page wasn't his. His analytics, rank tracker and AI visibility tracker were all blind to the highest-converting asset in his funnel.
- He had even rewritten that StoryChief article earlier, yet had no output system to defend it, expand it, or turn the finding into the next 20 placements.
- Takeaway: third-party placements can be the best-converting asset in a funnel, so the answer is a system that produces more of them, not another dashboard.

chunks.heading: What he is rebuilding: every result gets an action
chunks.text:
Using LinkDR research on "best ai presentation maker" (the keyword the StoryChief listicle ranked for), he got 99 results, 58 contact emails auto-extracted, Reddit threads at position #3, YouTube reviews from three weeks earlier, and an AI Overview citing competitors. The old report-style page leaves the work unstarted. The new version attaches an action to each result:

- **Listicle:** "Write insertion email", with the contact attached and the pitch drafted, personalized to what their list already covers, including dead tools they still recommend.
- **Reddit thread:** "Write comment", in the voice of the subreddit, with honest trade-offs and the tool mentioned once, like a human would.
- **YouTube review:** creator outreach.
- **Rollout:** V1 generates the prompt and the user fires it with one click. V2 executes through MCP connectors: "agents with hands, not dashboards".

chunks.heading: Closing the loop across products
chunks.text:
Ilias plans a portfolio loop where detection feeds production and production feeds verification:

1. AI SEO Tracker detects you're missing from the eight listicles ChatGPT cites for your category.
2. LinkDR drafts and sends eight pitches with contacts already found.
3. The tracker verifies when the citation appears.

He says outputmaxxing is now the bar for everything he builds. His closing point: "The fix wasn't another dashboard. It was an output."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism turns the workflow he used for Peel UI into an open-source Cursor skill that generates a Chrome extension's icon, brand guide, promo tiles, benefit slides and listing copy. The core lessons: explore many icon concepts first, derive a brand guide from the winner, and use full-bleed promotional slides rather than popup screenshots.

chunks.heading: Three-phase workflow for Chrome extension store assets
chunks.text:
Ilias treats the Chrome Web Store listing as a conversion surface: you can ship clean code and still "lose the click if the store listing looks like an uncropped Figma export." He built **Peel UI** (copy any UI element as Tailwind or CSS) and needed the full asset set: icon, brand guide, promo tiles, five benefit slides, listing copy. He wrote a three-phase workflow, packaged it as an open-source Cursor skill, and stopped opening Figma for every extension.

- **Phase 1, concepts:** generate 4-6 unrelated icon directions as 1:1 JPGs, compare them in a `preview.html` grid, pick one.
- **Phase 2, brand guide:** generate a 16:9 brand guide from the winning icon (hex palette, typography direction, button mocks, 24px toolbar glyph, voice tags). Every later slide references it.
- **Phase 3, store:** promo tiles, five benefit slides, and `product-details.md` listing copy.
- Install: `npx skills add Illyism/dev-skills --skill extension-store-assets`.

chunks.heading: What Chrome requires and the common listing mistakes
chunks.text:
Asset sizes Ilias works to:

- Extension icon: 128×128 source
- Small promo tile: 440×280
- Marquee promo tile: 1400×560
- Screenshots: 1280×800, up to 5
- Short description: capped at 132 characters

He names three common mistakes:

- Popup screenshots (a valid upload, but a weak listing)
- Hiring a designer per extension (fine if you have the budget)
- Generic purple clipboard icons, "same as the other forty dev tools in the aisle"

His reading of Google's guidance: favor promotional slides that explain the job. Show what the extension does, not what the popup looks like "zoomed to 90%." Store slides are concept illustrations of benefits, never literal screenshots.

chunks.heading: Phase 1: explore icon directions before committing
chunks.text:
Ilias generates 4-6 unrelated visual worlds before choosing anything. For Peel UI he got a sticker peel, a UI magnet, and a wand inspector. The sticker peel revealing code underneath won.

- Each concept is a 1:1 JPG; a `preview.html` grid lets him compare them.
- After picking, he sets `iconFile` in `brand.config.json` and deletes the rest.
- Prompts should avoid literal clipboard or marquee dev-tool clichés unless requested; icons should be fun, beautiful, and readable at 16px.
- His rule: never skip this phase. "Just make the icon" locks you into the first mediocre direction.

chunks.heading: Phase 2: a brand guide that keeps every slide on palette
chunks.text:
After the icon is picked, he generates a 16:9 brand guide poster: hex palette, typography direction, button mocks, a 24px toolbar glyph, and voice tags.

- The generator sends the picked icon as `input_reference`, so phase 3 output stays consistent.
- Peel UI's brand: neon magenta #FF2D8A and electric cyan #00E5FF, with a sticker-peel metaphor.
- The brand prefix lives in `promptPrefix` in the config and is prepended to every prompt.

chunks.heading: Phase 3: promo tiles, benefit slides, and listing copy
chunks.text:
The store phase outputs promo small (440×280), marquee (1400×560), five 1280×800 benefit slides, and `product-details.md`.

Peel UI's five slides, one idea each:

1. Hero value prop
2. How it works (3 steps)
3. Before/after (screenshot vs code)
4. Export formats (Tailwind vs CSS)
5. Production-ready classes

What makes a slide look store-ready, per Ilias:

- Background hits all four edges (full bleed, no letterboxing)
- Multi-column layout filling the 16:9 frame, not a small centered icon on empty space
- Concrete UI widgets with sample data (class names, code snippets, button states), not abstract icon rows
- Contrasting card pairs (before vs after, format A vs format B)
- Decorative elements bleeding off the canvas, plus a footer bar or three-icon feature row to anchor it

His rule: "One slide, one idea." Hero, picker, and export in one 1280×800 image reads cramped.

chunks.heading: The generator and config
chunks.text:
One `brand.config.json` per extension holds `productName`, `outputDir`, `iconFile`, a `brand` block (`promptPrefix`, `paddingColor`, `paddingPercent`), `concepts`, `brandGuide`, and `store` (promo and screenshots prompts).

- The script `generate.ts` calls OpenRouter **gpt-image-2** and resizes with sharp.
- Screenshots default to `fit: cover` with `paddingPercent: 0`, so the background runs edge to edge. He only raises `paddingPercent` above zero if he wants letterboxing.
- Run with `bun ... generate.ts --config=<path> --phase=concepts | brand-guide | store`.
- To regenerate only the slides, add `--screenshots-only` to the store phase.
- Prompting it in Cursor: "Run extension-store-assets phase 1 for my new extension. Output to public/_static/my-extension/"

chunks.heading: Listing copy and review checklist
chunks.text:
The skill writes `store/product-details.md` from a template, with a short description of 132 characters or fewer plus the long listing. Peel UI's short description (108 characters):

"Peel any UI element off the web. Click to copy clean Tailwind v4 classes or plain CSS, no DevTools digging."

His notes from the Peel UI run:

1. Run phase 1 every time.
2. Ban browser frames in prompts, because "models default to fake Chrome windows."
3. Fill the frame with multi-column layouts and sample data.
4. One idea per slide.
5. Check the 440×280 promo at thumbnail size; if the wordmark disappears, rewrite the prompt.
6. Do a visual review before shipping.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism lays out the repeatable backlink outreach process his agency MagicSpace SEO uses: pick keywords and competitors, find prospects, send short personalized emails, follow up 2-3 times, and track results. A Xnapper case study (100 emails, 10 links) shows what the numbers look like when outreach is personalized and incentivized.

chunks.heading: How Ilias gets 15+ backlinks a month with outreach
chunks.text:
- Ilias treats backlinks as the core of SEO success. His agency, MagicSpace SEO, consistently lands 15+ new backlinks every month by combining manual outreach with AI tooling.
- He cites three reasons backlinks matter: they are a key ranking factor (Google reads them as a signal of authority and relevance), they drive targeted referral traffic, and they build brand awareness and credibility.
- He considers manual outreach one of the most effective link building methods because it lets you target highly relevant sites, build genuine relationships with site owners, and secure contextual editorial links, "the most valuable kind."

chunks.heading: The five-step outreach process
chunks.text:
1. **Keywords and competitors.** Decide which keywords to rank for and which pages to build links to. Ilias uses LinkDR to find keywords, then Ahrefs to find the top 10 competitors per keyword. He exports the keyword and competitor backlink lists to CSV and imports them into LinkDR.
2. **Start an email campaign in LinkDR.** It finds prospects, generates personalized emails and tracks results. It includes an email finder, so no manual contact hunting. It filters prospects by criteria such as excluding competitor sites, low-DA sites, and sites outside the niche.
3. **Craft the outreach email.** See the principles and template below.
4. **Follow up strategically.** See the sequence below.
5. **Track and analyze.** He tracks open rates, reply rates, links acquired and time to conversion, then uses the data to find the best-performing templates and tactics.

chunks.heading: Email principles and template
chunks.text:
His four principles:
- **Personalize:** use the recipient's name and reference something specific about their site.
- **Provide value:** explain how the content benefits them and their audience.
- **Keep it concise:** get to the point quickly.
- **Include a clear CTA:** make the next step easy.

His current template: subject "Quick question about [their site]". It opens with who he is (MagicSpace SEO) and a specific compliment on the recipient's article. It then pitches a guide on a related topic with three bullet points of what it covers. It closes by asking if they'd like to check it out and offering to "write a custom intro if you'd like to share it."

chunks.heading: Follow-up sequence
chunks.text:
- He sends 2-3 follow-ups spaced 5-7 days apart, each from a slightly different angle: a gentle reminder, an added value proposition, then a final "break up" email.
- Follow-up #1 (5 days later, "Re:" the original subject) restates the topic and highlights three key stats from the guide that fit the recipient's audience, then offers the full article.
- Follow-up #2 (7 days later, subject "One last thing re: [topic] resource") is a last attempt that says no worries if it's not a fit and he won't bother them again. It sweetens the offer with an exclusive quote for readers, a custom graphic to accompany the link, and sharing the post across social channels (10k+ followers).

chunks.heading: Scaling with AI and LinkDR
chunks.text:
- Manual outreach works but is time-consuming, so Ilias has started using AI tools to scale it. LinkDR is the one he highlights.
- LinkDR is a managed service covering most of link building: sourcing publishers that fit your page, outreach and agreeing terms, writing the article, and tracking placements and AI answers.
- Pricing is per placed link, based on the publisher's Domain Rating.

chunks.heading: Best practices
chunks.text:
- Focus on quality over quantity: a few relevant, high-quality links beat dozens of low-quality ones.
- Offer genuine value by thinking about how the other site and its audience benefit.
- Build relationships, not just links; aim for long-term partnerships over one-off swaps.
- Be persistent but respectful: follow up, but accept a no.
- Keep testing and optimizing based on results.

chunks.heading: Case study: 10 links for Xnapper in 30 days
chunks.text:
Xnapper is a screenshot tool for Mac. The goal was high-quality backlinks to boost its SEO.

**Strategy:**
- Identified 100 relevant tech bloggers, productivity experts and Mac software reviewers.
- Used a personalized template highlighting Xnapper's unique features.
- Offered a free pro license to sites that reviewed and linked to Xnapper.
- Ran a 2-email follow-up sequence.
- Managed outreach manually to keep quality high.

**Results:**
- 100 emails sent, 25 replies (25% reply rate), 10 links acquired (10% conversion).
- Average Domain Rating of acquired links was 50+.

**Takeaways:** personalization was crucial for busy tech bloggers; the free pro license was an effective incentive for reviews; follow-ups mattered, since 30% of links came after the initial email; and manual outreach allowed better customization per prospect.

chunks.heading: Other link building strategies
chunks.text:
Ilias lists these alongside outreach:
- **Industry directories and lists:** niche directories and curated resource lists (he points to a list of directories for submitting a tool).
- **Social media and communities:** joining relevant Facebook groups, subreddits and other communities to find site owners and influencers.
- **Guest posting:** builds contextual links, establishes authority and expands audience; he scales it with AI.
- **Broken link building:** find broken links on other sites and suggest your content as the replacement; Ahrefs helps find opportunities.
- **Resource page link building:** find resource pages in your industry and suggest your content.
- **Digital PR and newsjacking:** create newsworthy content or tie expertise to current events to win links from news sites and publications.
- **Skyscraper technique:** find popular content, make something better, then pitch the sites linking to the original (popularized by Brian Dean).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism lays out a SaaS SEO playbook: know your audience and set 3-5 KPIs, research keywords by intent, publish content for each funnel stage, earn quality backlinks, fix technical SEO, promote, then measure and iterate. He backs it with Zapier, Ahrefs and Intercom examples.

chunks.heading: Why SEO matters for SaaS startups
chunks.text:
Ilias treats SEO as the most cost-effective, compounding channel for early-stage SaaS. He gives five reasons to start early:
- **Cheap acquisition.** Compared to paid ads, SEO gives affordable, consistent traffic and leads over the long term, which matters for startups with small budgets.
- **Compounding growth.** Results build as authority and rankings accumulate. Within 6-12 months, SEO "can become your top channel for new signups."
- **Brand awareness and credibility.** Ranking at the top for relevant keywords makes the brand visible and positions it as a leader in its space.
- **Market insight.** Keyword research shows the problems customers are trying to solve and the solutions they search for, which feeds product development and marketing.
- **Boosts other marketing.** High-ranking SEO content can be repurposed for social, email and sales enablement.

chunks.heading: Start with audience and goals
chunks.text:
Ilias says every SEO strategy starts with a deep understanding of the target customer: ideal users, use cases, pain points, jobs to be done, and the solutions they search for.
- Build detailed buyer personas and map the customer journey and funnel, from problem awareness to solution research to vendor evaluation and selection.
- Use that map to decide which keywords to target and which content to create at each stage.
- The ultimate goal is usually revenue growth, but he tracks leading indicators too: organic traffic, keyword rankings, backlinks and signups.
- Pick 3-5 core metrics, set "aggressive but realistic" targets, and get stakeholder buy-in on them.

chunks.heading: Keyword research process
chunks.text:
Ilias's keyword research is a repeatable sequence:
1. Brainstorm an initial list around the product's core features and benefits, from the ideal customer's point of view ("What would you search for?").
2. Expand it with Ahrefs, SEMrush and Google Keyword Planner to get search volume and difficulty. Look for relevant keywords with high volume but low to medium competition.
3. Go after long-tail keywords tied to specific use cases, features and pain points, as well as "head" keywords that define the product category. Long-tail terms have lower volume individually, but "they can really add up."
4. Categorize keywords by intent (informational, navigational, commercial investigation, transactional) and match each to a funnel stage.
5. Do competitor research: analyze what top competitors target to find gaps. Ahrefs shows any site's top organic keywords.

chunks.heading: Content strategy and on-page SEO
chunks.text:
Ilias maps the keyword list to a content plan with these page types:
- **Product and feature pages** for the core product, key features and major use cases, optimized for the most important commercial keywords.
- **Blog posts and articles** for informational, top-of-funnel keywords, to attract the audience and build authority.
- **Guides and tutorials** for "commercial investigation" keywords, helping buyers understand how to solve their problem.
- **Case studies and proof** for bottom-of-funnel searches, showing customers and data-driven results.
- **Comparisons and reviews** targeting "[your product] vs [competitor]" and "[your product] reviews," written honestly and objectively.

Prioritize by keyword priority and keep a calendar. His cadence target is at least 1-2 new optimized pieces per week.

On-page checklist:
- Target keyword in the title, meta description, URL and H1.
- Short, descriptive URLs.
- Title tag and meta description written for clicks.
- Keyword and variations used naturally in the copy, with keyword-rich headings and subheadings.
- Descriptive image alt text.
- Internal links to relevant pages.
- Better page speed and mobile friendliness.
- Yoast SEO can help optimize individual pages, and existing content should get an SEO audit and updates.

chunks.heading: Link building for SaaS
chunks.text:
Ilias calls backlinks from authoritative sites a key ranking factor, "votes of confidence." Quality beats quantity: "A few high-value links will do more for your SEO than dozens of low-quality ones." He avoids spammy tactics that risk penalties.

Tactics he recommends:
- **Guest blogging** on respected publications in the space, with a natural link in the author bio or body.
- **Digital PR:** pitch newsworthy data and stories to journalists, who often link back to the source.
- **Broken link building:** find broken links on relevant sites and ask them to swap in a link to your content.
- **Partnerships and co-marketing:** co-branded content, research, tools or events, with both sides promoting and linking.
- **Original research and data:** studies, surveys and data reports "tend to earn a lot of natural backlinks."

chunks.heading: Technical SEO checklist
chunks.text:
Ilias lists these technical priorities for SaaS sites:
- **Site architecture:** a logical, flat structure where every important page is reachable within 3 clicks of the homepage.
- **Navigation and internal linking:** clear menus, keyword-rich anchor text, and a sitemap.
- **Duplicate content:** consolidate with 301 redirects, rel=canonical tags or parameter handling.
- **Site speed:** optimize code, use caching, compress images, use a CDN.
- **Mobile:** responsive design, since Google uses mobile-first indexing.
- **Structured data:** Schema markup to help engines understand content and enable rich snippets that improve click-through.
- **HTTPS:** SSL certificate and migration, a small ranking factor and important for security.

Audit with Google Search Console, Screaming Frog and DeepCrawl, and fix anything hindering indexation first.

chunks.heading: Promote content, then measure and iterate
chunks.text:
Ilias says optimized content is "only half the battle"; it also needs promotion to earn engagement, social signals and backlinks.
- Share across social channels, both organically and with paid promotion, and engage in communities such as Reddit, Quora and Facebook/LinkedIn groups.
- Build an email list and send new content to subscribers, encouraging shares, comments and links.
- Reach out directly to influencers and publications; a mention from a prominent figure can amplify reach.
- Repurpose content into videos, infographics and slide decks for additional channels.

Measurement loop:
- Track keywords, organic traffic growth, backlink profile and conversions in Google Analytics, Search Console and Ahrefs. On-page metrics to watch: bounce rate, time on page and conversions.
- Update, expand or repurpose top-performing content, and find related terms to rank for.
- Run regular technical audits and monitor speed, mobile friendliness and crawlability.
- Reinvest the extra revenue into more optimized content and more high-quality backlinks.
- He calls SEO "a long-term, iterative process," not an overnight result.

chunks.heading: Professional SEO audits
chunks.text:
Ilias recommends combining ongoing in-house SEO with periodic outside audits, which can save founders time and surface missed issues.
- He points to SEO Roast (seoroast.com), a service he is associated with, covering analysis of current performance, critical issues and hidden opportunities, actionable recommendations, and competitor insights.
- Pricing runs from $180 for a public video audit to $3,735 for a full-service SEO audit and strategy.

chunks.heading: SaaS SEO case studies
chunks.text:
Ilias uses three companies as proof that a comprehensive SEO strategy drives SaaS growth:
- **Zapier:** comprehensive guides and tutorials on automation and productivity, long-tail keywords for connecting different apps, a free tool that recommends Zaps based on your tech stack, and backlinks from Forbes and Entrepreneur. He cites an estimated 1.8M organic visits per month and rankings for over 400,000 keywords.
- **Ahrefs:** in-depth data-driven posts and guides, free tools (backlink checker, website authority checker), influencer roundups and interviews, and promotion to 200k+ email subscribers and social followers. He cites over 500k monthly organic visits and top-100 rankings for terms like "SEO" and "backlinks."
- **Intercom:** content for every funnel stage, with educational blog content for informational keywords, product pages, guides and case studies for commercial keywords, a large library of video and webinars, and guest posts and partnerships with SaaS blogs. He says organic traffic has grown steadily year over year and drives a significant share of new signups.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism documents a wave of parasite SEO attacks on high-authority .gov and .edu domains (Duke, Michigan.gov, ca.gov, Wayne State), where spam PDFs rank #1 almost instantly for lucrative keywords. He explains why domain authority bias makes this work and gives site owners concrete steps to detect and prevent compromise.

chunks.heading: Parasite SEO on high-authority domains: what Ilias observed (Sept 2025)
chunks.text:
Ilias documented what he calls "one of the most aggressive examples of Parasite SEO I've ever seen": attackers compromising `.gov` and `.edu` sites and publishing thousands of spam pages, mostly SEO-optimized PDFs, that rank almost instantly for illicit, high-volume keywords.

- One Canadian `.gov` domain went "0 → 8M organic traffic in 24 hours".
- Compromised subdomains he named: `covididr.duhs.duke.edu`, `mienviro.michigan.gov`, `meetings.ctc.ca.gov`, and `wayne.edu`.
- The pattern shows up across domains that share the same CMS or software, which he reads as a sign they are fully compromised.
- The spam is not gibberish. It is well-structured, looks like a legitimate article, and includes calls-to-action that funnel traffic to illicit sites.

chunks.heading: Scale of the traffic: numbers from specific domains
chunks.text:
- **Duke University (DR 94):** a subdomain's organic traffic spiked to over 21.8 million visitors. Ilias exported over 1,200 compromised PDFs to a public Google Sheet. Per-PDF traffic estimates range from thousands to hundreds of thousands of monthly visits, across keywords from adult content to gambling to illegal services.
- **Michigan.gov (DR 91):** a compromised PDF ranks #1 for "ai undresser", a keyword with 70,000+ monthly searches (90,500 volume and $2.48 CPC in his keyword tool).
- **ca.gov:** over 3,000 compromised pages ranking for spam keywords, an estimated 2.1 million monthly visits.
- **Wayne State (wayne.edu):** thousands of compromised pages driving large traffic for illicit keywords.
- Government domains were also ranking for NSFW AI bot searches, the same results his own NSFW AI chatbots guide competes in.

chunks.heading: Why it works: Google's authority bias
chunks.text:
- Ilias's core claim: "Google heavily weights domain authority." Spam placed on `michigan.gov` (DR 91) or `duke.edu` (DR 94) inherits instant trust and ranking power.
- The algorithm "can't distinguish between legitimate government content and spam when both exist on the same trusted domain."
- That is why attackers target `.gov` and `.edu`: they get instant #1 rankings that would take years to earn on a normal domain, for keywords with real commercial value.
- The upside of authority is also the risk. High authority makes a domain "a high-value target for attackers."

chunks.heading: How he says to defend a high-authority site
chunks.text:
Ilias frames this as brand protection, not just a technical issue. His steps for universities, agencies, and large corporations:

1. **Audit for vulnerabilities.** The most common vectors are outdated CMS versions, vulnerable plugins, and misconfigured file upload forms. He suggests automated scanning of code, dependencies, and infrastructure with a tool like Aikido, or an immediate thorough manual audit.
2. **Monitor Google Search Console.** Check the "Pages" report for URLs you don't recognize. A sudden spike in indexed pages is a major red flag. Ahrefs or SEMrush can also be used to watch traffic.
3. **Configure robots.txt properly.** Disallow crawling of sensitive directories and file types, for example `/admin/`, `/uploads/`, `*.pdf$`, `/temp/`, `/cache/`. He notes this "won't stop determined attackers," but it can keep search engines from indexing spam if it does get uploaded to those locations.

chunks.heading: Detecting this kind of attack from the outside
chunks.text:
- A Google `site:` search on a suspect subdomain is a quick way to see the extent of a compromise.
- Keyword and traffic tools (he uses his own LinkDR keyword tool) show whether an authority domain suddenly ranks for off-topic, high-volume terms.
- Exporting the top pages of a compromised subdomain into a spreadsheet exposes the pattern: many PDFs, thousands to hundreds of thousands of monthly visits each, and unrelated spam keywords.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Google penalizes bad content, not AI content. Ilias lays out a repeatable workflow: pick a query with real intent, outline by hand, draft section by section with AI, then inject experience, optimize on-page, fact-check and iterate. A full post fits in about 90 minutes.

chunks.heading: Search intent first, then a manual outline
chunks.text:
- Ilias says Google doesn't penalize "AI content", it penalizes bad content. A post that shows experience, satisfies intent and is useful can rank whatever tool drafted it.
- Topic selection: pull queries from Google Search Console (positions 3-20), Ahrefs or LinkDR's keyword analyzer. Check which formats already rank, which questions are answered and what gaps exist, then decide the unique experience or data he can add.
- The outline is written by hand ("non-negotiable"), before AI drafts anything: Problem → Promise → Proof → Process → FAQs → Next steps.
- In the outline he adds the entities and phrases readers expect to see, and marks where screenshots, charts or personal anecdotes will go.
- Prompt for finding gaps: "You are an editor. Given this query: 'write blog posts with AI', list subtopics, entities, and FAQs the top 10 pages cover." Then ask for 5 gaps he can fill from hands-on experience.
- If starting from zero, he suggests seeding supporting content so new posts have internal-link fuel. Outrank is the tool he names for this: 30 SEO-ready articles in month one (code ILLY for 10% off; affiliate link).

chunks.heading: Drafting with AI section by section
chunks.text:
- Work one section at a time, with prompts that are specific, short and scoped to the outline.
- Example prompt: "Write a 120-180 word section that explains why outlines matter for AI writing. Constraints: no fluff, simple language, include one actionable sentence. Target reader: solo founder. Tone: practical."
- Cap paragraph length and word count, ask for bullets, examples or mini checklists, regenerate until crisp, and delete clichés.

chunks.heading: Inject E-E-A-T, the part AI can't fake
chunks.text:
He says this "is where rankings are won". Add:
- Your own screenshots, results and failures.
- Primary sources, with outbound links where helpful.
- Author bio, byline, and clear contact/about pages.
- Internal links from older, relevant pages (seeded with Outrank posts if needed).
- Visual content such as memes from MagicMeme, for engagement and shareability.

chunks.heading: On-page SEO checklist
chunks.text:
- Unique title tag containing the target phrase naturally (here "write blog posts with AI").
- H1 aligned with the title; the first 100 words answer the query.
- Descriptive subheadings, short paragraphs, scannable bullets.
- One primary CTA plus relevant internal links.
- Compressed images with descriptive alt text.

chunks.heading: Fact-check and de-template before publishing
chunks.text:
- Verify every stat and claim and replace them with primary sources.
- Remove generic filler such as "leverage" and "unlock".
- Read the post aloud and cut 10-20% for clarity.
- Run a plagiarism check if needed.
- He calls AI drafts "starting points".

chunks.heading: Publish, then iterate; the 90-minute workflow
chunks.text:
- Publish, request indexing in Google Search Console, and iterate on impressions and queries over the next 2-4 weeks. Add one improvement per day: a stat, a screenshot, an FAQ.
- 90-minute workflow for one post:
  1. Pick keyword and outline (15 min)
  2. Draft sections with AI (25 min)
  3. Add proof such as screenshots and examples (20 min)
  4. Optimize on-page and links (15 min)
  5. Publish and request indexing (5 min)
- Length: as long as needed to satisfy intent. Many queries are solved in 800-1,500 words when the post is specific and visual.
- Disclosure: if AI meaningfully assisted, he says disclosing editorially is good practice and can build trust with technical audiences.
- His summary: "Writing blog posts with AI doesn't hurt SEO, publishing low-quality, unoriginal, unhelpful content does."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias argues ChatGPT won't kill SEO but is rewriting it: the goal moves from ranking on Google to being cited, summarized and spoken about by AI answer engines. He lays out four bets: track AI visibility, earn citations from quotable content, write for AI summarization, and control your narrative.

chunks.heading: ChatGPT will not replace SEO, but it is rewriting it
chunks.text:
- Ilias's short answer to "Will ChatGPT kill SEO?" is no, but it "is rewriting the rules." His view comes from running SEO sprints for SaaS, building LinkDR, and launching AISEOTracker to track how AI tools actually mention brands.
- ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Gemini do two things at once: they answer questions directly, and they choose which sources to cite and summarize. He calls that second part "the new SEO battleground."
- He frames the shift as SEO evolving into "AI visibility optimization," not dying. His line: "If ChatGPT doesn't mention you, it doesn't matter if you're #1 on Google."
- ChatGPT is replacing some parts of the search journey, not all of it.

chunks.heading: The goal moves from ranking to being cited and retold
chunks.text:
- The old goal was to rank #1 on Google for a keyword. The new goal is to be the brand AI chooses to talk about when users ask questions.
- Ilias calls this "narrative SEO." The new game has three parts:
  - Get cited by authoritative content.
  - Be summarized well by AI.
  - Shape the narrative AI creates about your niche.
- Old-school tactics like keyword stuffing and random backlinks "won't cut it." AI reads deeper and picks what feels trustworthy, useful, and common across sources.
- His reframe: stop asking "How do I rank on Google?" and ask "How do I get cited, summarized, and spoken about by AI?"
- He says this frontier is "wide open."

chunks.heading: How ChatGPT changes the funnel
chunks.text:
- People now ask ChatGPT instead of Googling. His examples:
  - "Best tools for content repurposing"
  - "How to use AI for customer support"
  - "What's the best GPT-powered chatbot?"
- These used to be Google queries. Now they go to ChatGPT, so a brand will not show up unless it is part of the answer.
- His summary: SEO is no longer just about being found, it is about "being remembered and re-told."

chunks.heading: Ilias's four-part playbook for AI visibility
chunks.text:
1. **Track your AI visibility.** He built AISEOTracker to scan ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews and show whether a brand gets mentioned.
2. **Earn citations from real content.** Not PBNs or spammy guest posts. Create assets worth quoting.
3. **Write with AI summarization in mind.** Use clear structure, entity names, and helpful formatting, because "AI needs signal."
4. **Control your narrative.** Define what you want AI to say about your brand, then seed that message across your content, blog, and partnerships.

chunks.heading: Tools and projects Ilias ties to this work
chunks.text:
- **AISEOTracker** (aiseotracker.com): checks whether ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot and Google's AI Overviews mention a brand. He offers a free try and describes it as monitoring weekly.
- **LinkDR**: a product he built and mentions as part of his SEO background.
- **MagicSpace SEO**: another current project, alongside GenPPT.
- He is an exited founder (Officient).

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism explains GEO as optimizing content to be cited by AI search engines, not just ranked. He covers the three engine types, the Princeton study's tactics, and his daily manual routine of finding AI-cited listicles and paying for placement.

chunks.heading: What GEO is and how it differs from SEO
chunks.text:
Ilias defines Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) as optimizing content to get cited by AI search engines such as ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude and Google AI Overviews.

- Traditional SEO optimizes for keyword-matching algorithms and ranking among 10 blue links, with backlinks as the main authority signal.
- GEO optimizes for AI language understanding and targets citations in AI-generated answers. AI engines cite roughly 3-5 sources per response, so the competition is for a handful of mentions.
- His framing: "Instead of fighting for search rankings, you now present information to be selected as a source with credibility."
- He argues that if content isn't optimized for this, you become invisible, because the AI writes one synthesized answer instead of listing links.
- He stresses that GEO builds on SEO and doesn't replace it.

chunks.heading: Why GEO matters for a business
chunks.text:
Ilias says ChatGPT alone drives traffic to over 100,000 websites monthly.

- Evidence he cites: Vercel gets 10% of new signups from ChatGPT citations, and companies report 30-40% visibility improvements with proper optimization.
- AI search sessions run about 6 minutes, versus quick bounces on traditional search.
- Purchases can happen inside the AI interface, for example Perplexity's "Buy with Pro" one-click purchase.
- He argues that being the top citation in a generative answer can beat ranking #1 in Google for credibility and conversion.

chunks.heading: The three types of generative engines and how to approach each
chunks.text:
Ilias splits generative engines into three types, each needing a different approach.

**Google AI Overviews**
- They rely on the same crawling and indexing infrastructure as regular search, so master traditional SEO first. If Google can't find and understand the content conventionally, the AI Overview can't access it either.
- Needs: clean title tags, meta descriptions and structured data; a clear H2/H3 hierarchy; 2-3 sentence concise answers to the query; bullets and numbered lists.

**AI search engines (ChatGPT, Perplexity)**
- They run real-time searches on Google or Bing, aggregate top-ranking pages, rewrite them into a conversational answer, and attribute sources.
- Strategy: keep strong traditional rankings in Google and Bing, use headers and bullets the AI can parse, put the direct answer or definition in the first 2-3 sentences, and bold key terms.
- His conclusion: AI systems cite content that ranks well in traditional search.

**Training-data models (Claude, Llama, DeepSeek)**
- These remember brands that appeared most often on trusted sites while being trained.
- Strategy: publish regularly on news sites, industry blogs and trusted platforms; get mentioned in forums, reviews, podcasts and social media; think in years, not months. "This is a marathon, not a sprint."

chunks.heading: What the Princeton study found
chunks.text:
Ilias leans on the first systematic GEO study from Princeton researchers: 10,000 queries across nine domains, testing nine optimization strategies. Some tactics delivered up to 40% improvement in visibility in AI responses.

Which strategy works depends on content type:
- Debate/opinion content: an authoritative tone increased visibility.
- Factual content: statistics and citations dominated.
- Historical content: quotations performed best.
- Business content: fluency optimization showed strong results.

His takeaway: one-size-fits-all doesn't work, so tailor the strategy to the content type.

chunks.heading: Seven GEO tactics ranked by impact
chunks.text:
Ilias ranks these by measured improvement:

1. **Add compelling statistics (39.5%).** Turn "Many marketers struggle with content creation" into "87% of marketers report struggling with content creation, according to recent industry surveys." Bold the numbers, name the source, refresh regularly. If none exist, create them through surveys or analysis of your own data.
2. **Integrate credible citations (40.4%).** Every major claim gets a source, for example Gartner predicting a 25% drop in traditional search volume by 2026. Mix primary and secondary sources, keep them recent, and use inline "(Source, Year)" style.
3. **Include strategic quotations (38.1%).** Interview experts or pull quotes from conferences and podcasts. Attribute every quote. "Original quotes > recycled quotes every time."
4. **Optimize for fluency (35.2%).** Paragraphs of 2-4 sentences, simple active voice, 3-5 bolded key phrases per section, a subheading every 150-200 words, roughly 8th-grade reading level.
5. **Add technical terms (32.7%).** Define terms on first use, use them consistently, and consider a glossary for complex topics.
6. **Write authoritatively (30.1%).** Use definitive statements, avoid "might," "maybe" and "possibly," take clear positions, and back claims with evidence.
7. **Simplify complex ideas (15-30%).** Use analogies, break processes into steps, create visual hierarchy, and summarize in bullets.

chunks.heading: His daily 10-minute GEO tracking and outreach routine
chunks.text:
Ilias says you don't need expensive tools to track GEO. His routine for StoryChief:

- Every morning he spends 10 minutes asking ChatGPT and Perplexity money queries such as "What are the best content marketing tools?"
- He keeps a list of money queries on his phone (for example "best content marketing tools," "content management platforms," "social media scheduling software") and rotates through variations daily.
- When he sees listicles being cited, like "15 Best Content Marketing Platforms in 2025," he visits the article, finds the author's email with LinkDR, and pitches them.
- His pitch: "I saw your article was cited by AI platforms. I'm the [role] of StoryChief. Would love to get included in your next update. Happy to offer $500 for the mention, set up our affiliate program for you, or do a guest post exchange."
- Outreach works because it leads with "your article is being cited by AI" and offers real value. One publisher replied with rates of $300 per post or $200 per link insertion, do-follow.
- When he finds weak listicles getting AI citations, he writes better ones and reaches out to the same sites that linked to the weak ones.
- His framing: "I'm not begging for links. I'm offering to pay for placement in content that AI already trusts."
- He recommends starting manually to understand what works, then using AISEOTRACKER to find opportunities at scale and monitor GEO performance.

chunks.heading: Next steps he recommends
chunks.text:
- Audit AI visibility with AISEOTRACKER.com.
- Start with statistics: add 3-5 data points to top pages this week.
- Track citation rates monthly.
- Stay consistent. He compares the moment to Google in 1998: "The websites that adapted fastest to Google in 1998 dominated for decades. The same opportunity exists today with AI search."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias recounts going remote at 18 with design and web dev skills, freelancing, then founding Officient and moving through Paris, the Canary Islands and Switzerland. He distills a survival checklist (steady cash flow, in-demand skills, insurance, adaptability) and a mindset built on balance, constant learning, networks and embracing change.

chunks.heading: Early life and the case for freelancing
chunks.text:
- Ilias started at 18, fresh out of a Belgian school, with graphic design and web dev skills. He found a typical 9-5 back home unappealing and went remote instead.
- He freelanced in graphic design and web development, which let him work from anywhere (cafes in Chiang Mai, coworking in Bali, a balcony in Barcelona).
- He frames the goal as "collecting experiences, not business cards", and says the lifestyle is great for meeting people, learning cultures and juggling time zones.

chunks.heading: From freelancing to founding Officient
chunks.text:
- Freelancing was fun, but he wanted to "run my own online show", so he moved into startups.
- His first company was Officient, run from a workspace in Ghent. Three years in it had a strong team and a lively office.
- Along the way he built open-source tools with Vue.js, React and Next.js. Those ventures taught him social media and how brutal debugging can be.
- His view: there is always more to learn however hard you hustle. He decided the nomad lifestyle was the real prize, more than the startup game.
- He is now an exited founder of Officient, building MagicSpace SEO, LinkDR, AI SEO Tracker and GenPPT.

chunks.heading: Four things to sort out before becoming a nomad
chunks.text:
1. **Steady cash flow.** Online jobs, freelancing or your own business all work, but income must be reliable. Keep an emergency fund for unexpected hiccups.
2. **In-demand online skills.** Graphic design, web development, content creation, digital marketing, virtual assisting. Thriving depends on skills that are hot online.
3. **Travel and health insurance.** Solid coverage saves a lot of hassle abroad.
4. **Adaptability.** He compares the lifestyle to improv comedy: time zone shifts and income swings require flexibility.

chunks.heading: Practical problems he learned to handle
chunks.text:
- Bad Wi-Fi is the classic failure. His fixes: find a better cafe, get a faster VPN, or befriend a local with the password.
- He had to explain complex designs to clients over laggy calls.
- He also mastered tourist visas, health insurance, foreign bank accounts and public transit in new cities.

chunks.heading: Covid and the shift to remote work
chunks.text:
- When Covid hit, Officient went fully remote: the office became Zoom squares and coffee breaks became Slack emojis.
- Ilias used the new freedom to travel: Barcelona, Lisbon, the Douro Valley in Porto, and a few months in the Canary Islands where he learned to kitesurf.

chunks.heading: Where he lived afterward
chunks.text:
- **Paris:** about a year, working remotely from a small flat with an Eiffel Tower view while polishing his French. It taught him foreign banking, insurance and transit.
- **Canary Islands:** moved on a digital nomad visa and lived in a coliving space, where he met remote workers from many countries.
- **Switzerland:** worked amid the mountains and wrote blog posts about running a remote business. His takeaway: nomad life "isn't a sprint; it's a marathon". It means creating a home base in each place and adapting, not just finding the best cafes.

chunks.heading: Community and the nomad mindset
chunks.text:
- Location independence "doesn't mean being a lone wolf". Facebook groups, coworking spaces and cafe meetups give a worldwide network of remote workers who swap tips on workspaces and insurance problems.
- His four mindset lessons:
  1. **Balance is everything.** Alternate all-nighters with exploring.
  2. **Never stop learning.** Every job, project and city teaches something.
  3. **Your network is your lifeline.** Connect with nomads, join groups, build a social presence.
  4. **Embrace change.** Expect internet issues, late payments, even a pandemic, and adapt.
- His conclusion: being a nomad is "more than a lifestyle; it's a mindset, a celebration of freedom, and a relentless pursuit of living life on your own terms."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias contrasts a ramen chef who hired staff and can leave on busy nights with sushi owners who do everything themselves and never get a day off. He applies it to his SEO agency: document processes as SOPs so new hires can replicate quality, which also raises valuation and helped him sell his previous SaaS at a premium.

chunks.heading: Why Ilias hires a team instead of doing the work himself
chunks.text:
Ilias argues that a business owner who does everything personally is the business, and that this caps growth and freedom. He uses a story from his local neighborhood to make the point:

- A ramen shop owner opened a second location and spends busy Friday nights out with friends, because newly hired staff run the kitchen and serve customers.
- The sushi restaurant owners across the street never hired anyone, to save on expenses. They cook, serve and clean themselves, rarely take holidays, work weekends, and close the restaurant when they are sick.
- Ilias's summary of the sushi owners: "They are the business!"
- He notes the ramen chef's fame comes from press coverage (his digital PR tells a story of the chef having "traveled to Japan" to perfect his recipes), which draws visitors from across the city. Fame alone didn't scale it; hiring a team did.

chunks.heading: Ilias's own situation at MagicSpace SEO
chunks.text:
Ilias applies the lesson to his SEO agency in Switzerland, MagicSpace SEO.

- Right now it is just him and a co-founder, both doing client work themselves. His words: "We are the SEO agency!"
- His typical day covers content creation, keyword research, guest posting, link building and finding new clients.
- All of that serves one goal: improving website authority and boosting his clients' search positions.
- He concludes he can't do everything himself forever. As clients grow, he needs to hire more people to serve them, or he risks losing them.

chunks.heading: Scale by documenting processes as SOPs
chunks.text:
Ilias's key to scaling without losing quality is building standardized systems that future team members can replicate. He plans to turn his own way of working into standard operating procedures (SOPs), a blueprint of the agency's approach. Areas he lists:

- Using SEO tools correctly.
- Keywords: content gaps, topical maps, structure, content calendar.
- Writing: content briefs, content creation, editing, publishing.
- Link building: guest posting, handling payment, cold email outreach.
- Reporting: creating reports, sending them to clients, explaining them.
- Client management: onboarding clients, handling client requests.

chunks.heading: Why SOPs matter
chunks.text:
Ilias lists four benefits of documenting the processes:

- Smooth onboarding of new team members.
- Consistency even as the agency scales.
- Flexibility for him to step away at times.
- Higher business valuation if he ever wants to sell.

He frames putting these in place early as laying "the groundwork for scalable and sustainable growth."

chunks.heading: Teams and processes raise exit value
chunks.text:
Ilias says this approach is why his previous B2B SaaS startup (he is an exited founder of Officient) sold for a great price.

- He had built a team and processes that let him step away from the business and work on other things.
- The acquirer was willing to pay a premium for that.

chunks.heading: The risk of not building a team
chunks.text: If he doesn't do this, Ilias says he'll be stuck like the sushi owners, still doing everything himself even as the business grows. His advice to any business owner: think about how to scale operations so you don't have to be there all the time and can focus on the things you enjoy most.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism lays out a simple landing page formula: a short headline showing value and USP, a description with specific numbers and reasons, and 3-5 benefit bullets. He illustrates it with Pieter Levels' Nomad List, Interior AI and Photo AI pages and packages it as a reusable AI prompt.

chunks.heading: The 5-step landing page formula and why Ilias copies it across products
chunks.text:
- Ilias frames the "perfect landing page formula" as a simple, repeatable process for building a high-converting landing page.
- The core of the page is three parts, written in this order: headline, description, bullet point benefits.
- He calls the bullet points "the most important part of the landing page". They summarize the product and its benefits in a way that is easy to understand, easy to remember and easy to scan, because "most people don't read every word on a landing page. They scan it to see if it's worth their time."

chunks.heading: Headline, description and bullets: what each part must do
chunks.text:
- **Headline:** very short, simple to understand, concise, and shows the value and the unique selling point (USP).
- **Description:** specific numbers, benefits, reasons why, and the mission.
- **Bullet points:** 3-5 bullets, each with numbers and key points. Each starts with an emoji and states a concrete outcome.
- He packages this as a prompt for an AI "Conversion GPT": give it the formula and three worked examples, fill in your product name, and ask it to write "short, award-winning copywriting" in the order headline, description, bullets.

chunks.heading: Worked example: Nomad List
chunks.text:
Ilias uses Pieter Levels' pages as the reference pattern.
- Headline: "Go nomad and work remotely around the world"
- Description: "Join the #1 global community of 33,106 remote workers living and traveling around the world since 2014" (a specific member count and a founding year as proof).
- Bullets:
  - Attend 433 meetups/year in 100+ cities
  - Meet new people for dating or making friends
  - Research destinations and find your best place to live
  - Keep track of your travels and record where you've been
  - Join Nomad List chat and find your community on the road

chunks.heading: Worked example: Interior AI and Photo AI
chunks.text:
The same shape repeats, with an "instead of hiring an expensive professional" description.
- **Interior AI**
  - Headline: "Redesign your interior in seconds using AI"
  - Description: "Save money and use AI to redesign your interior from your laptop or phone instead of hiring an expensive interior designer"
  - Bullets: photo to AI redesign in seconds; choose a style (Modern, Minimalist, Contemporary); turn sketches and SketchUp files into photorealistic renders; Virtual Staging AI for empty homes in real estate; turn renders into 3D flythrough videos.
- **Photo AI**
  - Headline: "Create beautiful AI photos and videos without a camera"
  - Description: "Save money and use AI to do a photo shoot from your laptop or phone instead of hiring an expensive photographer"
  - Bullets: upload selfies to create your own AI character; take 100% AI photos in any pose, place or action; create 100% AI videos from any AI photo; run photo packs like AI Yearbook and Old Money; create AI-generated fashion designs with Sketch2Image™.
- Pattern: the headline names the outcome, the description gives the cost or time saving versus the human alternative, and the bullets list concrete features and use cases.

chunks.heading: Reuse one proven landing page across products
chunks.text:
Ilias embeds Pieter Levels' account of copying one landing page style across his products:
- Pieter copy-pasted the Photo AI and Interior AI landing page style onto Nomad List, and conversion went "from 1% to almost 4%".
- The lineage: Interior AI v2's page is a copy of Photo AI's page, which is a copy of Nomad List's page from a year earlier.
- Added elements borrowed from a heavily A/B-tested page (Tabs Sex Chocolate by @oliver__b1): press mentions and testimonials.
- Added the bullet point benefits list popularized by @NapierHolland.
- Sign-up and login are unified into one email box. A new user gets an account created after payment; an existing user logs in.
- Every added or changed element is measured with Simple Analytics event funnels, so what works and what doesn't is visible quickly.
- Having the same page across 3 projects saves time; Remote OK was next.
- Ilias presents this as the proof that a tested landing page structure is worth copying and reusing rather than redesigning each time.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism explains how to write SEO titles by treating the SERP as the brief: lead with the main query, stay around 40-55 characters, mirror winning patterns, match page type, and align title, description, H1 and slug. He adds a 10-step audit loop and a Cursor skill for bulk rewrites.

chunks.heading: Page title formula and anatomy
chunks.text:
Ilias treats the SERP as the brief for any page title. Bad titles usually fail because they are vague, bloated, mismatched, or clever when Google wants obvious. His starting formula is **primary keyword + useful modifier/benefit + brand**, used mainly to stop people writing titles like "Home".

- Weak to better: "Home" becomes "Client Portal Software for Accountants". "Products" becomes "Best AI Presentation Makers in 2026". "Pricing" becomes "Client Portal Pricing".
- A title tag is the HTML `<title>`, shown as Google's blue headline. It tells Google what the page is about and tells humans why to click.
- If the title is weak, Google may rewrite it. If it is too long, Google cuts it off. If it doesn't match the page, people bounce.
- His summary: "Better page titles are one of the highest-ROI SEO fixes because they sit at the intersection of ranking and CTR." The title should be "clear first", not clever first.

chunks.heading: Put the main query first and align everything around it
chunks.text:
The strongest pattern from his SEO Roasts is boring but effective: SEO title, meta description, H1 and URL slug should all point at the same primary phrase.

- Use the query people actually search. "Secure Collaboration Platform for Modern Firms" loses to "Client Portal Software for Accountants".
- Front-load the main phrase so Google and humans understand the page in the first few words.
- Keep slugs stable for the head term (e.g. `/best-ai-presentation-makers`) and update the title as numbers or years change ("10 Best AI Presentation Makers in 2026"). A slug like `/five-options` with a title that later says "10 options" creates a mismatch he calls a "tiny SEO goblin".

chunks.heading: Length: 40-55 characters, keep key words before the cutoff
chunks.text:
His practical sweet spot is 40-55 characters. He notes it isn't a law, since Google uses pixel width rather than character count, but it keeps titles readable and avoids truncation.

- Overlong titles kept appearing in roasts: a digital signage page with a 94-character title while competitors were closer to 60, a client portal title getting cut off, and a homepage title that needed to stay under roughly 60 characters.
- The rule: "Shorten until the words that matter appear before the ellipsis." If Google cuts off the benefit, the number or the query, the title is too loose.
- The goal is not exactly 60 characters. It is keeping the important words visible before truncation.

chunks.heading: Mirror the SERP and use proven title patterns
chunks.text:
Before writing a title, he searches the keyword and compares the top 10 titles side by side.

- Look for repeated words and formats: "best", "top", years, numbers, "software/tools/platform/service", and paired phrases like "client portal" vs "customer portal".
- This is "matching the market", not copying. If every top result says "best AI presentation makers" and yours says "AI slide creation solution", you have "invented a worse phrase".
- Patterns by intent:
  - How-to: `How to [Task]`
  - Definition: `What Is [Term]?`
  - Guide: `[Topic]: A Beginner's Guide`
  - Listicle: `[Number] Best [Tools]`
  - Checklist: `[Topic] Checklist: [Number] Tips`
  - Comparison: `[A] vs [B]`
  - Error: `What Does [Error] Mean?`
- Modifiers that keep showing up: Best, Top, Complete, Beginner's Guide, Examples, Template, Free, 2026. He warns that "Jaw-dropping", "Unbelievable" and "Shocking" make you sound like you sell miracle protein powder.

chunks.heading: Match the page type, avoid nothing titles, don't stuff keywords
chunks.text:
- The title should match the URL's job: pricing pages say pricing, support pages say support, docs say docs or documentation, login pages say login. In one roast a pricing URL was weaker because the title didn't match pricing intent, which he calls an easy fix.
- Ultra-short titles are as bad as long ones. "Home" and "About" are shrugs. A homepage title should say what the product does, e.g. "AI Customer Support Chatbot for SaaS Teams".
- Numbers and years work because they set expectations, but the page must match: "8 benefits" means the page clearly has 8.
- Google's guidance he follows: make titles unique, descriptive and concise, avoid boilerplate, avoid keyword stuffing, and match the page's language. Bad: "SEO Title Generator | SEO Title Tool | Best SEO Title Tags SEO". Good: "SEO Title Generator: Write Better Titles in 2026".

chunks.heading: Title audit loop and checklist
chunks.text:
His loop for fixing titles:

1. Pick the target keyword.
2. Search it in Google.
3. Pull the top 10 titles.
4. Note repeated words, numbers, years and modifiers.
5. Check page type and search intent.
