6. Write 5-10 title options.
7. Keep the important words under the cutoff.
8. Align title, meta description, H1 and slug.
9. Re-index the page.
10. Measure CTR in Google Search Console.

- "If a page has high impressions and low CTR, the title is often the fastest win." He adds "not always", but says to check it before launching "a 4-month content strategy".
- Pre-publish checklist: primary keyword near the front, matches page type, unique, around 40-55 characters, important part survives truncation, matches H1/description/slug, mirrors the SERP without copying, sounds human. "If yes, ship it. If no, tighten."
- He built the SEO Title Generator inside SEO Roast (seoroast.com) because this workflow kept coming up in audits: enter a keyword, pull top-ranking titles, see common words/length/structure, generate options, then grade the final title.

chunks.heading: Bulk-fixing titles with a Cursor Agent Skill
chunks.text:
For dozens of weak titles, he turns the rules into a reusable Cursor Agent Skill so he doesn't re-explain them each time.

- Create `.cursor/skills/seo-title-optimization/SKILL.md` (Cursor discovers skills from `.cursor/skills/` or `.agents/skills/`). The skill's description triggers on mentions of titles, title tags, SERP titles, metadata titles, CTR, truncation, or bulk title improvements.
- The skill encodes: primary query near the front; align title, description, H1 and slug; match page type; keep key words visible before truncation; 40-55 characters; clarity over stuffing; unique titles; mirror SERP patterns; don't change slugs just to match temporary numbers or years.
- Its workflow: identify the primary keyword, determine intent, compare top-ranking titles when SERP data exists, choose a pattern, draft 3-5 options, pick the most accurate and clickable one, and return a before/after table for bulk work.
- Example prompt: "Use the seo-title-optimization skill to audit all MDX blog post titles in content/blog. Return a before/after table with suggested titles around 40-55 characters when possible. Do not edit slugs."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism explains programmatic SEO as data plus templates plus automation producing thousands of useful pages. He backs it with client examples (MagicBuddy, WorkbookPDF, GradientPage), a four-stage implementation process, and a firm stance that quality beats page count.

chunks.heading: Programmatic SEO as a system: data, templates, automation
chunks.text:
Ilias defines programmatic SEO as systematically creating and optimizing web pages at scale using automation and data. His formula: "Data Source + Templates + Automation = Thousands of Valuable Pages".

- **Data sources:** public APIs, user-generated content, structured datasets, scraped data (when appropriate), and the company's own product or service data.
- **Templates:** dynamic page structures, variable content blocks, schema markup templates, meta tag frameworks.
- **Automation:** dynamic routing, automated page generation, intelligent internal linking, bulk optimization.
- Example: a recipe site holds a database of ingredients, cooking times and instructions, and one template generates pages like `/recipe/chicken-pasta` and `/ingredients/tomatoes/recipes`.
- Sites like Yelp and TripAdvisor rank for millions of keywords through code, not "an army of content writers".

chunks.heading: Why he favors it over traditional SEO
chunks.text:
He frames traditional SEO as writing individual posts, manual keyword research and one-off page optimizations, and programmatic SEO as building systems that scale and serve specific search intents.

- Traditional SEO scales linearly with effort. Programmatic SEO can scale exponentially once the system exists.
- It is a "blue ocean" strategy: target untapped search intent across thousands of specific pages.
- Technical barriers make the moat harder to copy, and there is first-mover advantage in underserved niches.
- It fits developers and technical founders: apply data structures, build automated systems instead of "endless blog posts".
- Systems can improve through automated testing and iteration, and expand into new markets and keyword spaces with little extra effort.
- His quality rule: "creating valuable pages that serve real user needs", not just many pages. Across dozens of clients, businesses that favor quality over quantity see the best results.

chunks.heading: Client implementations at MagicSpace
chunks.text:
Ilias describes three programmatic SEO builds from his agency, MagicSpace.

- **MagicBuddy (Telegram chatbot using ChatGPT):** thousands of pages are created dynamically when a user clicks a ChatGPT example they like, including city-specific pages via geolocation, built from user-generated content.
  - URL pattern `/ai/:topic` (e.g. "What is ChatGPT", "ChatGPT in Russian").
  - Each page has a unique title, description and conversation.
  - The bottom of each page shows 3 more examples, which are generated only if a user clicks them.
- **WorkbookPDF (personalized language workbooks as PDFs):** hundreds of dynamic pages per language, level and topic, plus blog, content and link-building help.
  - Patterns: `/:language/level/:level` (e.g. Korean grade 11, German beginner) and `/:language/topic/:topic` (e.g. French wine).
- **GradientPage (gradient wallpapers):** to reach designers, developers and indie hackers, they built free tools for CSS and UI gradients.
  - 500+ pages of CSS UI gradients, each linking to a color and hex code, "offering millions of potential pages".
  - Patterns: `/css/ui-gradients/:color` (e.g. after-the-rain, instagram) and `/hex/:code` (e.g. FFA647, 00FF7F).

chunks.heading: Other programmatic SEO examples he cites
chunks.text:
Ilias notes he has not worked with these companies, but sees lessons in them.

- **Nomad List:** thousands of pages targeting specific keywords and intents, a data trove on cities for remote workers.
- **TripAdvisor:** thousands of pages on travel keywords that rank and bring millions of organic visitors.
- **Yelp:** pages for essentially all business searches.
- **Zapier:** user-generated content creates pages for almost all "integration" keywords, so users can find and set up integrations between tools.
- **UserPilot:** built a database of tools in its industry and generated many articles programmatically to hit long-tail keywords.
- **Meme templates:** for viral-content sites, pages for popular templates (e.g. Spiderman Pointing, Vince McMahon Reaction on MagicMeme) are a programmatic strategy.

chunks.heading: Tool stack he recommends
chunks.text:
- **Google Sheets:** free, for collecting data from sources like Google Analytics, Search Console and Google Trends.
- **Claude (Anthropic):** "You need a good AI to generate content with"; he calls it one of the best.
- **Next.js:** dynamic routes to create pages targeting specific keywords and locations. He recommends it for its SEO capabilities.
- **OG image generator (ogimage.org):** automatic Open Graph images per page.
- **SEMrush (or Ahrefs):** keyword ideas, rank tracking, competitor analysis.
- **Screaming Frog:** crawl the generated pages to find errors and set up internal links.

chunks.heading: His four-stage implementation process
chunks.text:
Ilias lays out the process his team uses with clients.

1. **Strategic planning**
   - Use SEMrush or Ahrefs to find main keyword clusters and patterns in search intent.
   - Tip: focus on keywords with clear commercial or informational intent that can be templated.
   - Design the URL structure (e.g. `/city/:name`, `/product/:category/:item`), plan template variables, and map internal linking.
2. **Data foundation**
   - Pick a data source (SQL, MongoDB, or spreadsheets for smaller projects), structure it to match URL patterns, and clean and normalize it.
   - Create base templates, optionally use an LLM for unique variations, and "always review AI-generated content for accuracy and value".
3. **Technical implementation**
   - Next.js with dynamic routing matching the URL structure, proper meta tags and schema markup.
   - Quality control: automated duplicate-content checks, canonical tags where needed, monitoring page quality metrics.
4. **Launch and scale**
   - Submit the sitemap to Google Search Console, use indexing tools to speed discovery, and monitor indexing.
   - Track rankings, watch engagement metrics, and adjust templates from performance data.

chunks.heading: Learning resources and how he monetizes the topic
chunks.text:
- Courses he lists: MagicSpace Programmatic SEO Course (his own), a no-code course using Octoparse, Airtable and Webflow, Preetam Nath's course, PageFactory's free course, and Ian Nuttall's "Practical Programmatic" (about 3 hours of video covering keywords, data cleaning, page creation and indexing).
- He funnels readers to a free 15-minute SEO audit and the MagicSpace course, which offers production-ready code templates and video tutorials.
- His agency's stated approach: scalable high-quality content systems, lasting technical foundations, optimizing for both search engines and users, and measuring performance.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism's playbook for using X as a founder: post consistently, reply a lot, build in public, and weave product mentions into value-first content. Covers niche research, profile optimization, engagement tactics, cross-promotion of top content, analytics, and tooling, with examples of founders who grew via X.

chunks.heading: Why X is worth a solo founder's time
chunks.text:
Ilias calls X "the fastest place to build an audience as a founder."

- The feed rewards people who "post consistently, reply a lot, and share what they are building," and one good post can reach far beyond your followers.
- Buyers there (founders, developers, marketers, investors) follow people, not brands. That lets a solo founder compete with companies 100x larger.
- It is a news-first platform. He cites a 2021 Pew study: 69% of US Twitter users get news there, so timely, opinionated posts about your industry travel well.
- Other benefits he lists: targeted traffic, lead generation, real-time feedback, public customer support, competitor monitoring, and free tools (ads are optional).

chunks.heading: Proof from his own account and other indie hackers
chunks.text:
- **Ilias (@illyism):** started the year at 0 followers. He shared SEO tips, engaged with his audience, and reached 1,400+ followers. After Marc Louvion tweeted about his SEO services at MagicSpace, he got 20 solid leads in DMs almost overnight. He says Twitter became a top source of new business for his SEO agency, which went from $0 to $5,000 MRR in under a month. His takeaway: "It's important to connect with the right people."
- **Nick Buzz (UI design business):** went from struggling to $65k MRR in 3 months. He shared design process breakdowns instead of self-promotion, tweets regularly hit 100k+ impressions, and he took up to 10 calls a day from ideal prospects. Ilias's conclusion: building in public with tactical, value-driven content beat ads.
- **Marc Lou (ShipFast):** grew from 1k followers in July 2022 to 45k+ by openly sharing his journey. One ShipFast announcement tweet reached 167,000 impressions. He combined Twitter with Product Hunt, and Ilias's lesson is to build the audience first so the launch has social proof. Ilias cites Marc going from $1k MRR to $50k MRR in a year.

chunks.heading: Tools Ilias recommends
chunks.text:
- **Typefully:** best for writing and posting across X and LinkedIn. It has an AI writing assistant, a distraction-free editor, scheduling for tweets and threads, and publishes to X, LinkedIn, Threads, Bluesky and Mastodon. The free plan is limited to 10 posts a month with no AI.
- **Tweet Hunter:** best for AI content and growth on X. It has a library of 12M+ viral tweets, scheduling and queues, and analytics. It is X only, with plans from $29/month (AI on the $49 plan).
- **StoryChief:** for teams running content across many channels (collaboration, multi-channel publishing, SEO tools).
- **PostEverywhere:** schedules one post to X and 11 other networks from one calendar. It has bulk CSV scheduling, a REST API and a hosted MCP server, from $9/month with a 7-day trial.
- **Hypefury:** dropped X support in 2026, and its X analytics tool BlackMagic shut down on July 1, 2026. If you post on X, he says to use Typefully or Tweet Hunter.
- **MagicMeme:** for making meme content quickly.

chunks.heading: Building the audience
chunks.text:
- **Find your niche:** research hashtags like #buildinpublic, follow experts, micro-influencers, competitors and engaged users, and join those conversations.
- **Post value, not pitches:** insights, behind-the-scenes details, tips and actionable advice. Vary formats (threads, polls, quotes, infographics, memes), post regularly, and ask questions to get feedback.
- **Optimize the profile:** an informative bio that states your expertise and products, a link, links to your projects, a pinned tweet (a launch or best work), and a location set.
- **Engage daily:**
  - Reply to questions and comments, which improves the visibility of your tweets.
  - Like and retweet people in your community.
  - Follow back people who engage.
  - DM new followers to thank them.
- **Work with micro-influencers:** reply to and share their content (tagging them), and DM them discounts or free product in exchange for reviews.
- **Be patient:** "Consistency and persistence are key." You won't build a targeted audience overnight.

chunks.heading: Engagement tactics that turn followers into leads
chunks.text:
- **Spaces and AMAs:** set a date and promote it beforehand, and tag influencers and invite them to join. Provide value during the chat without heavy self-promotion. Afterwards, recap the highlights in a thread and turn the insights into blog posts.
- **Contests and giveaways:** give away products, discounts or premium access, and require a follow and a retweet to enter. Run joint contests with influencers to expand reach.
- **Polls and surveys:** ask questions about your niche or product, use images or video, and track responses in a spreadsheet for new product, content or feature ideas. Follow up with the results.
- **Exclusive value:** coupon codes, early access, sneak peeks, and Twitter-only reviews, how-tos and case studies.
- **Highlight user wins:** ask users how your product helped, share the best stories as threads or testimonials, and tag the users so they share them with their own followers.

chunks.heading: Promoting your product without hard selling
chunks.text:
The key is to "avoid overly promotional content," because followers quickly tune out hard sells. Weave product mentions in among the value you provide:

- Share product updates and explain which problem each new feature solves. Use images and video.
- Re-share the best reviews and tag the reviewers. Turn compelling stories into threads.
- Set up search alerts for your product name and handle, and respond to all feedback. Give support publicly so others see your responsiveness, and move to private if needed.
- Show use cases with real customers, step-by-step walkthroughs, and product mentions inside industry-analysis threads where the product solves the issue being discussed.

chunks.heading: Repurposing and cross-promotion
chunks.text:
- **Threads to blog posts:** expand your best threads into long-form guides, with images and examples, and link back to the original thread.
- **LinkedIn:** repost threads in relevant groups, highlight them on your profile, and ask connections to share them.
- **Product Hunt:** share your PH post at the same time as the Twitter announcement, ask followers to upvote, and thank those who did afterward.
- **Newsletter:** feature excerpts of top threads, turn threads into infographics, and promote your handle in every email.

chunks.heading: Analytics and his 11-step blueprint
chunks.text:
Track and refine based on: impressions, engagement rate (likes, retweets, replies), link clicks, top content, media performance (images, video and GIFs vs text), follower growth, demographics, and peak posting times.

His blueprint:
1. Set clear goals for followers, engagement, clicks and conversions.
2. Research your niche.
3. Grow the audience by consistently providing value.
4. Promote strategically, never overtly.
5. Monitor notifications and reply fast.
6. Engage followers with chats, contests, polls and perks.
7. Repurpose content.
8. Analyze the data.
9. Automate repetitive work with tools.
10. Be patient.
11. Plan a content calendar in Typefully or StoryChief and schedule ahead.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: MagicSpace (Ilias Ism, Sasha, Hiren) pulled Ahrefs data on the a16z AI Apps 50 list. Traffic is highly concentrated, organic dwarfs paid, and winners ship large indexable content libraries and category-owning educational content rather than relying on links.

chunks.heading: The a16z AI Apps 50 SEO study: what the data shows
chunks.text: Ilias and the MagicSpace team pulled Ahrefs data (October 3, 2025) for all 50 companies on a16z's AI Apps list to see who wins organic search and what separates winners from the rest. Findings below are the team's analysis, published under Ilias's byline.

chunks.heading: Market concentration and the organic vs paid gap
chunks.text:
- Combined, the 50 tools rank for 10.6M keywords, get 595M monthly visits, are worth $73.5M in traffic value, and have 1.6M backlinks from 476K referring domains.
- Ilias's read: the market is heavily concentrated. Canva (about 24% of traffic), OpenAI (about 19%) and Grammarly (about 5%) take roughly 65%; the other 47 fight over about 35%. The top 10 tools get 85% of traffic, the middle 20 get 13%, the bottom 20 get 2%.
- His lesson: "You're either top 10 in your category, or not! SEO is more brutal than ever." Being on the list doesn't mean winning.
- Paid search across all 50 tools is only about $268K/month against $73.5M in organic traffic value (a 274x ratio). His conclusion: "Organic is the only sustainable acquisition channel at scale."
- Heuristic: spending over $10K/month on ads while having massive organic traffic suggests organic isn't converting, "a product problem, not a marketing problem." Example: Grammarly has about $93.6K paid spend alongside 30M organic visits; Freepik has $69 paid spend with 52M organic visits.

chunks.heading: Focus on a few keywords, not keyword bloat
chunks.text:
- Most of the traffic comes from fewer than 1,000 high-volume terms. Grammarly ranks for 665K keywords, but its top 100 keywords drive about 80% of its traffic.
- Ilias argues most tools waste resources chasing long-tail keywords that bring 1-2 visits a month, and should "focus on the 1-5 keywords that matter."
- His method for this is the Blitz SEO framework (il.ly/blog/blitz-seo), which targets even a single keyword.
- Vertical depth beats breadth: OpusClip (video clipping) and Otter.ai (meeting notes) outperform generalists. "Own one category completely > weak presence in multiple categories."

chunks.heading: What separates winners: content volume, programmatic pages, category education
chunks.text:
- Content volume beats link building. Canva (4.3M keywords) and Grammarly (649K) show big content libraries beating selective high-authority linking. Pattern: "Every new template/tool/asset = new indexable page = new ranking opportunity." He calls this programmatic SEO and sells a course on it.
- Inventory-as-SEO works: Freepik's asset pages, Gamma's and CapCut's template libraries, Midjourney's community galleries, and Notion's template gallery each create thousands of landing pages.
- Free tools as lead magnets plus educational content at scale drive Grammarly's coverage.
- Category leaders own educational content: Perplexity (11M visits), Midjourney (2.5M), ElevenLabs (3.8M). Pattern: "How to use [category]" content beats "Why use [our tool]" content. MagicSpace builds this through "pillar posts."
- Developer tools win through problem-specific documentation (Cursor, Replit): "Problem-specific documentation > generic marketing content." Comparison pages (e.g. "Cursor vs VS Code") also work.
- Newer fast movers: Cursor (589K monthly visits, DR 84) and Lovable (317K visits, DR 89) show near-vertical traffic climbs.

chunks.heading: Domain Rating is not traffic
chunks.text:
- Authority doesn't equal visits. Canva (DR 93) and Grammarly (DR 90) convert authority into traffic efficiently, while some tools with similar DR get about 10x less.
- Examples of unused authority: Ada (DR 75, 9.5K traffic) and Crisp (DR 88 in the profile, 24.6K traffic, "They need more blog posts").
- Lesson: "Links without content strategy = wasted authority." He still says links are needed, and points to LinkDR for link building.

chunks.heading: Case study: Lovable's dead blog
chunks.text:
- Lovable has DR 89 and 317K visits, but Ilias says that excluding branded keywords it effectively ranks only for its homepage.
- Its blog posts on money topics get almost nothing: best-wedding-website-builder (0 traffic, 3 keywords), digital-portfolio-website-examples (0 traffic, 7 keywords), do-you-need-a-cto-as-startup (0 traffic, 1 keyword), what-is-vibe-coding (0 traffic, 1 keyword).
- His point: wedding websites and portfolio builders are valuable topics sitting dead; they "really need to improve this by a lot."
- Takeaway: a brand-driven traffic spike can hide a content strategy that doesn't rank.

chunks.heading: Where authority and brand do the work, and the greenfield cases
chunks.text:
- OpenAI (DR 92, 114M visits, 380K keywords): the product is the marketing. Product-led growth creates millions of natural backlinks, and its documentation ranks for thousands of technical queries.
- Anthropic (DR 88-89, 3.2M visits, 24.6K keywords): research papers as content marketing and AI-safety deep-dives earn backlinks from academic sources. An authority-first approach with fewer keywords but higher-intent traffic.
- Perplexity (122K keywords): "Be the answer engine, rank in the search engine."
- Near-zero SEO presence despite funding or buzz: Fyxer.ai (DR 36, 1 keyword), Serval (DR 11, 22 traffic), Combinely (DR 18, 102 traffic), Crosby (DR 22, 30 traffic). Ilias jokes that Crosby on the list looks like an a16z portfolio plug. His view: starting from zero means basic content strategy gives quick wins.
- Geography: B2C tools go global for volume (India-heavy); B2B tools stay US-focused for better conversion and monetization.

chunks.heading: How MagicSpace applies this
chunks.text:
- The core pillar is content marketing: 3-5 extremely high-quality blog posts a month for $5k/mo, which teach real users the platform and can be reused in social, newsletters and help docs.
- The offer stack: monthly SEO plans, SEO audits (a free 15-minute live audit), and paid "SEO roasts" (done for Cal, Resend, Tolt, Chatbase, Framer).
- Credentials cited: Ilias built and sold Officient ($500k+ MRR), has run 20+ products generating $10M+ in revenue, and has taught 1000+ students SEO. MagicSpace says it has helped 20+ products generate $10M+ through SEO.
- Side note: he acquired GenPPT (an AI presentation tool) a few months before this post and says it's "going well."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism argues that publishing is only the start and distribution is the real work. He lays out a 7-channel framework (Twitter thread, LinkedIn article, Pinterest pins, Reddit, Medium, newsletter, Quora) with timing and tactics for each, plus how to measure ROI per channel.

chunks.heading: Why one article should be distributed to seven channels
chunks.text:
Ilias argues that most creators publish and move on, and that distribution matters more than publishing:
- The typical workflow he criticizes: write, publish, tweet once (maybe), move on. He likens it to "building a store in the middle of nowhere and expecting customers to magically find it."
- "One well-distributed article will outperform ten undistributed ones."
- Competitors with "worse" content can get 10x the reach because they treat publishing as the beginning, not the end.
- Mindset shift: stop thinking "I need to write more content"; start thinking "I need to distribute better." "Content distribution isn't extra work. It's THE work."
- Quick audit: pull the top 10 posts by organic traffic and check whether each has been distributed to all 7 channels. He says a site with 20-50 posts likely has them getting about 10% of their potential traffic.

chunks.heading: The 7X framework: one article, seven formats
chunks.text:
When an article is published, Ilias wants it to become, at the same time:
- Twitter thread (immediate engagement)
- LinkedIn article (professional network)
- Pinterest pins (visual search traffic)
- Reddit post (community engagement)
- Medium syndication (backlinks and reach)
- Newsletter (owned audience)
- Quora answer (intent-based traffic)

Suggested timing: Twitter day 1, LinkedIn day 2, Reddit days 3-5, Medium day 7, newsletter day 8; Pinterest and Quora are ongoing.

chunks.heading: Twitter thread, cross-posted to other platforms
chunks.text:
- Don't just tweet a link: "Nobody clicks those anymore."
- Paste the article into Claude or ChatGPT with a prompt like: "Turn this blog post into a 10-tweet thread with a strong hook, key insights as individual tweets, and the link in tweet 1."
- Structure: tweet 1 is a controversial hook plus the link; tweets 2-9 are key takeaways with specific examples; tweet 10 is a CTA back to the full article.
- Use Typefully to schedule and auto-cross-post to LinkedIn, Threads, Bluesky and Mastodon. One thread reaches five platforms.

chunks.heading: LinkedIn native articles
chunks.text:
- Why: higher engagement than regular posts, stays on the profile permanently, and LinkedIn promotes native content over external links.
- How: use "Write article", paste the blog content with a more professional rewritten intro, add images, and say "Originally published on [YourSite]" in the first paragraph. End with a CTA back to the site.
- Bonus: tag relevant people and companies in the article to increase visibility.

chunks.heading: Pinterest: one pin per example
chunks.text:
- Pinterest is a goldmine for any content with visual elements, because users are actively searching.
- Create one pin for each example or tip in an article, each linking back to the post. Example: an article of "52 Cover Letter Examples" becomes 52 pins, each showing one example.
- Use Canva templates for consistency, or BlogToPin.
- The funnel: someone searches "cover letter example", the pin appears, they click, land on the site and convert.

chunks.heading: Reddit and Quora: answer questions, then link
chunks.text:
**Reddit** (users hate self-promotion):
- Find relevant subreddits, look for questions the article answers, write a genuinely helpful reply, then mention "I actually wrote a detailed guide on this: [link]."
- Sort by "new" and be the first valuable commenter, since early engagement brings more upvotes and visibility.
- Where text posts are allowed, format the article's insights as a post with "Full details in my blog post for anyone interested." Reddit posts can rank on Google, so this is SEO plus distribution.

**Quora** (he calls it the most underrated channel):
- Search for questions on the article's topic and write comprehensive 500-800 word answers using rewritten sections of the post. Use the blog outline as the answer structure to save time.
- End with "I wrote a complete guide on this: [link]."
- Why: answers rank on Google, Quora shows answers to people following topics, and traffic is high-intent.

chunks.heading: Medium syndication and newsletter
chunks.text:
**Medium** (100M+ monthly readers, ranks well in search), two approaches:
- Backlink play: rewrite the article slightly (different intro, condensed middle), publish with "Originally published on [YourSite]" at the top, and get a backlink from a high-authority domain.
- Canonical play: paste the exact article, then set Settings → Advanced → canonical URL to the original, so Google treats it as syndicated and SEO isn't hurt.
- Medium also surfaces posts to people who would never find the blog.

**Newsletter** (owned audience):
- Subject: "I just updated [Article Topic] with new data."
- Body: why it was updated, the 3 biggest takeaways, a CTA to read the full article, and a PS: "If this was helpful, forward to a friend."
- Pro move: segment the list and send different angles of the same article to different segments.

chunks.heading: Measuring ROI per channel
chunks.text:
- Track per channel: traffic, engagement time, conversions, and backlinks from syndication. He recommends Datafast for this.
- Common pattern he reports: Twitter drives the most traffic, LinkedIn drives the highest-quality leads, Pinterest drives steady long-term traffic, and Reddit drives either zero or huge spikes. Knowing this lets you prioritize.
- He claims an undistributed top-10 list of posts represents "$50k-500k in potential traffic value (based on search volume × cost-per-click)."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A hands-on tutorial on building a programmatic SEO site in Next.js. Prefer static generation for speed, drive many pages from one dynamic-route template and a data file, give every page unique metadata, ship a dynamic sitemap, and deploy on Vercel. Includes scaling notes for very large sites.

chunks.heading: Next.js is a good fit for programmatic SEO because of rendering and routing
chunks.text:
Ilias recommends Next.js for programmatic SEO (pSEO) because it handles the pieces a page-generation site needs:
- **SSR and SSG:** SSR gives search engines fully rendered HTML per request. SSG builds static HTML at build time, so pages load very fast, and speed is a ranking factor. For pSEO, especially large sites, he says SSG is often the ideal choice.
- **Dynamic routing:** one template can generate hundreds or thousands of pages.
- **Built-in SEO features:** components and APIs for title tags, meta descriptions, canonical URLs and image optimization.
- **API routes** for data fetching, form submissions or other server-side logic.
- **Ecosystem and DX:** the React ecosystem, fast refresh, built-in TypeScript support and an active community.
- **Deployment:** Vercel builds Next.js, so deployment and hosting are seamless.

chunks.heading: Starting a pSEO project: setup and data source
chunks.text:
Ilias's tutorial sets up the project and data layer like this:
- Needs Node.js with npm or yarn. Create a new Next.js project (his example is `my-pseo-site`, with TypeScript; TypeScript is optional) and run the dev server, typically at `http://localhost:3000`.
- The example is city pages with population data, using a static `data.json` in the project root as the data source.
- Each record gets a `slug` field so URLs are clean and SEO-friendly (e.g. `new-york`, `los-angeles`, `chicago`).
- In a real pSEO project, the data would come from a database, an API or a CSV file rather than a static JSON file.

chunks.heading: Page template and dynamic routes with the app router
chunks.text:
- Next.js uses file-system routing. A single template at `app/city/[slug]/page.tsx` handles every city page.
- The `[slug]` segment is a dynamic segment, so one file serves `/city/new-york`, `/city/los-angeles` and so on. The `params` object passed to the component holds the slug value.
- Template parts:
  - A `getCityData` async function that looks up the record by slug (in production this would hit a database or API).
  - A `generateMetadata` function for per-page SEO metadata.
  - A `CityPage` component that renders the page.
  - A `generateStaticParams` function. Ilias calls it "crucial" for SSG: it returns one `{ slug }` object per record so Next.js pre-renders every path at build time.
- Basic error handling shows a "City not found" message when the slug doesn't match a record.
- `toLocaleString()` formats numbers such as population with commas for readability.

chunks.heading: Unique metadata for every programmatic page
chunks.text:
- `generateMetadata` builds title tags, meta descriptions and canonical URLs dynamically from each record's data.
- Ilias calls this "essential" for pSEO, because every page needs unique metadata.
- In the example, the title and description are built from the city data, and each page gets a self-referencing canonical URL.

chunks.heading: Dynamic sitemap.xml
chunks.text:
- Create `app/sitemap.ts` (or `.js`) in the `app` directory. Next.js serves it automatically at `/sitemap.xml`, and the URL should be submitted to Google Search Console.
- Implementation steps:
  - Import the `MetadataRoute` type.
  - Import the data (in a real app, fetch it from a database or API).
  - Set a `baseUrl` to the real site URL.
  - Map over the records to produce one sitemap entry per page, using the slug for the URL.
  - Add the homepage (`/`) manually and combine it with the page entries using the spread operator.
  - Use `as const` in TypeScript to make the array read-only.
- `lastModified` should be the real last-modified date of the content, from the data source or CMS if available. The tutorial uses the current date only as a placeholder. `changeFrequency` and `priority` can be adjusted.
- For larger sites:
  - Past 50,000 URLs, or a sitemap over 50MB, split into multiple sitemaps with a sitemap index file.
  - For very large sites, regenerating the whole sitemap on every change is inefficient, so consider incremental updates that only touch changed pages.

chunks.heading: Deploying and next steps
chunks.text:
- Deployment on Vercel:
  1. Create a free Vercel account.
  2. Connect the Git repository (GitHub, GitLab or Bitbucket).
  3. Deploy. Vercel detects Next.js and configures build settings, so the defaults usually work.
  4. Optionally add a custom domain.
- Vercel rebuilds and deploys on every push to the repository and provides preview deployments, serverless functions and edge caching. Alternatives he lists: Netlify, AWS Amplify and self-hosting.
- Next steps he suggests for a more powerful pSEO site:
  - Fetch data from external APIs or a database (PostgreSQL, MongoDB).
  - Add user authentication and authorization.
  - Add richer content and features to pages.
  - Optimize for performance and scalability.
  - Use AI to generate or enhance content.
- He promotes the MagicSpace Programmatic SEO Course for advanced techniques, case studies and community.

chunks.heading: Background on Ilias and MagicSpace
chunks.text:
- Ilias is the author of the MagicSpace SEO blog. The page describes him as having built and sold Officient ($500k+ MRR), built 20+ products generating $10M+ revenue, and taught 1000+ students SEO.
- The page says the MagicSpace team has helped 20+ products generate $10M+ through SEO, and that 50+ founders have grown their SEO traffic.
- Services offered: SEO audits, monthly SEO plans, link building (linkdr.com) and strategy sessions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Case study of a 6-month SEO engagement for StoryChief, a content marketing SaaS up against Ahrefs, SEMrush and Backlinko. A mix of content, technical SEO, backlinks and conversion work grew organic clicks 6x, made SEO the source of 80% of leads, and replaced PPC that had a CPA above $2,000.

chunks.heading: StoryChief engagement: scope and approach
chunks.text:
Ilias, through MagicSpace SEO, ran a 6-month SEO and content marketing overhaul for StoryChief. StoryChief is an all-in-one content marketing platform (team collaboration, content creation, multi-channel distribution). It competed against Ahrefs, SEMrush, Backlinko and Neil Patel, and wanted more organic traffic and leads with less reliance on expensive PPC.

The engagement covered eight workstreams:
- High-quality content creation
- On-page and technical SEO optimization
- Strategic backlink acquisition
- Conversion rate optimization
- Video strategy improvements
- Affiliate marketing campaign enhancements
- Email nurture sequence refinement
- Weekly SEO consulting calls

Example content produced for StoryChief:
- "10 Best Screenshot Apps for Mac in 2024 (Free & Paid)"
- "Programmatic SEO Examples That Actually Work"
- "7 Powerful ChatGPT Prompts to Create SEO Content Faster"

chunks.heading: StoryChief results after 6 months
chunks.text:
- Organic search traffic grew 6x, from 8,000 to 44,000 monthly clicks.
- Significant boost in high-authority backlinks and organic traffic to key landing pages.
- 80% of leads now come through SEO.
- PPC was eliminated. Previous CPA on PPC was over $2,000+.
- Content distribution strategy improved overall.

chunks.heading: Ilias's argument for SEO over PPC
chunks.text:
- He frames SEO as the sustainable, long-term, cost-effective alternative to PPC for a B2B SaaS company.
- The shift from PPC to SEO "dramatically reduced customer acquisition costs": StoryChief went from $2,000+ CPA on paid to getting 80% of leads from organic.
- Even in a highly competitive market dominated by well-known SEO brands, a smaller player can compete by executing SEO well.

chunks.heading: Holistic SEO: combine content, technical and off-page work
chunks.text:
- Ilias credits the result to a "multi-faceted SEO strategy" rather than any single tactic.
- Content, technical/on-page SEO, and off-page work (backlinks) were run together, alongside conversion rate optimization, video, affiliate and email nurture.
- Traffic alone was not the goal: conversion optimization and nurture sequences were part of the package so organic visits turned into leads.
- A weekly consulting call kept the strategy tuned over the 6 months.

chunks.heading: Ilias's SEO track record and offer (as stated in the essay)
chunks.text:
- Built and sold Officient ($500k+ MRR).
- 20+ products generating $10M+ revenue through SEO.
- 1000+ students taught SEO.
- MagicSpace says 50+ founders have grown their SEO traffic with them.
- Services offered: SEO audit (live 15-minute or recorded), monthly SEO plans, link building (via LinkDR), and strategy sessions. Both audit formats include next steps and an intro to the services.
- Based in Switzerland.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism lists five reasons SEO is difficult: frequent core updates, technical SEO, scaling quality content, weaker link building tactics, and AI Overviews. His tactical advice: hybrid AI plus human content, diversified traffic, digital PR, and interactive tools. It ends as an agency pitch and the statistics are loosely sourced.

chunks.heading: Why SEO is hard: five forces Ilias names
chunks.text: Ilias frames SEO as "one of the most dynamic and complex disciplines" in digital marketing. It requires balancing technical expertise, creative content strategy and adaptation to algorithm shifts. His 2025 view is that AI, tougher competition and changing user expectations have made it harder. He lists five core reasons.

chunks.heading: Reason 1: Core updates keep rewriting the rules
chunks.text:
- Google ran four core updates and three spam-focused updates in 2024.
- He says the March 2024 core update took 45 days to roll out and cut low-quality content in results by 45%, beating Google's 40% target.
- He says the December 2024 update leaned on E-E-A-T (Experience, Expertise, Authoritativeness, Trustworthiness), hitting healthcare and finance hardest.
- Updates often demote previously working strategies "overnight". Recovering from a drop is a "Sisyphean" task, because drops rarely come from one issue. They come from a content ecosystem that fails evolving quality benchmarks.
- His adaptation playbook:
  - Monitor continuously with Google Search Console plus Ahrefs or Semrush.
  - Run regular content audits against E-E-A-T, especially for YMYL (Your Money or Your Life) topics.
  - Diversify traffic sources so organic search is not the only channel.
- He notes programmatic SEO (pSEO) sites can recover from updates.

chunks.heading: Reason 2: Technical SEO is the invisible foundation
chunks.text:
- Mobile accounts for 63% of global search traffic (2024 figure he cites), and Google "always" crawls sites on mobile. Responsive design has to be flawless.
- He says an August 2024 Core Web Vitals update tied rankings to LCP, FID and CLS.
- Enterprise blockers he lists:
  - Legacy CMSs that cannot support modern performance work.
  - Balancing rich media with page speed.
  - Coordinating dev, design and content teams.
- He says 58% of sites misuse structured data. Wrong schema risks being misread by search AI models.
- He says the 2024 BERT update favored contextual understanding over keyword density. His response:
  - Use NLP in content creation.
  - Do entity-based optimization aligned with Google's Knowledge Graph.
  - Keep refining semantic relationships inside content clusters.

chunks.heading: Reason 3: Quality content is hard to scale
chunks.text:
- He says Google's September 2024 Helpful Content Update formalized penalties for "content mill" tactics. 23% of domains relying on unsupervised AI articles lost SERP visibility.
- Scaling good content is still expensive. His 2025 enterprise survey figures:
  - Original research: 68% cite budget constraints.
  - Updating legacy content: 72% struggle to track ROI.
  - Multilingual localization: 54% report quality degradation.
- What works: a hybrid model. Use AI for ideation and drafting, and keep human editors for E-E-A-T elements like expert interviews and data validation.

chunks.heading: Reason 4: Link building and local SEO got harder
chunks.text:
- He says the March 2024 spam update hit private blog networks (PBNs). He cites Ahrefs data showing a 62% drop in PBN-powered rankings.
- He says nofollow and UGC links (Reddit, Quora) now appear in 37% of top-ranking pages, which shifts how links are earned.
- Modern link acquisition, in his view:
  - Digital PR tied to newsworthy data studies.
  - Content partnerships with academic institutions.
  - Outreach at scale with LinkDR (his link-building tool).
  - Tracking brand mentions (e.g. with Mention) to recover unlinked citations.
- For local SEO, he describes a 2024 "Near Me" update. Google Business Profiles increasingly need:
  - Real-time inventory integration for product businesses.
  - Hyperlocal, neighborhood-specific content.
  - Video testimonials.

chunks.heading: Reason 5: AI Overviews and AI search
chunks.text:
- He says Google's 2025 AI Overviews (formerly Search Generative Experience) answer 28% of informational queries directly, collapsing click-through on featured snippets.
- Early adopters benefit from:
  - Structured data markup for AI answer eligibility.
  - Conversational content built around question-and-answer pairs.
  - Authority positioning via Google's "Perspectives" filter.
- To adapt, he says to:
  1. Build voice search strategies for Alexa and Siri.
  2. Optimize for semantic search via knowledge panel eligibility.
  3. Create interactive tools (calculators, quizzes) that resist AI summarization.

chunks.heading: Bottom line and his SEO credentials
chunks.text:
- His conclusion: SEO in 2025 is harder than ever. Staying visible needs constant adaptation, deep expertise and a strategy beyond outdated tactics.
- He positions MagicSpace SEO as the fix and says it has helped 20+ products generate $10M+ through SEO, and that 50+ founders have grown SEO traffic with it.
- Background he lists: built and sold Officient ($500k+ MRR), 20+ products generating $10M+ in revenue, 1000+ students taught SEO, based in Switzerland.
- MagicSpace offers an SEO audit, monthly SEO plans, link building (LinkDR) and strategy sessions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A case study of a one-month SEO engagement with Aikido Security when it had 5 founders. Instead of publishing lots of new content, the work improved existing posts, restructured keywords, and used third-party listicles plus self-owned backlink pages to reach top-three rankings.

chunks.heading: Aikido Security's one-month SEO engagement: results and framing
chunks.text:
- Ilias's agency worked with Aikido Security when it was just 5 founders with a solid product that nobody could find in search.
- The engagement lasted one month, and Ilias says that was enough.
- Ilias says Aikido now has 100+ employees and generates "billions in revenue", crediting the work with the founders at the foundation stage.
- The outcome was #1, #2 and #3 rankings for their top keywords in that one month, without writing hundreds of new articles.
- Ilias frames the goal as an "SEO foundation they could build on", chosen together with the client, rather than ongoing content volume.

chunks.heading: Improve and restructure existing content before writing new
chunks.text:
- Ilias's first step is to look at every blog post the company already has and improve every article found.
- He then does a complete keyword restructure, looking at all of the company's top keywords and making sure the existing content gets into the results for them.
- His rule: "Improve existing content first." The aim is to make existing content rank, not to produce volume.
- The reasoning is that a young startup has no time to write hundreds of articles, so effort goes where it already has assets.

chunks.heading: Using other people's listicles and articles to reach the top three fast
chunks.text:
- Ilias does comprehensive backlink and listicle research: finding existing listicles and articles that rank for the target keywords.
- Getting the company into those third-party listicles and articles puts it in the top results immediately, instead of waiting for its own pages to rank.
- He argues this beats writing lots of content or wasting time: "use other listicles and articles to get into top results immediately."
- The focus is the results that matter, meaning the pages that already occupy the search results for the company's top keywords.

chunks.heading: Backlinks from your own pages
chunks.text:
- Ilias writes a few strategic articles and adds backlinks from his own agency's pages.
- The tactic is to leverage existing authority by writing pages that feature the client company, which he says boosts domain authority.
- He combines this with the listicle placements rather than relying on either alone.

chunks.heading: Focus on top keywords and know when the foundation is enough
chunks.text:
- Ilias's approach: look at all the top keywords, make sure the company appears in the results for them, and acquire #1, #2 and #3 spots for what matters rather than spreading effort widely.
- A small number of strategic articles, not a large content programme, completed the work.
- He argues one month can be enough to build the SEO foundation for an early-stage B2B SaaS, and that the stopping point should be decided together with the client.
- His agency's pitch is results "in weeks, not months", combining technical SEO with strategic content placement for B2B SaaS companies.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Case study of MagicSpace SEO's work with non-profit Bank.Green: growth strategy, brand identity, website and a tightly targeted keyword plan. Organic traffic grew from near zero in 2021 to 3.8K monthly visits with #1 rankings for the core topic keywords.

chunks.heading: Bank.Green case: strategy was a small set of high-intent keywords
chunks.text:
Ilias's agency, MagicSpace SEO, worked with Bank.Green (a non-profit that helps people move their money to banks that don't fund fossil fuels) in its early stages. The brief covered four things at once:
- A digital growth strategy.
- A website that attracts and converts.
- Brand identity and positioning.
- Rankings for high-value keywords such as "green banking" and "eco banks".

He frames the SEO goal as mission-driven. Rank for what eco-minded people search, so they switch banks and put consumer pressure on traditional banks to stop financing fossil fuels.

chunks.heading: Keyword focus: quality over quantity
chunks.text:
Ilias's stated takeaway is to avoid chasing thousands of keywords. Target a small set of highly relevant, high-intent terms instead, which in this case produced better rankings and more qualified traffic. The target terms were:
- "green banking"
- "eco banks"
- "sustainable banking"
- "is my bank green"

Bank.Green reached position #1 for all of them. Volumes reported: "green banking" at 350 monthly searches and "eco banks" at 200. These are small volumes, and the case shows that ranking first on niche, high-intent terms is a viable strategy.

chunks.heading: Results and timeline
chunks.text:
- Organic traffic: 3.8K monthly visits as of 2025.
- Pages indexed: 216.
- Growth curve: near zero in 2021, with significant growth starting in 2023, reaching 3.8K in 2025.
- Rankings are maintained years after the work, with steady traffic growth.
- Testimonial from Zak Gottlieb, Director at Bank.Green: "MagicSpace SEO was absolutely incredible during our early stages a couple of years back".

Ilias's point: SEO compounds and "continues to pay dividends years after implementation", so a solid foundation matters more than quick wins. The timeline also shows it took roughly two years before traffic really inflected.

chunks.heading: Combining brand, site and SEO from day one
chunks.text:
For an early-stage organization, Ilias bundled positioning, the website and the SEO strategy together rather than treating them separately.
- Brand identity: a cohesive visual and messaging strategy aimed at environmentally conscious consumers, which he argues helps a young organization stand out in a competitive space and build trust.
- Website: built to be user-friendly and optimized for both user experience and search engines. He notes the site still earned compliments years after launch.

chunks.heading: Non-profits can win with SEO
chunks.text: Ilias argues that non-profits can get significant SEO results with the right strategy and execution. Ranking #1 for terms like "green banking" lets a mission-driven organization reach people already looking to make responsible banking choices, amplifying the mission without paid acquisition.

chunks.heading: Credentials Ilias cites
chunks.text:
- Built and sold Officient ($500k+ MRR).
- 20+ products generating $10M+ revenue through SEO work.
- 1000+ students taught SEO.
- 50+ founders helped to grow SEO traffic.
- MagicSpace sells SEO audits (a 15-minute live audit or a recorded one), monthly SEO plans, link building (via LinkDR) and strategy sessions.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism explains Wono's attention framework (catch, hook, retain, convert) and the idea of Black & White ideas: concepts that reduce to a binary, sub-60-character title. He shows how to build one with ChatGPT using the "How Japanese Housewives Outsmarted Global Finance" example.

chunks.heading: The Black & White idea test: catch attention with a binary under 60 characters
chunks.text:
- Ilias, writing about a framework from Wono (the creator behind the viral "Mrs Watanabe" YouTube video), treats content as attention management in four steps: catch, hook, retain, convert.
- Catch: grab attention first, because the more you catch, the more you can funnel into later steps.
- Hook: engage the viewer so they want to keep consuming.
- Retain: keep them engaged for as long as possible.
- Convert: turn that attention into an action such as a like, share or subscription.
- The framework's point is that execution matters as much as the idea: even a remarkable idea falls flat without a plan for managing attention.

chunks.heading: Layered ideas vs Black & White ideas
chunks.text:
- The framework says to focus on the ingredients of an idea, not the idea itself.
- There are bad ideas and good ideas. Good ideas split into two types.
- Layered ideas are complex and multi-dimensional, and hard to convey in simple words. They are good at retaining attention but weak at catching it.
- Black & White ideas can be broken into a binary format in under 60 characters. Their concise nature makes them strong at catching attention.
- Their simplicity is the strength: they can be understood in a few words without losing substance.
- The binary shape sparks curiosity about the nuance behind it, and that curiosity carries attention into the hook, retain and convert steps.

chunks.heading: How to build a Black & White idea (the Mrs Watanabe example)
chunks.text:
- Start by having ChatGPT write descriptions around your topic, then ask it for a black and white title.
- Break the title down into smaller parts, keeping only the essence of the story.
- The resulting title: "How Japanese Housewives Outsmarted Global Finance".
- Under 60 characters (also the ideal SEO title length) is the signal that you have something to work with.
- The core is two counterpart thoughts inside one title:
  - Japanese vs Global
  - Housewives vs Finance
- Wono's example: a recording of a popular streamer reading the title aloud. The streamer's tone on "How Japanese..." shows the "catch attention" moment, then he opens the video with his fans and watches it fully (hook, then retain).

chunks.heading: Why the binary title works: tension in the reader's mind
chunks.text:
- Ilias says the framework creates "conflict and tension in the mind" of the reader, which leaves them intrigued and hooked. He links this to the Ovsiankina effect (the urge to finish an unresolved task).
- Catching and hooking attention is only the front half. After the title lands, the content still has to retain and convert that attention.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Case study of auditing Framer.com and its top 1000 customer sites by scraping them all and spotting shared problems. Shows how platform-wide SEO fixes beat per-site work, why clear Notion documentation matters, and how a one-off audit became a long-term AI SEO partnership.

chunks.heading: Auditing platforms at scale: scrape customer sites and fix patterns once
chunks.text:
Ilias and Sasha (MagicSpace) did a full technical audit for Framer, a platform with 32 people on the team and 1000+ customer sites. The audit covered Framer.com and its top customer sites.

- Ilias argues against checking sites one by one: "Scrape 1000 sites. Find patterns. Fix problems for everyone at once."
- Week one was research. They analyzed the top 1000 Framer sites, tracked issues in a spreadsheet, and used Screaming Frog SEO Spider to scrape every domain.
- Platform-wide fixes beat custom work per site. Framer needed improvements that helped thousands of customers, and broad solutions scale better.
- The approach suits SaaS platforms, website builders, and tools with many customer sites.
- Ilias frames Framer's core product as SEO, so being SaaS founders himself positioned them to suggest product improvements that help every Framer customer rank better.

chunks.heading: Common technical SEO blockers found across 1000 sites
chunks.text:
The scrape surfaced the same problems across customer sites:

- Missing H1 tags on 25% of sites.
- Canonicalization problems across domains.
- Nofollow issues hurting crawl budget.
- Lorem ipsum still live on customer sites.
- Duplicate content.
- Staging domains getting indexed.
- Truncated titles.

Ilias's takeaway is that these are platform-level defaults and templates, so they can be fixed once in the product rather than site by site.

chunks.heading: Deliverables: reports documented in Notion
chunks.text:
- Two reports were delivered: one for Framer.com SEO and one for customer site improvements.
- Everything was documented in Notion with screenshots and examples.
- Ilias's rule: "Document everything clearly." Dev teams can reference Notion reports later, and clear documentation prevents repeated questions.
- A 'website builder' keyword strategy was also built. It targets a competitive keyword with massive search volume, with a detailed Notion plan showing exactly what to build.

chunks.heading: From one-time audit to ongoing consulting
chunks.text:
- After the audit, they kept working directly with the dev team and answered technical questions in Slack, including sitemap generation strategies, hreflang implementation, and staging domain fixes, solving problems in real time.
- Ongoing consulting now covers technical SEO and AI SEO strategy. The relationship evolved from audit to strategic partnership.
- Ilias's view: "One-time SEO audits help. Ongoing consulting helps more." Questions come up and strategy shifts, and long-term partnerships deliver compounding results.
- Result: Framer implemented fixes from the recommendations, traffic grew consistently, rankings improved across competitive keywords, and the platform became more SEO-friendly for all customers. The audit covered 1000+ sites and identified issues affecting thousands of customers.

chunks.heading: AI SEO: getting ranked in ChatGPT and other AI tools
chunks.text:
- MagicSpace recently started AI SEO consulting for Framer, helping them rank in ChatGPT and other AI tools.
- They use their in-house tool, aiseotracker.com, for this work.
- Their service lineup around this includes a Platform SEO Audit, Technical SEO Consulting, AI SEO Strategy, and a Programmatic SEO course for scaling content across thousands of pages.

chunks.heading: MagicSpace credentials and offer
chunks.text:
- Ilias is credited with building and selling Officient ($500k+ MRR), 20+ products generating $10M+ revenue, and teaching 1000+ students SEO.
- MagicSpace claims to have helped 50+ founders grow SEO traffic and 20+ products generate $10M+ through SEO.
- Entry offers include an SEO audit, monthly SEO plans, link building via linkdr.com, and a 15-minute live audit or strategy session.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism ranks 12 link building tactics by cost, speed and scalability, based on 10,030 publisher quotes. Start with competitor link-gap outreach and "Best X" listicle insertions, compound with data pages and free tools, and filter targets by real traffic rather than DR. Links should also win citations in ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews.

chunks.heading: Competitor link-gap outreach as the fastest route to money-page rankings
chunks.text:
- Ilias's core method: pull the exact pages that already link to 2 or more of your direct SERP competitors. Those editors have linked to tools in your category, so the pitch is "relevant by definition."
- Steps:
  1. Enter your top 3-5 ranking competitors into a backlink checker (LinkDR's free one, or Ahrefs).
  2. Filter to Dofollow, 1 link per domain, and exclude customer asset subdomains (`cdn.`, widgets, badges).
  3. Require at least 1,000 monthly organic visits on the linking domain. He cites 43% of DR 30+ domains getting under 1,000 visits a month, so filter on traffic, not just DR.
  4. Pitch the author or editor directly with a specific reason your page adds value to their article.
- Cost: $160-$500 managed, or $90-$250 in DIY publisher fees. First link in 2-4 weeks. Scales without headcount.
- He ranks this and listicle insertions as the fastest ranking lift for money pages.

chunks.heading: "Best X" listicle insertions to win both Google and AI search answers
chunks.text:
- Ilias's logic: when a buyer asks ChatGPT or Google "What is the best [category] tool?", the answer engine reads the top-ranking "10 Best [Category] Tools" articles and synthesizes their picks.
- Getting added to 5-10 ranking listicles in your niche gives three wins at once:
  - Referral traffic from high-intent buyers comparing options.
  - A contextual dofollow backlink on a page already in Google's top 10.
  - Immediate inclusion in ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google AI Overview answers.
- Method: identify every ranking roundup where competitors appear, then negotiate your inclusion.
- Cost $160-$400, first link in 1-3 weeks.
- He states that pages ranking in Google's top 10 are the number one source pool cited by ChatGPT and Google AI Overviews, so a link strategy should serve ranking and AI citation together.

chunks.heading: Niche edits and guest posts: pricing evidence and execution rules
chunks.text:
- Niche edit (contextual insertion into an existing, indexed article): link equity transfers faster than waiting for a new post to index, because Google has already crawled and ranked the host page. Cost $160-$400, 1-3 weeks.
- From his analysis of 10,030 publisher quotes: 49% charge the exact same fee for a link insertion as for a guest post, and 38% charge less. Median publisher fee for a DR 30-59 guest post or insertion is $90-$100 upfront. 84% require upfront payment, and resellers mark up 1.44x. Median DR 30+ ask is $100.
- Rule for niche edits: never force an awkward exact-match anchor into an unrelated paragraph. Write a 1-2 sentence addition that improves the section so the editor keeps it permanently.
- Guest posts only work when written for a real publication's audience, not "generic AI filler to a link farm." What works in 2026:
  - Pitch an angle the blog hasn't covered (teardown, template, benchmark).
  - Include custom diagrams or real product screenshots.
  - Place the target link naturally, alongside 1-2 links to authoritative non-competing sources.
- Guest posts cost $160-$500 with a 3-4 week lead time. His outsourced offer runs from $160 per placed link.

chunks.heading: Passive link assets: original data pages and free micro-tools
chunks.text:
- **Original data/statistics pages**: journalists, bloggers and AI writers constantly search "<topic> statistics 2026". Publish proprietary numbers from your own database or customers and writers cite and link for free.
  - His example: LinkDR's Link Building Statistics page built on 10,030 publisher quotes. Every stat has a clean copy-paste citation sentence so writers can reference it in seconds.
  - Cost: $0 publisher fee (research time). 4-8 weeks to first links, compounding to DR 60-90+ editorial citations.
- **Free interactive micro-tools**: a narrow, zero-signup calculator, checker or generator "earns far more organic links than another 2,000-word beginner's guide."
  - Examples: LinkDR's Competitor Backlink Checker and Domain Email Finder; ROI calculators, template generators or graders that solve one painful step of the buyer's workflow.
  - Cost: $0 publisher fee, 1-3 days of dev. 4-12 weeks to links, evergreen for homepage and tool links.
- He treats both as compounding over 6-12 months.

chunks.heading: Low-cost and free tactics: PR quotes, mentions, broken links, partners
chunks.text:
- **Journalist quote platforms** (Featured, Qwoted, Source of Sources, Connectively-style feeds): among the safest ways to get DR 70-90 homepage links. $0-$300 a month, 2-6 weeks, low scalability because it takes founder time.
- **Unlinked brand mention reclamation**: when a blog, podcast show note or newsletter names your brand or founder without a link, send a friendly 3-sentence email thanking the author and asking them to make it clickable. Conversion "routinely beat[s] 25%" because the writer already vouched for you. Free, 1-2 weeks, capped by the number of mentions.
- **Broken link building**: in Ahrefs "Best by links" filtered to 404 on competitor or niche resource pages, find a dead guide with 20+ referring domains. Publish an updated replacement and email the sites linking to the dead URL. $0-$100, 3-6 weeks.
- **Integration, partner and customer links**: apply to the official integration directories of tools you connect to (Slack, Stripe, HubSpot, Notion, Zapier, MCP registries) and co-author a setup guide. These carry high topical trust and send qualified referral buyers. Free, 2-4 weeks, highly scalable for B2B SaaS and developer platforms.

chunks.heading: Directories for new domains, and second-tier links
chunks.text:
- For a brand-new domain (DR 0-15), start by submitting to vetted software and startup directories to establish an initial link graph and entity footprint, a baseline of about DR 25. Cost $0-$99 per directory, 1-7 days, a one-time batch. LinkDR keeps a curated list of 99+ startup and AI directories sorted by DR and traffic.
- **Second-tier link building** powers up pages that already convert, such as high-performing roundups. $160-$280, 2-4 weeks.

chunks.heading: The 90-day link building plan
chunks.text:
- **Month 1 (foundation and quick wins)**: submit to 15-20 curated directories, ship 1 citeable data post or free tool, and order 3-5 DR 30-40+ contextual backlinks to the homepage and primary service page.
- **Month 2 (competitor and listicle gap)**: run competitor backlink outreach to get added to the top 5-10 "Best [Category]" roundups ranking in Google's top 10.
- **Month 3 (scale and monitor)**: point monthly DR 40-60+ links at the highest-converting page-2 articles to push them into the top 3, and monitor every live backlink for uptime and dofollow status.
- Ilias's framing of the trade-off: doing outreach in-house costs about 35 hours of cold outreach per campaign. His service sells placements from $160 per link (15% off on monthly plans), most live in 3-4 weeks, paying only for verified live placements.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Ilias Ism's LinkDR essay analyzes a catalog of 10,030 publisher sites to show real link prices. Median guest post is $100 on DR 30+ sites, price is flat from DR 30 to 59, traffic matters as much as DR, and most publishers want upfront payment. It ends with practical buying rules.

chunks.heading: Link price is flat from DR 30 to DR 59, so pay for traffic and relevance, not DR points
chunks.text:
- Ilias's catalog covers 10,030 sites (as of 30 Sept 2026), built from publisher email replies (4,734 sites) and reseller price lists (6,885 sites).
- Median guest post on a DR 30+ site: $100. Average: $470, pulled up by a few expensive news sites.
- Median is about $90 at every tier from DR 30 to DR 59, then $140 at DR 60-69, $395 at DR 70-79, and $899 at DR 80+.
- Price tracks traffic as much as DR. Median rises from $70 for sites under 100 visits/month to $743 for sites over 250,000.
- Across DR 30+ sites, log price correlates 0.49 with log traffic and 0.45 with DR. Publishers price on both, traffic slightly more.
- 49% of DR 30+ sites with at least 1,000 monthly visits ask $150 or less.
- His advice: "Do not pay DR 60 prices for DR 50 sites." Pay more for traffic and relevance, not a few DR points.
- He uses medians rather than averages because a few very expensive sites skew the mean.

chunks.heading: Check organic traffic before buying, because DR can be bought
chunks.text:
- 43% of DR 30+ sites get under 1,000 organic visits/month; 24% get under 100.
- 31% of DR 50+ sites get under 1,000 visits/month.
- Median traffic by tier: DR 30-39 is 232/month, DR 50-59 is 1,132, DR 60-69 is 4,423, DR 80+ is 284,487.
- DR measures a site's own backlinks, and those can be bought too.
- His rule: "Check organic traffic before you buy, not only DR." A DR 55 site with 200 visits/month is not a DR 55 link in practice.

chunks.heading: Skip news sites unless needed, and expect restricted niches to cost more
chunks.text:
- News sites charge a median of $1,100 per guest post, about 11 times the $100 median of other DR 30+ sites.
- Casino, CBD, and other restricted topics cost a median of 1.33x the normal price on the same site (1,389 site/reseller pairs).
- Only 128 of 10,030 sites (1.3%) offer nofollow links only; 96% of publishers who state link type offer dofollow.

chunks.heading: Link insertions are usually not cheaper than guest posts
chunks.text:
- On 5,735 sites quoting both prices, 49% charge the same for an insertion as for a new guest post, and 38% charge less.
- The median insertion price equals the median guest post price.
- His read: many publishers charge for the link, not the article.
- He points to niche edits as the case where an insertion is the better choice.

chunks.heading: Compare resellers: the same site can cost twice as much
chunks.text:
- 1,135 sites appear on two or more reseller price lists.
- The priciest reseller asks a median of 1.44x the cheapest for the same guest post on the same site. Median gap: $40 per link.
- On 49% of these sites the highest price is at least 50% above the lowest; on 30% it is 2x or more.
- His advice: "If you buy from link lists, compare more than one seller."

chunks.heading: What publishers expect: terms to plan for
chunks.text:
Based on 4,057 publishers who stated at least one term (percentages count only those who stated that term):

- **Payment timing:** 84% want payment before publication, 16% after. His advice: pay only publishers you have checked.
- **Payment method:** 68% PayPal, 8% crypto, 7% bank transfer or Wise, 18% other.
- **Permanence:** 76% permanent, 24% time-limited. He advises asking for permanent links in writing.
- **Who writes:** 73% expect the buyer to supply the article, 21% either, 6% the publisher writes. Budget writing time or use a service that includes it.
- **Turnaround:** 89% publish within two days of receiving the article, 11% within a week.
- About 7% signal they reject AI-written articles.

chunks.heading: Publisher prices vs managed link building (LinkDR)
chunks.text:
- Publisher and reseller prices cover only the placement. They exclude finding the site, checking traffic, pitching, negotiating, writing the article, paying up front, and chasing disappearing links.
- LinkDR (his product) prices per link: $160 for DR 30+, $280 for DR 40+, $400 for DR 50+, $500 for DR 60+.
- Included: publisher fee, outreach, a new article, payment, live and dofollow checks, a full refund if the link isn't live in 60 days, and a free replacement if removed within 12 months.
- Most links go live in 3-4 weeks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Managed backlinks cost roughly $150 to $500 each, driven mainly by Domain Rating, real traffic and niche. The essay covers per-DR price tiers, red flags in cheap links, the true cost of doing it yourself, and budgeting from the link gap versus competitors.

chunks.heading: Backlink pricing by Domain Rating (2026)
chunks.text:
- Managed backlinks from a link building service cost about $150 to $500 each.
- Ilias's LinkDR per-link prices:
  - DR 30+ (100-10k visits/mo): $160
  - DR 40+ (500-20k visits/mo): $280
  - DR 50+ (1k-40k visits/mo): $400
  - DR 60+ (1k-80k visits/mo): $500
- Each price includes finding the publisher, outreach, a standard article, and the publisher's fee.
- Large vendors' public price lists sit in the same range: roughly $130 to $160 for DR 30+ and about $500 for DR 60+.
- Publishers themselves ask a median of $100 for a guest post on a DR 30+ site, based on 10,030 sites in LinkDR's link building statistics.
- The managed premium over that $100 covers finding and vetting the site, outreach, writing the article, paying up front, and replacing links that disappear.
- Ilias's rule: price rises with Domain Rating and real traffic. A site with real readers is worth more than a high-DR site with none.
- Data point: 43% of DR 30+ sites get under 1,000 visits a month.

chunks.heading: What drives backlink prices
chunks.text:
Ilias lists seven drivers:

1. **Domain Rating.** Higher DR sites have more links of their own and charge more.
2. **Organic traffic.** Real readers matter more than a high DR number.
3. **Niche.** Casino, crypto, CBD, and finance links cost much more because fewer sites accept them.
4. **Content type.** A listicle or product review usually costs more than a standard article. At LinkDR it adds 20%.
5. **Link type.** A link added to an existing article (a niche edit) is sometimes cheaper. In LinkDR's data, 38% of publishers charge less for it and 49% charge the same.
6. **Outreach method.** Custom outreach to relevant sites costs more than picking from a list of sites that sell to everyone.
7. **Approval.** Reviewing each site before placement takes extra work. At LinkDR it adds 20%.

chunks.heading: Pricing models for link building
chunks.text:
Ilias describes four models:

- **Per link:** pay for each placed link. Easy to compare and budget. This is LinkDR's model: pick a DR tier and a quantity, and see the total before paying.
- **Packages:** a fixed bundle, such as ten links at mixed DR, for one price.
- **Monthly retainers:** a set budget each month for ongoing link building.
- **Pay per result:** pay only for live links. He advises checking what "live" means and for how long.

chunks.heading: True cost of doing link building yourself
chunks.text:
- Buying the link is only part of the cost. You also find the site, pitch it, negotiate, write an article, and check the link.
- His example: if one link takes five hours and your time is worth $50 an hour, that is $250 before the publisher's fee.
- This is why he says many teams outsource link building even when they could do it themselves.

chunks.heading: Red flags in cheap backlinks
chunks.text:
- **Hundreds of links for under $100.** "Real publishers do not work for $1 a link."
- **"Guaranteed DR 70+ links for $20."** DR can be inflated with spam links.
- **No site list or sample URLs.** You cannot judge what you cannot see.
- **The same sites for every niche.** These sites sell to everyone.
- **Private blog networks (PBNs).** Built only to pass links, and Google targets them.
- His bottom line: a cheap link that Google ignores is not cheap, and a link on a spam network can hurt you.

chunks.heading: How to budget for backlinks
chunks.text:
1. **Find your gap.** Count the referring domains of the top three pages for your keyword, and use a backlink checker to see who links to competitors. Budget from the link gap between you and competitors.
2. **Pick a mix.** Most campaigns use mostly DR 30+ and DR 40+ links, plus a few stronger ones for key pages.
3. **Spread it out.** A steady pace each month looks natural and is easier to measure.

- Example first order: 3 DR 40+ links cost $840. With LinkDR's $25 credit on a first one-time order, the buyer pays $815.
- Most LinkDR links go live in 3-4 weeks.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: A practical guide to running cold email campaigns for backlinks. Covers using a separate outreach domain, warming it up, configuring DNS and mailboxes, and writing short, incentive-led emails that avoid common mistakes like broken variables and generic greetings.

chunks.heading: Cold-email domain setup: separate domains, warmup, and mailbox structure
chunks.text:
- Ilias says not to use the primary business domain for cold email outreach. Buy a lookalike domain instead, e.g. "try(name).com".
- Any fresh outreach domain needs warmup so emails land in the inbox, not spam/junk. Warmup means using the mailbox like a normal person: sending and receiving emails, subscribing to industry-relevant newsletters, signing up for some websites.
- Because manual warmup takes time, he recommends an email warmup tool. Before that, set up DNS records properly: SPF, DKIM, DMARC and MX.
- He recommends Google Workspace or Office365 for the best deliverability chances.
- Standard is 3 mailboxes per domain, with US-sounding names (e.g. "James Williams" as `james.w@(domain).com`).
- Give each mailbox a basic signature (name, title, company name) and forward everything it receives to your normal email address (Gmail: Settings > Forwarding and POP/IMAP > Add a forwarding address; Outlook 365: Settings > Mail > Forwarding > Enable forwarding, optionally keep a copy).

chunks.heading: Link-building cold email: what makes the email work
chunks.text:
- Link to your assets and theirs. Nobody wants to search for your site, so include a plain link to it (homepage, landing page, tool or blog post).
- One campaign opens with a short line like "you missed {our name} in your {post}". Both parts are hyperlinked: your name to your relevant content, their post to their page.
- A strong incentive is "key for any campaign". Examples: access to your affiliate program, free access to your platform or service, and offering assets they may need (images, screenshots, testimonials).
- Simplicity boosts engagement and open rates, makes replying easy, and clearly shows your value proposition.
- Subject lines: short and catchy, 5-7 words max. He says short subject lines get "2x higher open rates than long, detailed ones".
- Body: concise and focused. Use hyperlinks to reference pages, and include a link to schedule a call if needed.
- Use plain text, prepare follow-up emails in advance, and keep emails simple and personalized.

chunks.heading: Showing value to the prospect
chunks.text:
- The success of outreach hinges on showing how you benefit the prospect or their readers. Ilias's checklist:
  - Is your content useful for their audience?
  - Do you have a relevant, linkable asset?
  - Is your guest blog idea unique and engaging?
- Use tools like Ahrefs or SEMrush to find broken backlinks or outdated references on their site. Offering to fix these adds immediate value.

chunks.heading: Mistakes to avoid in outreach emails
chunks.text:
- Unoptimized subject lines: test emails to catch input codes or reference numbers leaking in.
- Broken variables: check personalization fields like `{{firstName}}` actually render.
- Grammar errors: proofread thoroughly, especially the subject line.
- Generic greetings: avoid "Dear Sir/Madam" or "To Whom It May Concern".
- Bad introductions: skip the "My name is... I'm the content manager at..." opener.
- Instead, grab attention with humor, a genuine compliment, or a simple question.

chunks.heading: Ilias's link-building service and credentials
chunks.text:
- He runs LinkDR (founder and CTO), which places backlinks for customers: it finds the sites, writes the articles and places the links, from $160 per link, with most going live in 3-4 weeks.
- His stated background: 10+ years in SEO and AI-powered content strategy; built and sold Officient ($500k+ MRR); 20+ products generating $10M+ revenue; 1000+ students taught SEO.
